content:
PLEASE Think Twice Before Booking This Tour!
This Was One of the Worst Experiences of Our Lives. During the Sunset Tour, Our Boat Capsized in the Open Sea, and We Were Left Waiting in the Water for Around 45 Minutes Until Local Fishermen Finally Rescued Us.
We Lost Our Phones and All of Our Personal Belongings. Despite the Financial and Emotional Impact, We Felt That We Received No Meaningful Support. To Make Matters Worse, We Were Even Asked to Pay for the Tour After the Accident.
After the Incident, the Company Told Us That the Person Operating the Boat Was Not Their Regular Captain. Hearing This Raised Even More Concerns About Their Safety Standards.
Please Don’t Take Chances With Your Safety. Before Booking, Ask Who Will Be Operating the Boat and What Safety Measures Are in Place. Based on Our Experience, We Cannot Recommend This Company.

If you are traveling to Zanzibar, look no further than Juma Private Tours. We established contact via WhatsApp before we even arrived, and from that moment, Juma was professional and helpful.
He met us on the beach to explain everything clearly and even moved dates around to accommodate us due to a change in the weather, but what really set him apart was how he went above and beyond. The swimming with dolphins and snorkeling was a once-in-a-lifetime experience that he made happen effortlessly, staying with us the entire time to ensure we were safe and having fun.
Beyond the tours, Juma treated us like family rather than just customers. He saved our group a significant amount of money by negotiating local prices for Jet Skis and even helped us get local Zanzibar T-shirts. To give you an idea of the value, the hotel was charging more than double for the exact same experiences!
Juma is 100% trustworthy and provides a 10/10 service. We will be recommending him to everyone we know!

content:
We had an incredible day with our guide, Juma! From start to finish, everything was perfectly organised and full of unforgettable experiences.
We began with a trip out to Mnemba Island, where we had the once in a lifetime chance to swim alongside dolphins in the wild, truly magical. Afterwards, we had a fresh platter of fruit served, we then went snorkelling in the crystal clear waters, surrounded by colourful tropical fish. The sea life was stunning, and Juma made sure we felt safe and comfortable throughout.
We also got to hold beautiful starfish, which was such a unique hands on experience, finally heading to Baraka Natural Aquarium. There, we swam with the most graceful sea turtles, a dream come true and a perfect way to end the excursion.
Juma was an excellent guide, very knowledgeable, friendly, and patient. He went above and beyond to make the trip special and memorable.
Highly recommend this excursion if you want adventure, relaxation, and memories you’ll treasure forever! 🌊🐬🐠🐢

content:
🇦🇹 Conclusion: A beautiful beach with white sand, crystal-clear water, and plenty of opportunities for water sports – especially attractive for Riu guests, as they can use some of the hotel's services and facilities. The only real downside is the sometimes pushy beach vendors.
Kendwa Beach Gallery offers a truly beautiful beach with fine, white sand and crystal-clear water. The setting is stunning and invites you to both swim and relax.
As a guest of the RIU Zanzibar, you also have access to restrooms and a beach bar, which makes your stay considerably more pleasant. However, the numerous beach vendors, some of whom are quite persistent, are somewhat bothersome – but then again, that's simply part of the experience on a public beach in Zanzibar.
On the other hand, I find the vendors with their permanent stalls very positive. Here you can browse and look around in peace without being constantly approached.
The beach is also surprisingly good for snorkeling. Directly below the restaurant, we were able to observe numerous beautiful fish – especially in the clear water, it's a real treat.
Another highlight is the wide range of water sports on offer. Jet skis are available and, compared to many other resorts, are really affordable. In addition, there are pedal boats, kayaks, and other activities. A particularly attractive feature: some of these activities are partially free for RIU guests.
Overall, a very beautiful beach with a good mix of relaxation, water sports, and entertainment. Guests staying at the RIU Zanzibar have a clear advantage here due to the additional amenities.
Verdict: A beautiful beach with powdery white sand, crystal-clear water, and plenty of activities. For RIU guests, the additional facilities and partly free water sports options make the experience even better. The only real downside is the rather persistent beach vendors.

If you are staying at RIU Zanzibar, you also have access to sanitary facilities and the beach bar, which makes spending the day here much more comfortable.
The only thing that can be a little annoying are the beach vendors, who can sometimes be quite persistent. On the other hand, this is simply part of the experience on a public beach in Zanzibar. I actually prefer the local sellers who have their fixed stalls, as you can browse at your own pace without being approached constantly.

Another highlight is the wide range of water sports activities. Jet skis are available and, compared with many other destinations, they are genuinely affordable. There are also pedal boats, kayaks and other activities. Some of these are even free for RIU guests, which is a great bonus.
Overall, a beautiful and enjoyable beach with plenty to do. The combination of stunning water, good snorkelling and a wide range of reasonably priced water sports makes Kendwa Beach Gallery well worth visiting.

The only thing that spoils the atmosphere is the pushy Maasai people who constantly follow you around, trying to convince you to buy a piece of wood with a carved inscription... but you'll also find wonderful souvenirs from the locals, which are truly charming, but be sure to haggle 🤣🤣🤣

The stay on the sandbank, however, is rather short, and the area tends to fill up with groups quickly. The lunch provided is simple but adequate for the setting, without anything particularly distinctive.
The staff is friendly and helpful, but the tour follows a fairly rigid schedule, so there's little room for customizing times or activities.
Overall: a nice experience to see Nakupenda without worries, but don't expect anything particularly exclusive or tranquil. Good for a half-day at the beach.

content:
I was here as part of a tour offered by my hotel. The sandbank itself is almost unrealistically beautiful and certainly deserves more than one star. Surrounding it are many corals and small reefs teeming with sea urchins and fish. And that's where the trouble really begins.
Every day, tourists are ferried in by boat for lunch and presumably dinner as well. Tables, chairs, and grills are set up (what an effort!) to offer seafood. The trash was collected, at least roughly.
What I found particularly disturbing was the way nature was treated. Tourists were touching corals, plastic bottles were lying everywhere, and there was constant noise. The boats were crashing into existing coral colonies, and animals were being actively caught to show the tourists.
Of course, there was no shade, except for the sails people brought with them. The temperature climbed to around 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), and I'm surprised no one collapsed. The white sand and its reflection made the sun simply unbearable. Everyone on the tour got a terrible sunburn, despite using sunscreen.
Once all the boats had arrived (around 50), it looked like a scene from a beach resort. No one was drinking alcohol, though; I suspect people were afraid of passing out. Instead, it was loud and crowded, which didn't do justice to this unique landscape at all.
I thought it was awful and just longed for the trip to end.
Bad tourism.

content: A rip-off for tourists. $30 for foreigners (30,000 shillings for locals), although that's still a lot... You arrive at the park, pay at reception, wait 15-20 minutes for a guide to be available (not a group trip, but solo or with family), and off you go. The first stop is a cage with 4 turtles where you can touch them and take photos, the second stop is a pen with 2 antelopes + 2 young giraffes + 2 zebras. You can feed each one and take a photo. The third stop is a square with pigeons. They give you food in your hand and take photos with the pigeons sitting in your hands. That's it!) 20 minutes maximum. It's interesting if you want to feel like you're in a petting zoo for 20 minutes for $30 and get some nice photos. There's no care for the animals here. They're kept here specifically (brought from the mainland) to make money.

content:
I visited Zakir Wildlife in Zanzibar and unfortunately left very upset and concerned about the treatment of the animals.
There was a monkey there with a large, clearly visible wound on her tail. What concerned me even more was her reaction to the handler. She appeared very scared of him, while at the same time she was extremely gentle and friendly with us. She willingly came to us, lay down, and allowed us to cuddle and interact with her. The contrast between how comfortable she was with visitors and how frightened she appeared around the handler was very disturbing to witness.
We asked the staff directly why the monkey was injured and why she was not receiving treatment. We did not receive a clear or convincing answer.
Afterwards, we contacted Zakir Wildlife through Instagram because we were genuinely concerned about her welfare. They told us that the monkey was at the vet.
It has now been about a month, and this monkey is no longer there, but theres no clear information what happened to her or whether she actually received proper treatment.
I sincerely hope she is alive, safe, and receiving veterinary care. However, the lack of transparency and the original condition of the animal are extremely concerning.
I am leaving this review because wildlife tourism should be about protecting and caring for animals, not simply allowing tourists to interact with them. If an animal has a serious visible wound, visitors deserve a clear explanation that appropriate veterinary care is being provided.
I strongly encourage anyone considering visiting to ask questions about the animals’ welfare and veterinary care before supporting this place

content:
I just came back from a safari in Tanzania and honestly… nothing prepared me for how incredible it would be.
From the endless plains of the Serengeti, to watching elephants walk peacefully in the wild, every moment felt like stepping into a nature documentary. The wildlife is absolutely unreal — lions, giraffes, zebras, and even the Great Migration if you're lucky.
But what made the experience truly special was the people. The guides are knowledgeable, passionate, and they make you feel the real spirit of Africa.
Tanzania is not just a destination… it’s a once-in-a-lifetime adventure.
If you ever dream of seeing the wild the way it’s meant to be — Tanzania safari is the place to go.

content:
What an incredible experience! 💙
After how much fun we had the first time, we decided to repeat the excursion… and it was even better! We swam with the dolphins again, and our guide did everything possible to ensure we could enjoy them for as long as possible. He was so attentive and professional that one of my children even got to touch one of the dolphins. When he came out of the water, he said, laughing, “It was hard and slippery!” 🤣🤣 A moment we'll never forget.
Afterward, we went fishing, and when we finished, they took us to a local house where they cooked the fish we had just caught in the most traditional way. It was an authentic experience, very different from any restaurant, and undoubtedly one of the most special moments of the trip.
The food was delicious: octopus in sauce, breaded octopus with a local recipe whose exact ingredients we don't know, but it was spectacular!, salad, sweet plantain… Everything prepared with so much love. I'm sharing a photo because, as they say, a picture is worth a thousand words.
The family who hosted us was lovely. They didn't speak English, and we didn't speak their language, but that wasn't a problem at all. Sometimes you don't need to speak the same language to understand each other. Their hospitality, their smiles, and the warmth with which they treated us said it all.
Thank you from the bottom of our hearts for giving us memories that will stay with us for a lifetime. If you're thinking about taking a trip with them, don't hesitate. We went back... and we would do it again a thousand times!

content:
We booked a snorkeling tour to Mnemba Island on June 18, 2026. The tour was very well organized, and we were picked up from the beach right on time. Plenty of fruit and water were provided along the way.
Unfortunately, our guide's English wasn't very good, making communication rather difficult, and there weren't many explanations.
Another issue was that the tour took us to places that were absolutely overrun with other tour boats. The snorkeling spot was so crowded that we were afraid of colliding with another boat.
When we visited the sandbar, we were able to anchor a little away from the hustle and bustle, which was truly wonderful.
When the topic of a possible dolphin sighting came up, we were shocked. Two dolphins appeared and were practically chased by all the boats (around 20 of them). People were jumping into the water to swim with them. Thankfully, the two dolphins took flight. After that, we didn't feel like looking for any more. Visiting another beach further north was nice enough, but ultimately we didn't quite understand what we were supposed to be doing there. Since the guide's English wasn't good enough, he couldn't really explain it. All the boats went there, and behind the beach was a market selling nothing but tourist trinkets – definitely not worth the trip. It was completely overcrowded.
All in all, we wouldn't book this tour again. The lovely visit to the sandbank and the rather scenic boat trip along the coast unfortunately couldn't compensate for the other negative experiences.

content:
Safari for the whole weekend, an unforgettable experience, from scratch the logistics were well managed, in hands of the best tour guides! Picking up in time, help in every moment ( Abdul was with me all the time ), I didn’t want to pay for fancy accommodation so I experienced rural houses which I loved, the guide was after my needs at every moment with every detail. We took ferry to the big city and then a train to Morogoro, and then a driver took as to the town near the park. Traffic is crazy so it’s really important the driver makes you feel secure. First day it took around 6 hours to get to the hotel that’s why they pick you up early in the morning.
The guide at the safari park ( Mikumi ) was super energetic and fun, he answered to all my questions and he was very attentive too the full day, definitely the best!!! Animals were everywhere and you have the chance too see them very close.
At nights the main guide ( Abdul)takes you to a safety place to eat, which it’s good to know since sometimes food here can be risky for delicates stomachs. We also visited the Masaai village and it was such a great adventure to see how they live, they are super friendly with tourists and I loved a lot the dancing and singing part. I highly recommend these people !

content:
Great company great owner. We stayed near this beach and from our beach We were quoted 100usd for two people for the dolphin tour. We decided to drive around and ask around. This owner gave us the best offer directly without bargaining back n forth which saved us time. We also drive to nungwi and it was cheaper like 50 usd for two but it's shared trip with maybe 8 other people And We didn't want to drive 50mins for that. So We made the arrangement with the owner the night before. He prepared lots of fruits for us way more than enough for two. His customer service was great He asked for our feedback And made sure that we were not pushed by the skippers to come back. We saw dolphins And were able to swim with them 3 out if 4 attempts. We then snorkeled at one or two spots before we went for the break at the sandbank. The sandbank was so nice one of the best beaches i have ever been to. We had the option to snorkel here again but it was getting a bit cold for us so we skipped it. Some people found starfishes here.
The service was quite professional We had a local guy called cappuccino And the skipper was Mobi. Cappuccino was guiding us in the water the also took a swim ring with him for safety the whole time we snorkled.
The trip from this beach to the dolphin spot was taking longer than expected. Due to the low tides And shallow water the boat was going at a very slow speed the whole time. So it took almost 1hr each way. Plan that into your Overall time. We chose to leave at 7.30am (actually left around 7.40) And got back just after 12.10pm.
To Avoid the crowd i suggest departing at6.30am as suggested by the owner but it was too early so we asked for 7.30am ourselves. There were a lot of boats already. If you want to take photos of the dolphins make sure you do that before leaving for snorkeling as you won't be able to turn back and see the dolphins again Once left.

We then snorkeled at one or two spots before we went for the break at the sandbank.
The sandbank was so nice one of the best beaches i have ever been to.
We had the option to snorkel here again
but it was getting a bit cold for us so we skipped it.
Some people found starfishes here.
The service was quite professional We had a local guy called cappuccino And the skipper was Mobi.
Cappuccino was guiding us in the water the also took a swim ring with him for safety the whole time we snorkled.
The trip from this beach to the dolphin spot was taking longer than expected.
Due to the low tides And shallow water the boat was going at a very slow speed the whole time.
So it took almost 1hr each way.
Plan that into your Overall time.
We chose to leave at 7.30am (actually left around 7.40) And got back just after 12.10pm.
To Avoid the crowd i suggest departing at6.30am as suggested by the owner
but it was too early so we asked for 7.30am ourselves.
There were a lot of boats already.
If you want to take photos of the dolphins make sure you do that before leaving for snorkeling as you won't be able to turn back and see the dolphins again Once left.

content:
We first met Abdillah during a tour to Stone Town and Prison Island and were so impressed by his service that we wanted to book a second tour with him. This time, we visited Jozani Forest.
Jozani Forest, the largest and only protected rainforest on the island, is truly fascinating. It’s home to the Red Colobus monkeys, which are native only to Zanzibar. The rainforest is impressive for its diverse flora and fauna, and although not originally native, the mahogany trees are a beautiful sight.
We were lucky enough to see a large group of Red Colobus monkeys up close. Unfortunately, we couldn’t visit the part of the jungle with the mangroves, as it was inaccessible due to the high tide.
All in all, it was another great day with Abdi. We felt well taken care of, and he treated us with water and great company.
Thank you, Abdi! You are such a kind person, and we would gladly book more tours with you and highly recommend you to others!

We met him on the beach and we were immediately seduced by his kindness, his positivity, his respect and his sense of human contact. On top of that he offered us a very competitive price for the excursion, including fruit platter, snorkeling gear, and barbecue meal.

content: Old Slave Market - today, this site is home to a Catholic cathedral and a monument erected in honor of the victims of slavery. It is known that in the mid-19th century, approximately 40,000 slaves passed through Zanzibar annually. The British put an end to this practice in the late 19th century, and Bishop Edward Steere, whose body rests in the cathedral, took an active part in the fight against slavery. The descent into the cells where men, women, and children were held before the auction is shocking. A cell measuring 5x3 meters - without water, access to fresh air, or food - held 50 men or 75 women and children. Those who survived these inhumane conditions were put up for auction. Those who survived proved to be the "strongest" - "people dealt this fate to people," as always.

content:
The Anglican church, Christ Church Cathedral, was built on the site of a former slave market in Stone Town (in the old part of Zanzibar City, the capital of Zanzibar – the Stone Town area was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000). What shocked me most was the fact that the slave trade was abolished by order of the Sultan only at the end of the 19th century, in 1873!
Zanzibar was under Portuguese rule from the late 15th century until 1698, when the island was taken over by the Sultans of Oman. It then became a center of trade, including the slave trade – due to its strategically advantageous geographical location in the Indian Ocean, Europeans eagerly sourced labor for their colonies. According to historians' estimates, between 1830 and 1873, approximately 600,000 people were sold here as merchandise, and many more slaves were held here en route to their destinations. It was the largest slave market in East Africa.
In 1861, Zanzibar became a British colony. By then, many activists were campaigning for the abolition of slavery. British (Scottish) explorer and physician David Livingstone, as well as Anglican Bishop Edward Steere, were particularly active. After the final abolition of slavery in 1873, Bishop Steere laid the foundation stone for a church intended to symbolize freedom from tyranny. The cathedral, completed in 1879, is built of coral reef stones, combining various architectural styles with distinct local and Arabic accents.
Zanzibar seceded from the British Empire in 1963. In January 1964, a revolution took place, resulting in the country becoming the independent Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba. Three months later, in April of that year, it formed a new state – Tanzania – with the Republic of Tanganyika, while retaining significant autonomy (including a separate government and president).
Next to the cathedral stands the Slave Memorial, created by Swedish sculptor Clara Sörnäs in 1998. Since 2006, the East African Slave Market exhibition has been open – a visit forces one to reflect on humanity. Visitors can see, among other things, two rooms in the damp and cold basements where slaves were held in incredibly cramped conditions, as well as an exhibition of materials and photographs relating to this shameful practice (the transport of slaves, the trade, their destinations, the abolition of slavery, and the new forms of slavery occurring in the 21st century).

content:
The cathedral in Stone Town is an absolute treasure and a must-see for anyone visiting Zanzibar. Its stunning architecture stands as a testament to the island’s rich history and cultural diversity. The beautiful stained glass, high ceilings, and intricate details inside the cathedral make it a truly peaceful and inspiring place. The history behind the cathedral is fascinating, and learning about its significance added so much depth to our visit.
What made the experience even more special was the artisan shop located nearby. The shop features incredible artwork and pictures, many of which are inspired by Zanzibar’s history, culture, and natural beauty. The artists’ craftsmanship is remarkable, and it’s a fantastic opportunity to support local talent while taking home a meaningful souvenir.
Overall, the combination of history, spirituality, and art makes this cathedral a place that touches your heart and leaves a lasting impression. Whether you’re exploring the historical landmarks of Stone Town or simply looking for a moment of quiet reflection, this cathedral should definitely be on your itinerary.

content: Fascinating ruins and history especially about Princess Salame who was born in 1844 and was favoured daughter of Said bin Sultan, the first sultan of Zanzibar (and also ruled as Sultan of Oman which is where he came from). The ruins are now in a poor state but enough remains to imagine the scene with the sultans large harem of consorts using the multiple baths, heated pools and sauna. Princess Salame before she died in Germany wrote extensively about the palace. Entrance is good value (note year 2024) at around 12000tsh for adults and 5000tsh for children. Nice team running the site who tell me that there are negotiations between Oman and Tanzanian governments about renovating the palace to it's original glory. Would be amazing to see if they ever manage to move ahead with that.

content:
To wade through the history of Zanzibar move a little north towards Bububu and reach Mtoni Palace Ruins. It islocated just north of Maruhubi, built between 1828 and 1834 for Sultan Said. The land believed to be belonged to Saleh bin Haramil, the Arab trader who imported the first cloves to Zanzibar. Mtoni means ‘place by the river’. This is the oldest Palace in Zanzibar.
Read the history before you are there.
One of Sultan Said’s daughters, Princess Salme later took the name Emily Ruete in her book, describes Mtoni Palace in the 1850s and her life.
Salama bint Said was born on 30 August 1844 and she spent her initial years in huge Mtoni Palace, 8km north of Stone Town. After parents death she moved to Kisimbani, one of her estates. Finally moving to Stone Town. Here she became close to her neighbor, a German merchant, Rudolph Heinrich Ruete (born 10 March 1839; died 6 August 1870) and became pregnant by him. She fled to Germany. Her memoirs give insight into the history of Zanzibar.
Feel the history of beautiful Zanzibar with reading it and visiting the place. Good luck.

content:
If disappointment were a water sport, Coconuts Kite Zanzibar would be world champions.
From the moment I arrived, it felt less like a kite school and more like an experiment in how little effort can be stretched over an entire day. Organization was apparently optional, communication was a fun guessing game, and time moved at its own mysterious pace—mostly backward.
The vibe? Imagine enthusiasm being actively discouraged. Any questions were met with the kind of silence usually reserved for awkward elevators. Equipment looked like it had lived several previous lives and was now just tired of existing.
The beach itself is beautiful—though that’s entirely Zanzibar’s fault and in no way thanks to Coconuts. In fact, the highlight of the experience was realizing that simply standing still and staring at the ocean was infinitely more rewarding than engaging with anything offered here.
If you enjoy confusion, waiting around for no clear reason, and wondering how a place managed to get such a good location while doing absolutely nothing with it, then congratulations—you’ve found your spot.
Everyone else: do yourself a favor and keep walking. The wind deserves better.

You can cook your own food and you have a spacious apartment with bedroom, living room, bathroom and a terrace.
We felt very welcome and can definitely recommend!

By the end of my first day the intimidation had evaporated and was replaced with a sense of confidence, a lot of fun, and eagerness to go back the next day.
The team exhibited the utmost professionalism and kindness, guiding me step by step in selection of gear, teaching me the technical and safety protocols with the kite and board, and accompanying me in the water, showing me how to ride and providing detailed feedback and support until I was riding happily across the water!
I would go back in an instant, and highly recommend those looking to learn and enjoy kitesurfing in a positive, safe and fun environment to head to Coconuts Kite!

Such a wonderful team. School really well located, which allows you to practice at high tide in front of the school and at low tide in the lagoon (they provide you bikes to join the lagoon in 5 minutes 😀). My wife took lessons with Brown and made amazing progress and obtained an IKO certification. Thanks to him she gained confidence and a lot of experience.
I brought my own gear (Hydrofoil, surf and kites), Elisa and Ema (the owners) stored it for me at the school. Even if I didn't take lessons, Chaar (one of the beach boy of the school) helped me for every take-off or to land and fold my kite. Special thanks to him, a really nice guy always smiling and kind.
We were blessed by perfect wind conditions but the cherry on the cake was to find this great school and team. Price are really reasonable and Elisa is really flexible. She provides you information each day about the wind and if it's ok to kitesurf. To finish, the place is so beautiful, and riding in the lagoon is kind of magic. We recommend them without hesitation.

content:
Our experience in Jambiani was unfortunately overshadowed by constant harassment from some beach vendors. Saying “no” was often not respected. We were repeatedly approached, whistled at to get our attention, and sometimes followed or pressured to continue the conversation after refusing. Instead of feeling able to relax, we felt we had to stay on guard whenever we walked along the beach.
We were also uncomfortable seeing children approach tourists asking for money or trying to attract attention. Whether encouraged by adults or not, it created an uneasy atmosphere and raised concerns about the involvement of children in tourist interactions.
We found that several beachfront restaurants offered disappointing value for money, with prices that felt high compared with the portion sizes served. In contrast, local restaurants away from the beachfront, e.g. Banana restaurant, provided better meals and better value during our stay. We also found that the Blue Oyster - beachfront - is really receptive to feedback and the food is delicious
The beach itself is beautiful, and many local residents going about their daily work, such as fishermen and seaweed harvesters, were respectful and did not disturb visitors. However, travellers looking for a peaceful and uninterrupted beach experience should be aware that this was not our experience in parts of Jambiani, and because of the above we don’t recommend Zanzibar.

content:
Zanzibar/Jambiani has real beauty — I’ve visited three times in five years because I wanted to believe in it. I won’t be returning.
The beach experience has deteriorated significantly. Declining vendors is now met with hostility, passive-aggressive comments, and verbal abuse. Not occasionally — consistently. “La asante” and walking away no longer works.
The food situation is equally frustrating. Restaurants are charging European prices for portions that wouldn’t satisfy a child. You’re paying Lisbon prices for a quarter of the plate.
If you’re coming to genuinely rest and recover, manage your expectations carefully. The paradise you see in photos requires a lot of work to access — and increasingly, it’s not worth the effort.

content: This wide beach is perfect for a quiet, intimate getaway away from the larger resorts and large tourist groups. Located in the southeastern part of the island, it's far from the major resorts. Even in peak season, it's relatively quiet, and everyone can find a secluded spot away from other beachgoers. There are fewer Maasai than in other locations. Jambiani stretches for over 2 km. It's entirely covered in fine, snow-white sand that resembles powder. The ocean water is crystal clear and warm, but the bottom isn't exclusively sandy; both small stones and larger boulders can appear. Starfish, crabs, and sea urchins are often found on the shore. Therefore, wearing special rubber water shoes is recommended. The beach is also often covered with algae, brought in by the strong tides that occur in this area. Furthermore, it's worth knowing that the tides here are quite high. During this time, only sunbathing is possible, not swimming in the ocean. If you love beautiful beaches, exciting attractions, good restaurants with delicious food and authenticity, you will love this place.

About Jambiani
Jambiani is one of the best beaches on the South coast of Zanzibar, known for its calm atmosphere, long stretch of white sand and some tourist activities like Kitesurfing. The village is situated in the middle between Paje and Makunduchi beach. The beach is an ideal destination for tourists looking for beach vibes and unique things to do while in Zanzibar.
Jambiani Beach is also known for its stunning ocean views and breathtaking sunrise in the morning. Visitors can also participate in many activities like Caves, Dolphin Tours, Snorkeling at Michamvi, Kiteboarding, and fishing trips.
Accommodations in Jambiani range from budget-friendly guesthouses to luxury resorts. You can choose the one that suits your budget and preferences. There are also many restaurants and cafes serving fresh seafood and other local and international dishes, including vegetarian options.
This travel guide to Jambiani will cover all you need to know about this beautiful beach.

content:
The beach is very beautiful. Long and wide. The sand is perfectly white. However, the sand is often covered in seaweed and algae. Furthermore, if you're hoping to observe marine life, there's not much to see here. Due to the ebb and flow of the tide, the seabed changes position by about 200 meters. It's difficult to sail out far enough into the ocean (without a boat) to see anything. At low tide, the ocean is also very far away, and it's difficult to reach it. There are tons of sea urchins in the very shallow pools.
In short, it's great for sunbathing alone. It's also great for swimming with kids. If you want to swim at any time of day or just watch something underwater, this is a different beach.

content: Excellently arranged snorkeling trips from Bob Sele, based at HuShop, just a 2 minute walk from Mr Kahawa on the beach front. Bob took time to chat to us and find out what we specifically wanted from a personal snorkeling trip, then gave good location advice to suit our requirements. Our first trip with him was to Tumbatu Island, and that remains our favourite. We enjoyed it so much we also took 2 more snorkeling trips to Pongume and Mnemba with Bob during our stay in Zanzibar. He took very good care of us on all our boat trips, and kept us entertained out of the water 🤣. He was always friendly, trusting, very comfortable to be around, and agreed a fair price. He really listened to us so he understood our wishes and could tailor our trips accordingly. He just wanted us to have a good time and for the trip to suit our taste. We'd recommend him to anyone for private trips, but he also organises group tours. The drivers he arranged for our pick ups and drop offs were safe, good drivers and friendly. Everyone at the HuShop itself was lovely and they have a good selection of authentic art and artifacts. They weren't pushy at all, allowing us to browse comfortably, a welcome change from some of the stores in Paje.

content:
We visited both the Tazari Caves and the Chameleon rescue center. Both were very nice and the guide (Belo, if I understood correctly) was fun and easy going!
The caves were small but nice and easy, good for beginners, maybe a little boring for experienced cavers. The guide was nice, making jokes about how the shapes of rocks reminded that of animals and objects. We didn’t get much geological info, which is a bit of a shame.
The chameleons were very nice and cute, and the guide was very well informed about them, telling us fun facts and stories. You could tell that he is specialized in them rather than the caves history!
Overall a very nice experience for a reasonable price (10$ for the cave, 5$ for the chameleon).
Only downsides were:
- lack of geological information
- the guide was continuously touching stalactites and stalagmites, which could ruin them in the long run
- the guide often grabbed the chameleons to show them to us, even if they seemed scared and wanted to hide, which seems a bit unethical

content:
We departed from Nungwi by tuk-tuk for 20,000 shillings roundtrip and reached the cave in 20 minutes. The driver was waiting for us.
Here, you can not only visit two large caves but also a small chameleon farm. Zanzibar Island was once underwater, a seabed; millions of years ago, shifting plate formations pushed the island up, and these caves are clear evidence of this area's marine past. Millions of years ago, seawater currents created these labyrinths. Once on the surface, and gradually covered with a layer of organic matter, these caves became filled with land dwellers—bats and insects. According to the guide, traces of ancient human habitation were also found here, namely clay cooking utensils. Gradually, groundwater flowed into the crevices of the rocks, forming stalactites under the cave roofs, some of which are over 1,000 years old. Water is still gently dripping, so you can see the process of creating these bizarre shapes. I should note that I wouldn't recommend the second cave for older people or children. Since it's not a walk-through cave, there's a feeling of air shortage, a steep descent, and many of the passages are very narrow or low. The second cave is definitely not suitable for those with a fear of confined spaces. The first cave is quite comfortable to visit. A guide accompanies you throughout the tour and explains everything in great detail and interest. Flashlights are also provided. The video shows how the flashlights illuminate beautiful sections of the cave walls and ceiling, allowing you to admire the lacework of white crystals that completely cover the walls and ceiling. You can discern the outlines of various virtual animals, such as a turtle, a snail, a shark, or a giant baobab tree. A visit to the cave costs $10, but add another $5 for a visit to a wonderful small chameleon farm. The total time is at least an hour.

content: This cave system is located next to Mbuyuni Village, in just about 10-15min drive form Nungwi and Kendwa. It is really easy to find it, lots of shields and signs will show you the way from the main road. Some local guys will greet you at the entrance, where you can discuss the about the entrance fee. If you visit the Chameleon farm, which is right next to the Cave, you can get an even cheaper price for both attractions. There is no electricity inside the cave. Bring your own flashlight if you have one because those, they provide are rather creepy. You should wear proper shoes and light clothes, it can be hot inside. Since this is a natural cave with many narrow and low passes, it is not recommended for disabled people. Inside of the cave you can see different sized stalactites and stalagmites and dozens of dripstone formations. Make sure you don’t touch them to keep them as beautiful as they are. The cave is the habitat of bats, lizards, cave scorpions and other creatures, so watch your steps and try not to disturb them. The guide will show you in about 1h around and tell some information about the cave’s history but you shouldn’t expect a geology or archeology lesson. In our opinion it is worth to visit the cave and we would recommend it for thoughtful tourists.

content:
I don't usually give many reviews of attractions, but I think it's necessary to talk about Nungwi Beach (Nungwi Public Beach on Google Maps, not Nungwi Beach).
This beach is nothing like the ones on the east coast. The sand isn't any finer or whiter. In September, the beach was covered in seaweed, both on the sand and in the water; in fact, nobody was swimming there. I also noticed that there were more Maasai or local acrobatic troupes than tourists. Because the beach is narrow and hemmed in by rocks and a hotel's thatched terrace, it's impossible to reach another nearby beach at high tide. It's also worth noting that, in addition to being accosted by the Beach Boys, there are many drug dealers and cocaine sellers.
There are other beaches, like the hotel beaches or Nungwi Beach itself. For the latter, too, if the tide is high, access through the village isn't straightforward. You have to ask for directions or go through the hotels.
Really, the only real draw of Nungwi is perhaps the sheer number of souvenir shops.

content: In Nungwi, where the northernmost shores of Zanzibar meet the vast Indian Ocean, the beach hums with a rhythm that feels eternal. The sands, cool and fine underfoot, stretch endlessly, kissed by water so clear it mirrors the sky. Fishermen anchor their dhows after the day’s work, their wooden boats carrying whispers of centuries-old traditions. Nearby, a local artisan threads beads onto bracelets, her fingers moving deftly as laughter ripples from children chasing the tide. The air is warm, scented faintly of salt and the smoke of seafood grills along the shore. By twilight, the world seems to pause—only the sound of waves and murmured conversations remain. Nungwi is not merely a beach; it is an experience of connection: to the land, to its people, and to the stories carried in every grain of sand.

content:
The beaches are incredible. For starters, there aren't many people, and you can walk along the fine sand until you find a secluded spot. The ebb and flow of the tides are quite interesting: until midday, the tide is rising, so there are areas where you have to wade through the water to get across—a little adventure. From then on, and for the rest of the day, the tide goes out, and the sandy shore widens. I especially recommend spending the morning on the beach; the atmosphere is much more peaceful, partly due to the high tide. In the afternoon, which is also worth seeing, the locals come out to practice various sports right on the water's edge.
There are a few pushy people trying to sell you mango-coconut snacks, decorative items like bracelets, or boat trips for typical water activities... although this is somewhat unavoidable. They approach and leave with a smile, which is what matters.

I personally found the prices in their shop a bit high, but we definitely took home some beautiful jewelry as souvenirs.

content:
My visit to Maasai World was an incredible and eye-opening experience. It offers a deep dive into the Maasai culture, which is so unique yet sadly disappearing. Learning about their traditions, lifestyle, and history was both interesting and enriching, and it made me realize how important it is to preserve and support this culture.
Maasai World isn’t like the professional museums you might find in Europe—it has a more authentic and grassroots feel, but that’s part of its charm. While it’s not polished in a commercial sense, the experience is real, personal, and full of potential. You can tell they’re passionate about what they’re doing, and I truly believe Maasai World is going to be a great success in the future.
If you’re interested in cultural experiences and want to understand more about the Maasai people, I highly recommend visiting. It’s a beautiful way to connect with a way of life that deserves to be remembered and celebrated.

content:
The Old Fort is one of Stone Town's most iconic landmarks and a delightful place to explore the city's history. Built by the Omanis in the 17th century, this stone fort is distinguished by its thick walls, inner courtyard, and tranquil atmosphere. Today, it serves as a cultural space, housing small craft shops, events, and activities, giving it a vibrant feel without losing its historical essence. While not spectacular in size, it's a very pleasant place to stroll, relax, and soak up the Stone Town vibe. Its central location also makes it easy to include in any itinerary. In short, Zanzibar's Old Fort is a highly recommended stop. A charming historical gem that blends history, culture, and local atmosphere right in the heart of the city.

content:
Our visit to Old Fort was a lovely experience and a great way to soak in a bit of Zanzibar’s history and culture. Located right in the heart of Stone Town, the fort stands as one of the oldest buildings in the area and gives you a glimpse into the island’s past.
The structure itself is quite striking, with its high stone walls and simple yet strong architecture. While it may not be as ornate as some other historical sites, it has a raw, authentic charm that reflects its historical significance. Walking through the fort feels like stepping back in time.
What makes the experience even more interesting is how the space is used today. The inner courtyard is lively, with small shops selling local handicrafts, souvenirs, and artwork. It’s a nice place to browse, pick up something unique, or simply sit and take in the surroundings.
There’s often a relaxed and cultural vibe here, sometimes with local performances or events adding to the atmosphere. We enjoyed just spending some time wandering around and observing the mix of history and present-day life.
Overall, the Old Fort is not just a historical landmark but also a cultural space that brings together the past and present of Zanzibar. It’s definitely worth a visit while exploring Stone Town.

content:
The Old Fort in Stone Town is one of those places where history is literally beneath your feet.
Thick coral stone walls, darkened by time, the scent of the sea, old limestone, and something spicy—all of this instantly transports you back to the era when Zanzibar was a center of the spice and slave trade.
The fort was built in the late 17th century by Arabs from the Sultanate of Oman. They had just recaptured the island from the Portuguese and were strengthening their position. They maintained a garrison here, defended the harbor, then served as a prison, and later even as a warehouse and train station when the British arrived with their own rules.
This place has a rich history, full of changes, like Zanzibar itself.
Today, the fort looks stern, but vibrant.
Inside is an amphitheater where concerts and festivals are held, surrounded by souvenir and spice stalls, women selling fabrics, and children kicking a ball around.
You sit on a rock, looking at the towers, listening to someone singing in Swahili, and you realize that history hasn't stopped here—it's just shifted to a different rhythm.
I climbed the wall and looked down at the old town—white facades, tin roofs, the sea in the distance. And I thought: Zanzibar isn't just an island, it's a place where everything has mixed—Arabs, Africans, Indians, Europeans—and each has left their mark. The old fort stands as a reminder of this—rough, beautiful, and honest.

content:
As the name suggests, Old Fort truly lives up to its heritage a city built from stone, rich in history and timeless beauty. Dating back to around the 18th century, this was once the royal palace area, and walking through it feels like stepping into another era.
You’ll come across old cannons, gun storage areas, and elevated platforms once used for defense fascinating reminders of the town’s strategic past. There’s also a theater space where performances and cultural plays are held, adding a touch of artistry to the historical setting.
One thing that stood out to me and something every cat lover will appreciate is how many beautiful cats freely roam around the gardens. They’re calm, friendly, and almost part of the town’s charm. You can easily spend time just taking photos of the cats, the stone buildings, and the lush gardens around.
The view from Stone Town is spectacular, especially facing the ocean. From here, you can spot large ships, ferries, and container vessels gracefully moving across the turquoise water a perfect blend of history meeting modern trade.
As the sun sets, Stone Town transforms into a lively scene with its night market. The air fills with the aroma of freshly prepared street food seafood, grilled meat, and local treats. One drink I particularly enjoyed was a refreshing sugarcane juice mixed with ice, made fresh by local vendors.
Stone Town is more than just a historic site; it’s a place that combines culture, ocean views, architecture, and authentic street life. Whether you’re exploring during the day or enjoying the lively evenings, it’s a spot that captures the true essence of Zanzibar historic, vibrant, and full of character.

content:
Old Fort (Swahili: Ngome Kongwe), also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, Zanzibar, Tanzania.
It is the oldest building and one of the main tourist attractions in Stone Town.
It is located on the main waterfront, adjacent to another iconic building in the town, the House of Wonders.
It was built by Omani Arabs after they expelled the Portuguese in 1699. Over the years, it has served various purposes, including as a prison and a tennis club.
In the courtyard, there are some remains of earlier buildings, including those of a Portuguese church.
Old Fort is one of the main attractions for visitors to Stone Town, and its courtyard has been adapted to serve as a cultural center with souvenir shops selling tourist-oriented merchandise. It also features an open-air amphitheater where live music and dance performances are held most evenings, a restaurant, and a tourist information desk. It is also the main venue used for major events such as the Zanzibar International Film Festival and Sauti za Busara (an African music festival held in February each year).

content: In Stone Town, the Old Fort, or Ngome Kongwe, rises with quiet strength, a relic of Zanzibar’s past that has transformed into a vibrant cultural hub. Built in the late 17th century by the Omanis to fend off Portuguese attacks, its sturdy, weathered walls now embrace a more peaceful rhythm. By day, its courtyard hums with the chatter of artisans selling hand-carved wood and intricate jewelry, while the amphitheater comes alive with the rhythmic beat of taarab music, weaving Swahili traditions into the air. As the sun sinks into the Indian Ocean, the fort becomes a gathering place for dreamers and storytellers, each sharing tales that echo through the arches of its ancient corridors. The Old Fort is no longer a site of defense but a living bridge between the Zanzibar of history and the island’s boundless future—a space where every visitor, local or traveler, feels the pulse of a heritage that refuses to fade.

content:
The Old Fort of Zanzibar, also known as the Old Arab Fort, is one of the most prominent historical landmarks on the island of Zanzibar, located in the Fardhani district near the coast.
History of the Fort:
• Establishment: It was built in the late 17th century by the Omanis after liberating the island from the Portuguese, to protect it from any future invasion attempts.
• Architectural Structure: It is characterized by its defensive design, surrounded by thick stone walls and circular watchtowers.
• Uses:
• Initially, it served as a defensive fortress and administrative center.
• In later periods, it was used as a prison and trading center.
• Later, it became a venue for cultural and artistic activities.
Importance:
• Culturally: It is a symbol of Zanzibar's Omani and Arab heritage.
• Touristically: It attracts thousands of visitors who explore its rich history and its unique location overlooking the ocean.
• Currently: It is used as a cultural center, hosting art festivals and heritage exhibitions, such as the Zanzibar International Film Festival.
The fort is located near other attractions such as the Forodhani Gardens, making it an integral part of exploring Zanzibar's culture and history.

content: Built around 1700 by SeyyidSeif bin Sultan of Ya’aruba Dynasty who ruled Oman from 1692 to 1711 D. This site was once occupied by Portuguese chapel and small fortified houses before their total expulsion from East Africa in 1698. The Oman Arabs replaced the Portuguese remnants by construction of western side of the fort. Some of chapel remnants can be seen on north western corner wall of the fort until today. In 1836, Seyyid Said himself added eastern half of the fort for the purpose of keeping his garrison. The Omanis partially demolished the Portuguese chapel and a Portuguese merchant house and incorporated them in the construction of what was described in 1710 as a ridiculous little Fort. In the later years it was used as a prison. In 1905, the fort was used as a railway station and a deport. The front passage was constructed in 1946 to house ladies club. From 1964, it is used for cultural performances. Currently, it is a home for several festivals such as ZIFF, Sauti za Busara (Sound of Wisdom) etc.

content:
The old Fort in Zanzibar, also known as the Arab Fort or Ngome Kongwe, is a historical and architectural landmark located in Stone Town, Zanzibar City, Tanzania. Here are some key points about it:
1. **Historical Background**:
- The fort was built by the Omanis in the late 17th century (1698) after they had driven out the Portuguese. Its primary purpose was to defend against the Portuguese and any other potential invaders.
- The fort was constructed on the site of a Portuguese chapel and garrison.
2. **Architecture**:
- The fort is characterized by its large, sturdy stone walls and defensive towers. Its design reflects traditional Omani military architecture.
- Inside, there is a large, open courtyard, which originally served as a prison and later was used for military barracks and other administrative purposes.
3. **Cultural Significance**:
- The Old Fort is one of Stone Town's most important cultural sites and is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
- It hosts a variety of cultural events, including the Zanzibar International Film Festival (ZIFF), music performances, and other community events.
4. **Modern Use**:
- Today, the fort is a popular tourist attraction. Visitors can explore its historical architecture, shop at a number of small shops and stalls selling local crafts and souvenirs, and enjoy performances at the amphitheater within its walls.
- The site has been adapted to serve contemporary cultural purposes while preserving its historical integrity.
5. **Restoration and Preservation**:
- Efforts have been made to preserve and restore the Old Fort to maintain its historical and cultural significance. These efforts are part of broader initiatives to preserve the heritage of Stone Town.
The Old Fort remains a testament to Zanzibar's rich history, blending African, Arab, Indian, and European influences over the centuries.

Visitors can sample dishes such as Zanzibari biryani, grilled seafood, and samosas while enjoying live music and entertainment.
Another popular activity at the Old Fort is shopping for souvenirs and handicrafts.
The fort is home to a number of shops and stalls selling traditional Zanzibari items such as spices, textiles, and jewelry.
Overall, a visit to the Old Fort in Zanzibar is a great way to immerse yourself in the island's culture and history while enjoying delicious food, live entertainment, and shopping.

content:
A strategic fort on the road to Mizingani, this building dates back to the Omani era in the 1700s. It was used as a garrison for the Sultan and later a train station.
The Old Fort in Stone Town is an impressive historical building, now a commercial and cultural center. As soon as you walk through the gate, you see the grandeur and scale of the fort, with its towering walls and imposing gate.
The fort is home to a variety of shops selling everything from handicrafts and handmade jewelry to clothing and souvenirs. I was impressed by the beauty of the items on offer, which represent the rich cultural heritage of Zanzibar.
A feature of the Old Fort was the large and beautiful courtyard, which is full of green grass where I sat quietly and away from the hustle and bustle of Stone Town. I enjoyed sitting under the shade of the trees and watching the world go by while drinking a refreshing fruit juice from one of the local vendors nearby.

Other cultural activities are also held there.
There are also a few small art galleries and souvenir shops within its walls.

Zanzibar's old fort was built by Omani Arabs after expelling the Portuguese in 1699. It was used as a garrison and prison in the 19th Century. Also used as terminal of the Zanzibar Railways 1905 to 1928. A new guard house was built in 1947 and used as a ladies club. And an amphitheatre was added in the 1990s.

content: The Old Fort, also known as the Arab Fort, was built by the Arabs in 1699 on the main quay opposite the Forodhani Gardens. In the 19th century, it served as a garrison and prison, and from 1905 to 1928, it served as a depot for the Zanzibar Railway. In 1947, a new guardhouse was built, which served as a ladies' tennis club. In the 1990s, an amphitheater was added, which currently houses the Zanzibar International Film Festival.

content:
Certainly not as strong as our European castles, but if you're already exploring Stone Town, it's worth a visit.
The structure houses several shops selling local handicrafts (such as the famous Tanzanian batik) and a cultural center where henna dyeing, drumming, and Zanzibari cooking courses are held. The square is used as an open-air theater, and in the evenings, there are often taarab music and ngoma dance performances.

content:
The Old Fort, also known as Arab Fort and other names, is a fort located in Stone Town. It is the oldest building in Zanzibar and a major tourist attraction in the city. Situated on the main waterfront, it is close to another landmark, the House of Wonders.
It served as a garrison for soldiers, a prison in the 19th century, and a station for the Zanzibar Railway from 1928 to 1945.
It was also used as a warehouse during the construction of the Zanzibar Railway, which connected Stone Town to the village of Popopopo.

There are also several souvenir shops to buy some local finds and a lovely cafe that turns into a bar at night. Visit my Instagram (kelledstyle) for more pictures and my blog for more info :)

content:
The Old Fort (Swahili: Ngome Kongwe), also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar. It is the oldest building[1] and a major visitor attraction of Stone Town. It is located on the main seafront, adjacent to another landmark building of the city, the House of Wonders (former palace of the Sultan of Zanzibar), and facing the Forodhani Gardens.
'It was built by Omani Arabs after expelling the Portuguese in 1699. It was used as a garrison and prison in the 19th century

content:
Our visit to Freddie Mercury Museum was a special and slightly nostalgic experience, especially if you’re a fan of music or someone who appreciates cultural history.
Located right in the heart of Stone Town, the museum sits in the very house where Freddie Mercury (born Farrokh Bulsara) spent his early years before moving abroad. That itself makes the visit quite meaningful — you’re literally stepping into a place connected to one of the greatest musical legends of all time.
The museum is relatively small, but thoughtfully curated. It showcases photographs, personal stories, handwritten lyrics, and memorabilia that trace Freddie Mercury’s journey — from his childhood in Zanzibar and schooling in India to his rise as the iconic frontman of Queen. ￼
It doesn’t take very long to explore (roughly 20–40 minutes), but if you take your time reading through everything, it becomes a much richer experience.
Opening hours: 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM daily ￼
Duration: Less than an hour is usually enough ￼
Entry fee: $10 for non-residents (approx.) ￼
One thing to keep in mind — this is not a large or highly interactive museum. It’s more of a compact, personal tribute rather than an expansive exhibition. So managing expectations helps.
We found it to be a nice stop while exploring Stone Town — especially given its central location, making it easy to combine with nearby attractions. The experience is more about appreciating the roots and early life of Freddie Mercury rather than expecting a grand museum setup.
Overall, if you’re even remotely a fan of Queen or enjoy music history, it’s definitely worth a short visit. It adds a unique cultural layer to your Zanzibar experience.

content:
You stand in this house, close your eyes, and suddenly everything is there.
Not as an exhibition.
Not as an object.
But as movement within.
The walls disappear, time loses its sharpness, and somewhere between the first note and the second heartbeat, something begins that is greater than memory. A voice rises, not loudly, but necessarily. It no longer bears a name; it carries people. Millions. It lifts them up, makes them stomp, laugh, cry, recognize each other. We will rock you—not as a title, but as a promise. A rhythm that rises through your legs, through your chest, until you realize that you've been participating all along, without being asked.
Here, in these narrow rooms, nothing matters except one thing:
A person has decided not to let their life be small.
Farrokh becomes Freddie.
Not by chance, but through courage.
Through getting up every day against fear, against doubt, against loneliness.
Through the will to make one's origins not a prison, but a springboard.
Through the quiet decision to trust one's own voice until it grows strong enough to carry others.
You see photographs, letters, sheet music—and suddenly you understand:

content:
The Freddie Mercury Museum: A Bittersweet Disappointment
As a Freddie Mercury fan, my visit to the museum left me with mixed feelings, leaning towards disappointment. While it's exciting to have a space dedicated to a legend like him, the experience is marred by two major problems.
The first, and most hurtful, is the hypocrisy of a museum celebrating the life of a gay icon like Freddie existing and profiting in a country where homosexuality is prohibited and criminalized. It's an unacceptable contradiction that borders on exploitation, and as a fan and a gay man, it fills me with deep indignation. How is it possible that they profit from his legacy while people are persecuted and oppressed for being who they are in this country? This situation completely overshadows any positive aspects of the visit.
Furthermore, the museum is expensive for what it offers. The collection is quite limited and doesn't justify the entrance fee. Perhaps I was expecting something more profound about Freddie's life and work, but what you find is a modest exhibition that leaves you wanting more. The value for money is poor, which only intensifies the feeling that they're exploiting Freddie's name without offering anything worthy of him.
In short, for me it was a bittersweet and somewhat frustrating experience. The moral dilemma and the high price mean I can't enthusiastically recommend it to other fans. I'm sorry.

content:
The first ever Museum dedicated to the world legend Freddie Mercury, located in Shangani, in the heart of Zanzibar Stone Town, officially inaugurated on Sunday the 24th of November 2019, in order to commemorate the 28th anniversary of the beloved passing of the rock legend.
The Freddie Mercury Museum is officially partnered with Queen Productions Ltd. in the United Kingdom, who have loaned us exclusive pictures of Freddie Mercury throughout different stages in his life. This project aims to showcase a detailed accord of the birth town of Farrokh Bulsara, his roots with the Zoroastrian religion, his childhood and upbringing in Zanzibar, followed by his schooling in Panchgani, and then the rest of his journey to becoming one of the greatest stars of all time.

content: Finally, a museum dedicated to Freddie Mercury in his homeland. Little is known about Freddie's early years, as he was born in Stone Town's public hospital on September 5, 1946. Almost nothing is known about his childhood in Zanzibar and India, and even less about the Zoroastrian religion followed by the Parsi community to which his family belonged. In this museum, you can find answers to many of your questions, discover many unpublished photos, and insights into Zanzibar society at the time, the Zoroastrian religion, and the Parsi community. There's also, of course, tons of memorabilia, drawings by Freddie, lyrics from songs he wrote himself, stage costumes, and much more! If you go to Zanzibar, you absolutely must stop by.

content:
I visited Jozani Forest on an organized excursion and consider it a must-see for anyone visiting Zanzibar. It's the island's only national park and offers a true immersion in nature, along trails surrounded by lush tropical vegetation of ancient trees, palms, and typical forest plants.
The main attraction is undoubtedly the famous Zanzibar red colobus monkeys, an endemic species that lives exclusively here. You'll encounter countless of them along the trail: they're accustomed to human presence, move freely among the trees, and often cross paths, allowing you to observe and photograph them up close without disturbing them.
The tour is well-organized, with guides who explain the characteristics of the forest and the local fauna and flora, making the visit even more interesting. If you're in Zanzibar, I highly recommend including Jozani Forest in your itinerary: it's an experience that allows you to see a side of the island completely different from its splendid beaches.

content:
Visited Jozani Forest during the low season in late May, and honestly it was one of the highlights of our trip to Zanzibar. We were welcomed by the head guide, who was incredibly friendly, energetic and passionate about the forest. From the first minute until the end of the tour, he kept the experience fun with great jokes while also explaining everything in detail about the wildlife, ecosystem and history of this iconic forest.
We saw the famous Red Colobus monkeys in their natural habitat, squirrels, different birds and learned a lot about the animals and plants living there. The mangrove boardwalk was also beautiful, especially seeing the black crabs moving through the mangroves. It felt very authentic and peaceful, not overly crowded, which made the experience even better.
You can really tell the guides care about the forest and want visitors to understand why this place is so special for Zanzibar.
Only advice: bring strong mosquito repellent because the mosquitoes are very active in the forest. Other than that, absolutely worth visiting.

content: A hopeless place, totally not worth the money. Let's start by saying that before I arrived, I asked a friend from Zanzibar who knows the island and its attractions very well about this place, and he replied that if I went anywhere else and took a path into the forest, of which there's no shortage, it would be exactly the same as this park. We pay $12 for the entrance fee and another $10 for a guided tour. The guide leads us through the bushes for 40 minutes, telling us stories about the surrounding plants, trees, and remnants of the reef. Unfortunately, this place truly deserves the name "bushes." I managed to see five monkeys, and of course, I understand that they don't wait for tourists and that it's accidental, but I would have seen the same monkeys if I had stood patiently by the main road. Part of the route to the mangrove forest lies outside the park. There are local homes there, and the monkeys sit in their yards like dogs. This road is directly opposite the park entrance. At the end, the guide mentions several times that you can tip him generously for what I consider a rather dubious walk through the thicket. I suggest spending that money on something better. Like food.

content:
The tour organized by Zantour, which includes the Butterfly Center, Jozani Forest, and the mangrove walk, is overall well-managed, although very "traditional" in its nature.
The Butterfly Center is nice, a short but pleasant visit: little explanation is given, but seeing the different butterflies up close in a tranquil environment is worth it. It's not a particularly memorable experience, but it's a good start to the day.
The Jozani Forest is definitely the most interesting part of the tour. The close encounter with the colobus monkeys and the local plant varieties is the main reason it's worth it. The Zantour guide was clear and helpful, although the route follows the usual route used by all groups, so there's a bit of traffic around.
The Mangrove Walk is short but evocative. The wooden walkway allows you to see the roots up close and understand how the mangrove ecosystem works, even though the visit only lasts a few minutes.
In short: a well-organized, convenient, and interesting package that gives you a glimpse of the island's natural beauty. It's not exceptional or particularly in-depth, but it's a good choice if you want to see multiple places in a single, hassle-free trip.

content:
Visiting Jozani Forest was one of the highlights of my trip to Zanzibar. This lush and peaceful nature reserve offers a rare glimpse into one of the island’s last remaining natural treasures—and it absolutely lives up to the hype.
The forest is home to the endangered Zanzibar red colobus monkey, which is found nowhere else in the world. Seeing them up close in their natural habitat was both exciting and heartwarming. They’re surprisingly calm around visitors, and the guides are great at making sure tourists don’t disturb them.
Beyond the monkeys, the forest itself is stunning. Towering mahogany and eucalyptus trees create a cool canopy overhead, while butterflies and birds flit through the undergrowth. The air feels fresh and earthy, and walking the trails is a refreshing escape from the beach heat.
One of my favorite parts of the tour was the mangrove boardwalk. It winds through a surreal, otherworldly landscape where you can see crabs scuttling along the roots and learn about the importance of mangroves for the local ecosystem.
The guides are knowledgeable, friendly, and passionate about conservation. They explained not just the wildlife but also how the community is involved in protecting the forest.

content:
We decided to take a half-day trip that included a stop at Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park. The journey itself was already quite an experience, offering a firsthand glimpse into the reality of corruption, with around 8–10 police checkpoints seemingly set up just to collect bribes. While this is worth mentioning, it does not influence our rating of the park itself.
The park is undeniably beautiful, showcasing lush nature and a rich variety of flora and fauna. It was a pleasure to observe the animals in their natural habitat, and our guide provided plenty of interesting information about the different plant species.
Unfortunately, the negative aspects outweighed the positives for us:
Mass tourism: Visitors are herded through the park in groups of approximately 40 people, which significantly diminishes the experience.
Tipping culture: Even during the initial briefing, there was already a strong emphasis on tipping the guide.
Disregard for rules: While sensible rules are explained—such as keeping a respectful distance from the monkeys—they are largely ignored. Most visitors end up crowding the animals, and the guides do little to enforce these guidelines.
Littering: One of the rules is to avoid leaving trash behind, which is ironic considering the park is littered with plastic waste. Rangers don’t seem to take any initiative to clean up or maintain the area.
In the end, Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park felt like just another location in Zanzibar being exploited to the maximum for tourism. A real shame, considering the natural beauty and ecological importance of the area.

The forest is home to the endemic Zanzibar red colobous monkey, one of the rarest primates in the world. Jozani Forest history reflects the reflects the delicate balance between human activity and environmental preservation.

Jozani Forest offers an engaging experience best suited for a short 1–2 hour visit. While the natural environment
is certainly intriguing, the tour itself lacked cohesion. The first portion took us through dense forest where we heard some birds but saw very few. We encountered a couple of red colobus monkeys along the path and later came across a tree with several monkeys resting quietly—an interesting but brief highlight.
Unfortunately, the organization of the tour left something to be desired, and we lost contact with our guide midway through. Fortunately, we were able to reconnect with our driver, who then brought us to the mangrove section of the forest. This area, with its unique ecosystem and tranquil atmosphere, was arguably the most captivating part of the experience.
Overall, Jozani is worth a brief visit, particularly if you’re interested in Zanzibar’s biodiversity, but it is not an all-day activity.

The park covers a very large area and is crossed by one of the country's main roads. Here, you can see the monkeys crossing the road via a very long rope ladder that connects the two parts of the forest above the road. I personally saw baby monkeys crossing the forest with their cubs clinging to their mother's body—a stunning sight.

content:
Jozani Park or Jozani Forest is the largest National Park on the island of Unguja (Zanzibar). Here you can observe several species of monkeys, including the rare Red Colobus - an endemic species that is found only on the island of Unguja. They are characterized by the fact that they do not eat ripe fruit and have only four fingers. Along with the monkeys, you can also meet a miniature frog (adults are up to about a centimeter long), an elephant shrew, over 200 species of butterflies, land crabs, biting ants and many other interesting animals. You will also get to know many plants, huge trees laden with mangoes (the fruit's bark is a favorite of the Red Colobus), eucalyptus, tamarind, etc.
Be sure to visit the mangrove forest.
A wonderful place for walking, taking pictures and getting to know different types of plants and animals.

content:
I didn't particularly enjoy this visit. It might be interesting for someone who has never seen monkeys before, but otherwise, I don't think the ticket price is worth it. I did the short tour, which lasts about 75 minutes, so I can't comment on the longer treks.
What bothered me most was that tourists were allowed to get far too close to the colobus monkeys. Some even went so far as to press themselves against them to take selfies. This is undoubtedly stressful for the monkeys and clearly disrupts their behavior.
The monkeys stay close to groups of tourists, hoping to get food, which is also undesirable.
The mangrove section is a bit more interesting, and at least the animals are left undisturbed there.
However, the road leading to the mangrove is in very poor condition. It's a shame, because with the revenue generated by the park, we could at least maintain it a little better.

The Jozani Forest tour is divided into three parts.

All the explanations seemed rehearsed and simply recited.
At the end, the promised tip was collected.
All in all, the tour lasted about an hour.
It was nice to have seen it once, but it's not something we'd do again.

content:
Experiences from the 3-hour tour:
Jungle:
Beautiful jungle with countless mahogany trees (I'd never seen anything like them before). Lots of monkeys, tiny frogs (they're amazingly small and very cute!), butterflies, and birds. We only noticed the snakes by their rustling. This was perfectly fine with the venomous green mambas and Indian cobras, and the (non-venomous) 6-meter pythons.
The mangroves at the end of the tour were very impressive, but require an additional 15-minute walk each way in the sun.
Clothing: I would recommend closed shoes (absolutely essential) and, despite the heat, long clothing (personal opinion), as we were actually a bit afraid of the venomous snakes – probably unfounded, since the snakes slither away before people get too close.
It was very hot (late September) and we had to do a lot of walking in the tropical heat, sometimes on dusty roads with no shade.
In conclusion: three hours was a bit long for the experience, but I wouldn't have wanted to miss the mangrove forests. I don't know if the mangroves are included in the one-hour tour.

content:
Booked this tour because my room wasn't ready and thought the drive through the towns would be interesting.
Thus, I consider the drive which was about an hour really engrossing. The monkeys were cute and our guide Shaeeb was committed to environmental conservation which was fantastic. He explained the salinity and uniqueness of the mangroves (similar to the swamps in Florida) which is fascinating considering this is the same seawater from the magnificent turquoise Indian Ocean. The mangroves protect the island from flooding and there used to be a lot more. The forest is beautiful and used to house the extinct Zanzibar Leopard…videographic evidence suggests that the leopard is still alive, illusive but not extinct. The last sighting was in the 80’s so thats a nice little mystery.
Another interesting story was the introduction of the Eucalyptus tree to the forest in an attempt to control water levels but its invasive and not attempts are being made to remove these massive trees. Consequently, there are magnificent uprooted trees which I found awe-inspiring.
I enjoyed my time here. As someone who was not driving, I found the drive, the monkeys, the mangroves and the forest for $80 plus tip worth it.
This is Africa and Im happy to support the local economy 💜🇹🇿

Highly recommended, don't miss it!

content:
We went on this excursion expecting to see lots of monkeys. We can't give a price because it was included in a day trip, but what's certain is that it's not worth more than €10 per person! The guide picked us up and added us to a group for a walk, with no explanation about the monkeys, only an explanation about a plant. The terrain was uneven, so wear sneakers. After walking for 30 minutes along a dangerous road, we spotted three monkeys. After that, we had to get back in the car with the guide to see some mangroves for another 30 minutes—completely pointless. The visit was rushed. We were told not to approach the monkeys closer than 3 meters, but when tourists from other groups got within a meter, he said nothing. Lots of unwritten rules were ignored.
Furthermore, there's a fantastic wildlife park next door with reptiles, turtles, etc., which belongs to the same park, but it's impossible to visit it unless you pay significantly more! Shameful!
A waste of time and money, I don't recommend it. We saw ten times more monkeys at our hotel in Jambiani and even got close to them in their natural habitat (Mahi Mahi Hotel).
