content:
Extremely disappointed, we live in Zanzibar and we do not recommend this place. The forest is supposed to be visited with a guide, but most guides just take you around a roadside area to see three millipedes and two monkeys. It's a tourist trap like few others. Josiani is supposed to have a mangrove, a large forest, etc.
Before paying at the entrance, we were told that it was possible to visit without a guide (the regulations are posted after the entrance where you pay, so it's impossible to see them). Then, once we paid, we were told it was impossible without a guide (which we completely understood). We then asked for our money back so we could leave without visiting, since we were at the entrance and hadn't seen anything yet. And then, because it's easier to take money but more complicated to give it back, what followed was a series of incoherent and false explanations designed to lead us in circles and make us give up. Then, seeing that we were standing firm and remaining very calm, the staff and a guide began to threaten and verbally abuse us in a racist manner: "You'll never get your money back, leave, this isn't Europe, this is Africa," they laughed. Imagine if we had said the same thing to a Tanzanian visitor? "This isn't Africa, this is Europe, so leave!"... I absolutely do not recommend this place. There are many other places on the island, less than 5 km away, where you can see monkeys and a couple of woodlice with a much more respectful attitude. Avoid at all costs.

content:
Enchanting Encounter with Nature: Jozani Forest, Zanzibar
Nestled in the heart of the captivating island of Zanzibar, Jozani Forest stands as a sanctuary of natural wonder and biodiversity. My recent visit to this verdant paradise left me spellbound, and I'm eager to share my experience.
From the moment I stepped foot into Jozani Forest, I was greeted by a symphony of exotic birdcalls and the rustling of lush foliage. The air was infused with the earthy scent of the forest, instantly transporting me into a realm untouched by time.
As I embarked on the guided tour through the forest's winding trails, I was mesmerized by the sheer diversity of flora and fauna that surrounded me. Towering mahogany trees, delicate ferns, and vibrant orchids adorned the forest floor, creating a tapestry of colors and textures that seemed straight out of a dream.
However, the true highlight of my journey was encountering the rare and majestic red colobus monkeys, which call Jozani Forest their home. These endangered primates, with their striking crimson coats and expressive faces, captivated my attention as they swung gracefully through the canopy above. Witnessing these beautiful creatures in their natural habitat was a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I will cherish forever.
But Jozani Forest is not just about its charismatic inhabitants; it's also a crucial conservation area dedicated to preserving Zanzibar's rich biodiversity. Through sustainable ecotourism initiatives and community involvement, the forest serves as a beacon of hope for the protection of our planet's natural treasures.
In addition to its ecological significance, Jozani Forest offers visitors a chance to reconnect with nature on a profound level. Whether you're a seasoned adventurer or a casual nature enthusiast, exploring the tranquil pathways of this forest will leave you feeling rejuvenated and inspired.
In conclusion, my visit to Jozani Forest was nothing short of magical. It's a place where the rhythms of the natural world unfold in perfect harmony, and where every moment is infused with a sense of wonder and discovery. If you find yourself in Zanzibar, don't miss the opportunity to experience the enchantment of Jozani Forest for yourself.

Don't be fooled: YOU DON'T VISIT ANY PARK WITH THE MONKEYS. You visit a small forest and they explain things about plants (usually lies because they supposedly show you plants that are good for everything: cancer, prostate problems, erections, libido, bacterial infections, etc.). 15 minutes and that's it. Afterwards, they tell you to get back in your car and follow them to a road where there are some red-headed monkeys in plain sight, right next to a stall selling food for tourists and food to feed the monkeys (TRUE). 5 minutes and back to the car where they take you to the mangrove forest, which, yes, is beautiful, but it's another 10 minutes. They tell you 3 interesting facts and that's it. They ask for a tip and goodbye.
A fraud. Everyone in the tour group thought the same. Unbelievable. One of the worst experiences I've ever had in national parks.

content: We were really disappointed with this place. I don't recommend going there. The entrance fee is 25,000 Tanzanian shillings, not including the mandatory, limited tip for the guide. They take you into a mahogany forest with ferns at its base—this is just a way to waste some of your time during the hour-long tour. Then they take you out of the forest to see monkeys. When you reach the junction where you're supposed to turn left into the forest, I advise you to take the road on the right, because that's where the monkeys are. This way you'll avoid paying the 25,000 entrance fee unnecessarily. You can't get lost; it's a straight road. You'll see the monkeys on your right near the huts of the local people. A little further on, you'll find the mangrove where you can take a short 5-minute walk. That's the gist of it. The guide's three-sentence summary is practically useless. So unless you're a mahogany enthusiast, I advise against visiting Jozani Forest. It's much better to explore the monkeys and mangroves on your own...

content:
Watching red monkeys is simply a delight. There are so many wonderful specimens in their natural habitat, so many tiny babies clinging to their mothers. It's cute and amusing. But there's not much room to walk there. A walk involves searching for monkeys over a 200-meter stretch and photographing them.
There are also mangrove swamps, with wooden walkways running across them. Occasionally, you might spot a crab. But if you've seen mangrove forests in the Amazon or Sri Lanka, you'll be saddened by the modest size of the Zanzibar mangroves.
So, I give it a 4.

content: Challenging tour! We did the long jungle trek. The guide led us for 3.5 hours through the deepest jungle (a total of 3 km). He led the way with a machete, pushing through dense foliage, stooping through branches, and crawling over and under fallen tree trunks. In some places, the jungle was very swampy. The leaves and trunks have thorns, and the branches are barbed. You should dress accordingly; flip-flops won't get you far. Long pants are also a good idea if you don't want scratched feet. Definitely bring water! Along the way, the guide told us a lot about the plants and animals in the national park. One section of the path was swarming with ants, and our guide simply said, "You have to RUN!" It actually worked quite well. The smaller mangrove forest is also beautiful.

content:
English text below
Jozani is one of the few places in Zanzibar where nature is taken care of and protected in the sense we understand it in Europe. So you can only move around here with a guide and you definitely won't pick or pet anything here (which is only good). The park is divided into three parts, between which you need to drive a short distance by car. In the first you will find a rainforest with many plants. Some of them you may know from Europe, but more like small plants and not big trees like here. The second part is probably the most popular. Here are monkeys that you can observe very closely. Be careful, you are not allowed to feed or touch them. But it is still an experience. And the last part is the mangrove forest. Here it depends a lot on whether the tide is high or low. We were lucky with low tide, so you could see a tangle of roots and many crabs among them.

content:
the Jozani Forest National Park in Zanzibar is an incredible experience that left me in awe of the natural beauty and biodiversity of this unique ecosystem.
Our guide was very knowledgeable and provided us with a lot of interesting information about the different species of mangroves that grow in the area, as well as the various animals that call the mangroves home. We saw a variety of crabs, and even some monkeys swinging through the trees above us.
The walk itself was quite easy and took us along a boardwalk that wound its way through the dense mangrove forest. The trees were tall and majestic, with their roots stretching down into the water below, creating a labyrinth of tunnels.
One of the highlights of the walk was spotting the rare red colobus monkeys that are endemic to the area. Our guide was able to point out several of them to us, and we were able to watch them foraging for food in the trees.
Overall, I would highly recommend a visit to the Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk to anyone who loves nature and wants to experience the unique beauty of a mangrove ecosystem. It's an unforgettable experience that will leave you with a newfound appreciation for the incredible biodiversity of our planet.

content:
After the turtle tour in Nungwi, this was the most wonderful experience for us here in Zanzibar!
Monkeys, which are only found here in Zanzibar, roam freely in the wild without captivity or any other restrictions, completely free and not at all shy. It was beautiful to watch these magnificent animals move about in their natural habitat. Our guide was very friendly and gave us many valuable tips about the flora and fauna. Here, they truly take care to protect and preserve nature, and the forest in particular. A truly wonderful atmosphere in this tropical forest. Definitely worth a visit and the $12 entrance fee!

Pros: You see monkeys. And quite a lot of them, actually.
Cons: You basically have no choice but to walk through the forest with a far too large group (over 20 people in our case), as you'd be completely lost on your own. There are no signs or anything like that in the entire forest.
We didn't understand what our guide ultimately had to say about the forest, which is why it wasn't a big deal for us that he only spoke broken English.
After about 30 minutes of walking through the forest, we were directed to a parking lot where several taxi drivers were waiting for us. There, the guide explained that the advertised mangrove forest wasn't accessible on foot. In a rather chaotic scene, all the visitors were then crammed into whatever taxis were available. (Naturally, this ride cost extra.)
Conclusion: It's doable, but definitely not a must-do.

content:
A nice trip through the tropical forest. Ticket (25 k TSh / 12 $) includes entrance fee, guide services and walk through three areas. First is the small forest near the ticket office, where you can see monkeys. Then you enter bigger forest and can see some known trees, like mahogany or eucalyptus. The third part, mangrove forest, of the trip requires you to either walk 2-3 km or take a car (your own or rent something at the parking lot, they charged us 3$ pp). It was my favorite part of the trip, a stroll on the bridges over the roots of trees growing in water. Altogether, trip is an interesting alternative to the beach activities, although do not expect wonders. You just spend 1-2 hours in the forest and learn basics about it and take nice pictures of monkeys.
You can get there by taxi or local bus. I recommend the bus, it costs 1k TSh from Paje (any bus that goes to stone town is fine).

content:
Interesting and definitely recommended. My tip, addressing the previous reviews: Don't book through the tour operators at the hotel. Book a private guide. This way, you can decide how long you want to spend at each stop. It worked perfectly for us over two days, and I can't understand the €150 per person mentioned here. For €100, we saw Changuu Island, Stone Town (including the museum), the Spice Farms, the Zaaso Animal Welfare Organization, Jozani Forest, and the Nungwi Aquarium over two full days (it's impossible to do it all in one day). This included entrance fees, a private guide, a private driver, and drinks. Highly recommended. I'm happy to help if you're interested.
Now, about Jozani Forest. If you take your time there, you have the opportunity to observe the monkeys up close. It's really recommended for photographers. The mangrove forest on the other side, with its natural boardwalk, is also beautifully laid out and worth a visit.

The forest is divided into a jungle-like area teeming with wildlife and a mangrove forest.
In the first section, with a bit of luck, you might spot some small snakes and squirrels, as well as, of course, the red colobus monkeys. Once you've found them, don't let them disturb you and take your time photographing them.
The second part of the excursion leads into a mangrove forest. It's not particularly spectacular, but you can enjoy the peace and quiet.
Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they need such a tour. However, it's a nice change of pace from a beach holiday and offers insights into the magnificent natural beauty of Zanzibar.

content: We visited Jozani Forest Park in Zanzibar in August 2018. There you can see blue and red koula monkeys. The blue ones live solitary lives, while the red ones live in groups. We visited the small park with our guide in the morning and saw many monkeys. With a bit of luck, the red koula monkeys are all gathered in one spot, and you can observe them up close as they climb, hang from branches, or enjoy eating leaves. You are not allowed to touch or feed them. They won't hurt you and seem to enjoy being photographed, remaining completely undisturbed. There were also some baby monkeys when we were there. There's a forest you walk through where you might spot a blue koula or two. We highly recommend a visit to this park. The entrance fee is $5 per person. It's an amazing experience to be so close to a monkey.

content:
We booked this excursion as a hotel tour with air-conditioned bus service from the Royal Zanz Beach Resort.
The bus wasn't full, which was very pleasant. We had a total of three guides through Fisherman Tours (an experienced local operator), who spoke English, German, and Swahili.
The drive to Jozani and Prison Island was very interesting; you can see the local life firsthand along the road. From the construction of huts and houses to the dalla-dalla buses of the locals and the tuk-tuks carrying countless workers and market vendors... the tour guides are very knowledgeable and answer all our questions.
In the Jozani and mangrove area, it looked like another planet to us. (It looks as if the earth acts as a saltwater filter, allowing life to develop there over the centuries.) It was a short but interesting excursion. The short hike along the boardwalks was quite interesting and varied. We continued walking through the forest for a while afterward.
The past was briefly explained here as well.
All in all, in short: a great day trip for $70-90 per person. A welcome change from the usual hotel routine.
Highlights:
- Bus ride
- Very close encounter with red colobus monkeys
- Hike along the boardwalks
- Hike through the jungle
Best regards and have a nice day

content: As a nature lover, I loved the forests and the monkeys. The guides were quite knowledgeable and I heard them explaining details of the forest in a number of different languages. I liked the idea that a percentage of the proceeds from the park fees go to help the local community. Why shouldn't the locals benefit from tourism? As a resident of Tanzania, I see all too often the tourist dollars being funneled outside of the country with a minimal amount of benefit reaching the local residents. The park fee subsidizes local farmers and damage to their crops caused by allowing the monkeys to stay in their locality. Please be advised that there are signs posted on the highway prohibiting photographing the monkeys without paying the park fee. Do not risk losing your camera. This is a government law. Some might feel offended by this... feeling that their freedom is being restricted. They usually just want something for nothing. Be happy as you share in the conservation efforts of Jozani Forest.

content:
Visited today and really enjoyed it. At 15,000 TZS per person, the entrance fee is very fair for what you get.
Our guide Omar was excellent – friendly, patient and clearly passionate. He started by explaining why the centre exists and how it supports local farmers and forest conservation, then walked us through the whole butterfly life cycle, showing us what the caterpillars and cocoons actually look like up close. We got to see where the butterflies live and were shown the incubator where the pupae are kept until they emerge.
After the guided part, we had time on our own in the small but beautifully kept garden to watch the butterflies and take photos. Omar stayed nearby the whole time and happily answered any questions we had. To finish, he showed us the chameleons, which was a nice bonus.
The whole visit was peaceful and relaxing – a lovely change of pace from the beach. Highly recommended, especially combined with a trip to Jozani Forest.

content:
This is a fantastic little place to stop. We visited while travelling from east coast of Zanzibar to Stone Town.
We gave Juani Forest a miss after mixed reviews and opted for this instead.
$7 per person entry which goes directly to support local butterfly farmers and the community. A brief but a detailed discussion about the life cycle of butterflies and how they're farmed here, with lots of items to look at including the most incredible shiny golden chrysalis! You can then wander around the netted garden for as long as you want admiring the plants and butterflies and any other creatures you may find!
There's also another section outside the butterfly garden where they move the chameleons to (so they don't eat the butterflies) and we were able to hold a chameleon and watch them change colour.
100% worth a visit!

place_name: Chumbe Island Coral Park (CHICOP) Head Office
content:
This was, without a doubt, the best snorkeling experience in Zanzibar, and the coral reefs here are the healthiest I've ever seen! Chumbe Island truly offers a private island experience, with the unique opportunity to see wildlife in their natural habitat. Spotting the massive coconut crab, the largest land-living crab on earth, was an absolute highlight.
What really impressed me was Chumbe’s dedication to ecotourism, where all income supports their impactful conservation and education initiatives. I was fortunate to meet students and community members on a day trip, learning about the marine protected area, forest reserve, and broader environmental issues. Their commitment to community engagement is inspiring.
To the entire Chumbe team: thank you for such a warm welcome and the meaningful work you do. And for anyone visiting, I highly recommend climbing the lighthouse at golden hour for a breathtaking view of this unique island. Chumbe is truly one of a kind!

place_name: Chumbe Island Coral Park (CHICOP) Head Office
content: Chumbe Island Coral Park is a true gem in Zanzibar! The ecological focus of the park is impressive, and you can really feel the effort put into preserving the environment while providing a unique and beautiful experience. The coral reefs are stunning, and snorkeling in these clear waters is an unforgettable experience for nature lovers. The park itself is well-maintained, and the natural beauty of the island—from the lush green surroundings to the pristine coastline—offers a perfect escape. The staff are friendly, knowledgeable, and always ready to assist. If you're looking for a serene, eco-friendly adventure, Chumbe Island is a must-visit!

We visited this park on a Sunday with a 19-month-old baby. It's a large park, but it seems neglected in places, which is a shame. We spent the whole day there. But the park really comes alive after 3 pm. In the morning, apart from the zoo, there isn't much to do.
There's a zoo section (a good experience, especially for the baby, even though we didn't feel completely free because a zookeeper was giving us a tour without us asking). There's also a swimming pool area with several pools and slides; it was great.
And various attractions that start in the afternoon: video games for younger and older children, camel rides, a miniature train ride, children's games, etc.

content:
I was extremely disappointed by the treatment and behavior of the park staff. Based on my experience, I would not recommend visiting this place.
Before making the trip, I called the park and spoke with a staff member in English to ask about the ticket price. I was told it was 5,000 TSH. I repeated the question to make sure I had understood correctly, and they confirmed the same price.
After driving a long distance to get there, I was surprised to be told that the actual entrance fee was USD 15 per person. When I politely asked for an explanation, the staff showed no interest in acknowledging or correcting their mistake. Instead, they accused me of handing the phone to someone who spoke the local language, which was simply untrue.
Everyone can make mistakes, but what truly matters is how those mistakes are handled. Unfortunately, the staff’s attitude was unprofessional, dismissive, and disrespectful. As a visitor, I expected much better customer service.

I DO NOT RECOMMEND!!!
I do not recommend visiting. For MZUNGU, meaning foreigners, it offers nothing interesting for $15 per person. It's a modest "amusement park," with attractions for local children, but it's too expensive for them to enjoy.

I am very disappointed with ZANZIBAR PARK, which I revisited after four years. It was much cheaper before and offered a bit more.
So, I DO NOT RECOMMEND!!!

content:
We read good reviews and decided to visit this park with the kids. We arrived at 10:00 a.m. Our first disappointment awaited us at the entrance: the 5,000 entrance fee is only for Tanzanian residents. Although the website doesn't mention this at all. They told us to pay 15,000 TZ (480 rubles) per person. Fine. Judging by the price list, this price includes absolutely everything. The park itself is in a sad state. It seems like they rarely clean up after the animals. The walking paths are basically cleaned. There are swings and slides for children. They are old and poorly maintained. From 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m., not a single attraction was working. Everything was closed, including the children's play area. Horse and camel rides start at 4:00 or 4:30 p.m. - the website says so - no doubt about it. But what about everything else?!! There are only a few animals. We quickly looked at everything and decided to take a dip in the small pool. They tried to charge us 500 rubles per person for swimming again (15,000 tz). They claimed our tickets were only for the park, and the pool was separate. After much arguing and bickering at the ticket counter, they offered us a free swim. They did us a favor, thank you. But we were no longer in the mood or in the mood. Especially since the pool is far from the entrance.
We regret the waste of time. Perhaps it's better after 4 pm. We won't check.

content: Cheetah's Rock is the MOST AMAZING and special place where incredible humans care for incredible animals. They are focused on caring for the psychological and physical happiness of the animals. They are a critical link to preserving and conserving animals who are endangered by habitat loss, human/animal conflict, inbreeding and so many other pressures which are risking their populations. You will not only have the most wonderful up close experiences but you will also learn why Cheetah's Rock is a critical and highly ethical link to the survival of multiple species. Every animal is cared for, loved and treated as a precious life. Visiting Cheetah's Rock will enhance your life but also provide funds critical to continuing their mission. Don't miss an unforgettable visit to this magical place.

content:
Visiting Cheetah’s Rock was without doubt one of the highlights of my holiday in Zanzibar and an experience I will never forget. Coming face to face with a cheetah and even being able to stroke such a magnificent animal was truly surreal. It felt like a once in a lifetime opportunity and something I never imagined I would experience.
The entire visit was incredible from start to finish. Getting so close to so many beautiful animals, learning their individual stories, and seeing the care and respect they receive was both inspiring and moving. Every animal encounter felt special, and it was clear how much love, dedication and expertise goes into caring for them.
Jenny and her team are doing truly inspirational work. Their passion for animal welfare, conservation and education shines through in everything they do. It was evident that the wellbeing of the animals is always their top priority, and hearing about the rescue stories made the experience even more meaningful.
This is so much more than an animal attraction...it is an unforgettable, educational and deeply rewarding experience. I left with amazing memories, a greater appreciation for wildlife conservation and a huge admiration for everyone involved.
Thank you, Jenny and the entire team, for such a remarkable day. I absolutely loved every minute of it and cannot wait to return on my next visit to Zanzibar!! 🫶🏾🐆💗

content:
My wife and I had such high expectations of this ‘trip’ but unfortunately the staff and organization seem to be the biggest downfall for our experience. When booking my wife did email to let the staff know that we would want picture opportunities together because let’s be honest the main attraction to this place is the photo/video opportunities, my wife even mentioned that we would be happy to pay extra for this. We were told there would be staff to help with this and it would be at no extra cost.
At no point do they inform you that there are NO opportunities to eat throughout the day, you are offered water and prosecco but no food, we were collected from our hotel at 12pm & didn’t arrive back to the hotel until 8:30pm, ideally if they had told us this when booking we could have arranged some form of pack lunch! My wife has health issues which means she has to eat throughout the day little and often, however when we told staff this they still made sure we put our bags into a reception office and just said ‘no sorry we don’t have food here, there isn’t anywhere you can get any food either’
Our group had a total of 21 guests which is way too many, this was discussed throughout the day with other guests and everyone said the same thing, the day is far longer than it needs to be because of the amount of people to animal ratio - 2 bush babies to 21 guests and everyone gets to feed them twice? Then 4 lemurs to 21 guests.. you can imagine the waiting around, we are avid animal lovers and have our own animal rescue rehab farm in the UK so we totally understand the day is controlled inevitably by the animals and how they are feeling but the animals weren’t the problem.
Staff who lead the tour were quite demeaning and rude, not to us as such but others it was quite embarrassing hearing how one man spoke to people. The staff who are in the black shirts (locals) were so pleasant and as helpful as can be.
When it came to the ‘main event’ the images with the beautiful Latifah OBVIOUSLY with myself and my wife being together and it also being our honeymoon we wanted our pictures to be together, with this being such an expensive trip too we wanted to be sure our only images were perfect. After our pictures were taken with the cheetah we then checked them and noticed every picture that was taken was blurry and their finger was infront of the camera, when we mentioned this to staff and asked if there was any chance we could try and just get one more we were told ‘No’
We were then split up for the next encounter so again my wife was allowed another picture but not with myself? I was able to brush the cheetah but not with my wife? It was all very badly organized and honestly not worth the money at all, many other people were told they couldn’t join in due to colours they were wearing? At no point was this sent or mentioned in the email so this other couple didn’t get to have any Involvement in some things which was such a shame. we felt like we had wasted a day of our holiday from start to finish with this trip. We have done experiences like this all over the world and we haven’t ever had this experience.
Honestly I wouldn’t recommend this trip to anyone, if it was ran by the local men it would have been such a nicer experience and this isn’t due to ‘rules’ at all we completely understand how it works. Just lack of communication and breakdown of the day prior to booking. If it was explained how it ACTUALLY would be, we would have saved our money and not bothered.
However one positive I can add is that the animals are all well taken care of and it is clear how clean enclosures are kept.

content:
Cheetah Rock is such an amazing experience. They were so kind in responding to our inquiry for tour availability and accommodating our request to fit this into our stay while in Zanzibar. They offer pickup from your hotel which is such a great benefit. Our driver/guide was so sweet and knowledgeable and ensured we made it there and back safely. Once we arrived we were greeted with the workers who provided fresh coconut water while we went over the rules and regulations.
One thing to note, and they make you aware at the time of booking is to not wear stripes or bold colors if you want to interact with the zebra, which you definitely want to do lol
After the briefing you are led to an enclosure where you meet bush babies. There you can feed them and let them interact with you. This was such a sweet experience and they are so adorable. Then you have an enclosure with monkeys and they are so fun and energetic. The babies are so cute as they take food and play around the enclosure. There's also an enclosure with hyenas as well as lions and of course the cheetahs. With the cheetas, you are able to sit near them to take photos and brush them if they are in the mood. Its such a surreal experience to do this. They are such special creatures. You're also able to meet and feed the zebra if they're feeling up to it. If you're able to attend this tour, I think you should do it. You learn so much about the animals as well as conservacy for them and how they are rescued and how they're raised ethically. The owner as well as workers are all so knowledgeable and passionate about the animals and what they do and it shows. It's an eye opening experience that will leave you with more of an appreciation for the animals and those who strive to ensure safe lives for them.

content:
Cheetah’s Rock was easily one of the things I was most excited about during our time in Zanzibar and I’m so glad we went. I’m always conscious about the ethics of wildlife encounters, so knowing that Cheetah’s Rock is a not-for-profit conservation centre focused on rescue, animal welfare and education made this experience so much more meaningful.
Our guides JJ, Kevin and Mario were absolutely fantastic. Their knowledge and passion for the animals really came across throughout the experience. We didn’t just get to see these incredible animals up close — we learned their individual stories, how they came to be at Cheetah’s Rock, their behaviours and personalities, as well as so much about wildlife and other animals found across the African continent.
One of my absolute favourite moments was meeting the bush babies! Getting to see these tiny, fascinating animals so close was incredibly special and something I’ll remember for a long time.
Another highlight is the education behind the experience. Hearing the rescue stories of the animals and understanding the work that goes into their care and conservation made seeing them up close feel like a privilege rather than simply a tourist attraction.
We were also lucky enough to meet Jenny, the founder of Cheetah’s Rock, who came out to see us during our visit. Hearing from someone who has dedicated so much of her life to these animals and seeing the passion she has for their welfare made the experience even more memorable.
The animals are treated with respect and are never forced to participate in encounters, they have the choice to interact or not. Where possible, the goal is rehabilitation and eventual release back into the wild, while those who cannot be released are given a safe and caring home.
If you’re visiting Zanzibar and love animals, I would absolutely recommend Cheetah’s Rock. Come for the incredible opportunity to see these beautiful animals up close, but you’ll leave remembering their stories, the people caring for them and everything you learned along the way.
A truly unforgettable experience and one I’m very happy to have supported.

content: This was amazing! The founder and her staff work tirelessly to rescue and rehabilitate wild animals that have been abandoned, were living in poor conditions or being illegally traded. Most of the animals can’t be returned to the wild for various reasons (they’d be poached, not survive, need ongoing medical treatment etc), however, the goal is for future generations to gradually return to the wild. They use positive reinforcement training, no punishments or sedation or de-clawing/de-fanging. It was amazing to see the care and love the staff have for all the animals and we were able to have contact with some of their animals using the positive reward approach (grooming a cheetah was a particular high-light).

We cannot recommend Cheetah's Rock highly enough!
My sister and I initially booked the Great Wildlife Tour, and we were so impressed that we immediately decided to book the VIP Otter Tour as well. Without a doubt, these were some of the most incredible experiences we have ever had.
One of the things that stood out the most was how much we learned about the animals. Having grown up with many animals ourselves, we are familiar with animal behaviour and care, but Jenny and her team still taught us an incredible amount. Their depth of knowledge and genuine passion for educating visitors, while sharing the unique stories of each animal, made the experience truly special.
The VIP Otter Tour is a private experience where, if the otters choose to interact, you even have the opportunity to play with them. During the Great Wildlife Tour, we met many different species, observed them up close, and, in some cases, interacted with them. At no point did it feel like the animals were being forced to perform for tourists.
What impressed us the most was that the welfare of every single animal always comes first. It is obvious that Jenny and her team are deeply passionate about what they do. The tours help fund the sanctuary and provide care for rescued animals, but every interaction is carefully considered and only takes place when it also benefits the animals.
For example, playing with the otters provides them with important enrichment and stimulation. Other interactions help animals become more comfortable with handling by veterinarians or caretakers, reducing stress when medical treatment is needed. Every animal is treated as an individual, and the team carefully considers whether an animal actually wants to interact with visitors. If an animal prefers not to participate, it is simply left alone. The animals always have the choice to walk away.
It is also clear how much trust exists between Jenny, her team, and the animals. You can immediately see that the animals have had positive experiences with their caretakers. Even during demonstrations, such as with the zebra, it was obvious that everything was based on trust rather than force, and the animals could leave the interaction whenever they wanted.
Beyond the tours themselves, the work this sanctuary does is truly inspiring. Many of the animals have been rescued from heartbreaking situations, saved from death, or given a second chance after suffering terrible circumstances. By booking a tour, you are directly supporting this important conservation and rescue work.
The only small criticism we have is not directed at Cheetah’s Rock, but at some of its visitors. Unfortunately, not everyone treats the animals with the care and respect they deserve. The team sometimes has to step in, and in our opinion, anyone who continues to behave disrespectfully should simply be asked to leave. We honestly cannot understand such disrespect towards these amazing animals and work of the team.
All in all: This was truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience, and we are so grateful we had the opportunity to visit. If you are traveling to Zanzibar or Tanzania, we wholeheartedly recommend booking one of these tours. And if you cannot visit, consider supporting this amazing sanctuary with a donation. Jenny and her team are doing extraordinary work, and they deserve every bit of support they can get.
Lara & Alicia

content:
I visited Cheetah's Rock Wild Animal Rescue & Conservation Centre in Zanzibar on 28th June, and it was the highlight of my trip.
The staff were extremely knowledgeable, kind, and clearly passionate about the animals. It was obvious how well cared for the animals are and how much trust they have in their carers.
My favourite part was meeting the cheetahs, especially Latifa. Being able to stroke her, and later brush Bailey, was a truly unforgettable experience. I completely fell in love with them, especially when Latifa looked straight into my eyes.
I also spent time with the adorable bush babies, who jumped onto us and even climbed onto my head for food. Other memorable experiences included stroking and feeding a zebra and feeding the monkeys.
All the animals we interacted with were incredibly gentle, affectionate, and trusting.i
I also saw beautiful white lions, a huge tiger, peacocks, lemurs, tortoises, baboons, dik-diks, hyenas, and more.
This was one of the best experiences I have ever had and the most memorable part of our Zanzibar holiday. I would highly recommend a visit to anyone travelling to Zanzibar and would love to return one day to spend more time with the adorable otters and interact again with Latifa and Bailey.
A truly unforgettable experience

content:
Some places stay with you long after you’ve left. Cheetah’s Rock is one of those places.
We visited for the Great Wildlife Tour and the VIP Otter Experience, and without exaggeration, it was one of the most magical experiences of our lives. It’s incredibly difficult to put into words how special this place is.
What touched us most wasn’t just being so close to these incredible animals. It was seeing the love, trust, and respect between the animals and the people who care for them. Every interaction is based entirely on positive reinforcement and the animals’ wellbeing. Nothing ever feels forced or staged. You can tell that every decision is made with the animals’ best interests at heart, and that makes the experience unlike anything else.
Meeting Jenny was a privilege in itself. She is one of those rare people whose passion is completely contagious. Listening to her story and seeing what she has built was deeply inspiring. She hasn’t just created a sanctuary, she’s created a place where people leave with a different perspective on animals, conservation, and the responsibility we have towards them.
Her team deserves just as much praise. Every single person we met was kind, knowledgeable, passionate, and genuinely devoted to the animals in their care. You can feel that this isn’t just a job for them. It’s a calling.
When we got home, I found myself searching for another place in the world like Cheetah’s Rock because I simply wasn’t ready to let the experience go. I couldn’t find one. That made me realise just how extraordinary this place really is. There is nothing else quite like it.
Thank you, Jenny, and to every single member of your wonderful team, for sharing your world with us. You gave us memories we’ll carry with us for the rest of our lives.
If you’re visiting Zanzibar and you love animals, don’t hesitate. Go. It may very well become one of the most meaningful experiences of your trip, just as it was for us 🐾❤️

content: We had the combined otter tour. The day started early. Transfer was included. It was wonderful and so much fun. We learned a lot about otters and played with them :) Afterwards, we had two hours for lunch at a beach restaurant. The otter time is limited to two people to avoid overexerting the animals. Then other guests arrived for the rest of the tour. We visited various animal enclosures, were able to interact with the animals, and received a lot of information. It was a fantastic and interesting tour. The animals there are well cared for. They were all taken in because they were no longer suitable for release into the wild. It's a great facility. The manager was also there when we were allowed to sit next to the cheetah. It was an unforgettable experience! :-) The tour fees cover the animals' upkeep, veterinary care, and other expenses. I highly recommend this tour to everyone, whether young or old. Book well in advance, especially if you're interested in the otters. It's absolutely worth it! :-)

Of course, you now have beautiful pictures of yourself with the wild animals, but you can tell that it's somewhat of an Instagram tourist spot.
Many of the animals are rescues that can never be released back into the wild. I did notice occasionally that the animals pace nervously or boredly along the fence, but knowing this is normal, it's fine, and you know that it helps the animals.
I would definitely come back again; it's a truly unique experience and absolutely worth the price. Thank you so much!!

content:
Regarding the criticism in the previous review!
This criticism does not reflect the impression one gets on-site. The animal shelter is run with great dedication, and it is understandable that a significant portion of the income goes directly into the animals' care – for example, food, grooming, and medical treatment.
Another important aspect is the financing: The transport of the rescued animals is organized and paid for privately, as are all operating costs. There is apparently no government support. Veterinary services, supplies, and necessary medications are expensive, especially when certain items have to be flown in. Against this backdrop, the income appears to be a necessary foundation for the shelter's operation.
Furthermore, this is an institution that saves animals from being euthanized, as they are often no longer fit to be released into the wild. The responsibility encompasses not only the animals themselves but also the entire organizational and financial risk. All costs are covered independently, including the salaries of the staff, who provide daily care for the animals under professional supervision.
The living conditions also differ from the description in the review. The enclosures appear well-maintained and designed to meet the animals' needs. The absence of blankets in the cages reflects natural living conditions – animals in the wild also lie on soil, grass, or similar surfaces. The design aims to create an environment that is as natural as possible while also ensuring safety.
The facility serves to protect animals that are often no longer able to survive in the wild. The focus is on their care, stabilization, and – where possible – eventual release back into the wild.
The offered visits can also be seen as a contribution to funding and raising awareness about animal welfare. Overall, a much more nuanced picture emerges than presented in the initial criticism.
Finally, it is regrettable that platforms like Google are used for such reviews without any firsthand experience on-site or a demonstrable understanding of animal care. Reviews should ideally be honest, objective, and respectful. This standard is not met in the present criticism.
These reviews are also intended to be informative and supportive. After nine visits to Cheetahs Rock
It was one of the most impressive experiences I've ever had the privilege of witnessing. The way the animals are cared for there is truly remarkable. Everyone on the team has made it their mission to ensure these rare and beautiful creatures have everything they need. If more people did this, the world would be a better place. Every bit of support is invaluable.

content:
I was absolutely thrilled with my visit to Cheetah’s Rock. It quickly becomes apparent how much heart, expertise, and genuine dedication go into the work done here. The animals are clearly the top priority. You can immediately see that this isn't your average "zoo," but a true conservation and rescue center where animals are rescued from difficult circumstances and endangered species receive professional care.
I was particularly impressed by the animals' medical care. Experienced veterinarians come directly to the rescue center for necessary examinations and treatments, or are flown in when needed. Together with the dedicated animal keepers, the team ensures that each animal receives individualized care and finally finds safety and a life appropriate to its species.
The enclosures are spacious, beautifully designed, and tailored to the animals' needs. Lions, cheetahs, pumas, lemurs, bushbabies, hyenas, and even crocodiles have plenty of room and appear relaxed and healthy. Everything is handled with great respect, calm, and responsibility, without causing any stress for the animals.
What I found particularly wonderful was that animal welfare isn't just a buzzword here, but is truly practiced. Every visitor is shown, in an impressive and respectful way, how important responsible treatment of wild animals, species conservation, and sustainable animal welfare are. You take away not only wonderful memories from this visit, but also a much greater awareness of the need to protect these magnificent animals! 🥰
This visit was one of the most impressive animal experiences I've ever had. Honestly, no safari can compare, because here you don't just see animals, you also understand how important genuine animal and species conservation is. You feel the special connection between humans and animals and experience firsthand how much love and work goes into every rescue.
A very special thank you to Jenny and her entire team for their tireless dedication, their love for the animals, and the incredible work they do there every day. I highly recommend supporting this unique project and visiting it yourself. An absolutely unforgettable experience! ❤️

content:
Sad but true. Our experience at Cheetha's Rock.
The responses to reviews/criticisms from owner Jenny sometimes read like the reactions of an unusually quick-tempered operator, rather than an objective assessment of visitor feedback.
The fact that criticism is quickly portrayed as a request for "special treatment" suggests a lack of openness to honest feedback.
The claim that interactions are based on the animals' natural rhythms also raises questions, especially when the animals are simultaneously presented in a highly staged manner.
The discrepancy between the stated goal and the reality is striking, at least to outsiders. In my opinion, the tone with customers is more patronizing than reflective, which gives the impression of a certain resistance to criticism on the part of the owner. On-site, I was reprimanded and embarrassed in front of a group of tourists, almost rudely and extremely unprofessionally, after I politely asked if I could take another picture of the cheetah. Terms like "treatments" are used here to describe tourist interactions with animals.
Regardless, the experience itself remains at least questionable. If interactions supposedly follow only the animals' natural rhythms, it seems somewhat contradictory to visitors when fixed program points, clearly timed sequences, and very obviously staged moments are simultaneously part of the tour.
The flow already feels highly regulated, while visitors are mostly rushed from station to station in a short amount of time.
When animals are also clearly part of demonstrations, the question remains: where exactly is the line between experiencing the animals and the staged performance?
All in all, a disappointing experience, quite apart from the way tourists are treated here!

If interactions supposedly follow only the animals' natural rhythms, it seems somewhat contradictory to visitors when fixed program points, clearly timed sequences, and very obviously staged moments are simultaneously part of the tour.
The flow already feels highly regulated, while visitors are mostly rushed from station to station in a short amount of time.
When animals are also clearly part of demonstrations, the question remains: where exactly is the line between experiencing the animals and the staged performance?
All in all, a disappointing experience, quite apart from the way tourists are treated here!

As someone who absolutely loves animals, I can say that I was incredibly happy not only to see the animals in this place, but also to realize that they live in truly wonderful conditions. Huge thanks to Jenny and her entire team for taking such great care of the animals — I really appreciate it 🤍

Es sollte ein Highlight unserer Sansibar Reise werden, der Besuch im Cheetahs Rock!
Leider hat er bei mir einen sehr gemischten und am Ende eher ernüchternden Eindruck hinterlassen.
Bei der Ankunft wurden wir gemeinsam in einer größeren Touristengruppe empfangen.
Programmpunkt Nr. 1 - Zahlung!
Das „Abenteuer“ schlägt mit 160 USD pro Person zu Buche, ein Preis, der naturgemäß gewisse Erwartungen wecken könnte.
Nach der Bezahlung ging es los, die ganze Touristengruppe im Pferdemarsch hintereinander gereiht, relativ zügig durch die einzelnen Gehege zitiert.
Der Ablauf erinnerte dabei an einen straff organisierten Durchlauf als an ein Erlebnis.
Dann die ersten Tiereindrücke.. auch ziemlich ernüchternd. Kleine Gehege, trübselige Stimmung und das Gefühl von auffällig angespannten Tieren.
Die Löwin sprang mehrfach an die Gitterstäbe, sobald Besucher oder Pfleger vorbeigingen, und fletschte die Zähne. Ähnlich unruhig und gereizt wirkten auch der Puma und die Streifenhyänen, zurückzuführen auf derer vor kürzlich verabreichten Impfung, so die Aussagen vor Ort.
Während der Führung wurde immer wieder eindringlich und obszön drauf hingewiesen, wie wichtig unsere Finger und Gegenstände seien. Bloß nicht an die Tiere verlieren. Werden hier Tiere pauschal 'kriminalisiert'" ?

I was initially hesitant about booking a tour to Cheetahs Rock, as I was unsure whether the animals were truly well cared for.
I'm so glad I finally did it; the experience was fantastic, and you could tell how passionate all the staff are about their work with the animals. At no point were any of the animals forced to do anything—quite the opposite, in fact. Some of the cheetahs simply weren't in the mood to interact with people that day, so they weren't allowed near us. Before meeting the cheetahs, we received clear instructions on how to behave, and Jenny, the founder, constantly monitored our body language. Each cheetah was rewarded for exhibiting desired behavior, but there was never any form of punishment. The explanations and stories about how the animals came to be at Cheetahs Rock were wonderful. I also appreciated that the staff always made sure everyone got plenty of photos with the animals and that the cheetahs had a chance to interact with everyone.

This place offers a very special and unique experience. While you learn a lot during the tour, you get up close and personal with wild animals. It's an extraordinary experience!
For me, it was worth the entrance fee and the 5 hours spent here.
Be sure to read the information on the website. Avoid bright, patterned, flashy clothes, because because of this you may miss the zebra feeding, for example.
Importantly, this place is not a zoo or circus, and was not created for the entertainment of people. This is an animal 'shelter', an animal 'home' established to accommodate injured, rescued wild animals, where visitors can experience what it's like to be up close with a zebra, cheetah, etc. while learning.
The tour is very educational, you can learn a lot. The staff is very kind, helpful, they know a lot about animals and they provide information in a very interesting way. They do their work with all their heart and soul, so that the animals that come here have a better fate.
I definitely recommend it, with your visit you will contribute to improving the world, or at least the fate of the animals here. Thank you for your work!

content:
In November, we had the opportunity to visit Cheetah’s Rock – an experience we won't soon forget. What was particularly moving was that we also got to meet the founder, Jenny, in person. Her warm, calm nature and the deep respect she shows the animals immediately impressed us.
Cheetah’s Rock is a recognized sanctuary for rescued animals – from rare white lions to Sykes' monkeys and lemurs, to otters and zebras, animals of all kinds and with diverse stories find a safe home here. The team works with incredible love, patience, and respect. Nothing is forced; every animal is free to retreat at any time.
If you're ever in Zanzibar, I highly recommend visiting Cheetah’s Rock and supporting this invaluable institution. For us, it was the absolute highlight of our vacation!
The visit is very informative and goes far beyond simply taking tourist photos. You learn a great deal about the animals' stories and the important work being done here. The animals' well-being is always the top priority, and the team consistently ensures that visitors behave respectfully. The animals appear well-cared for, calm, and friendly.
I'm not usually a fan of traditional zoos, but Cheetah's Rock is something completely different. The interactions here serve a clear purpose: Since veterinary care is difficult to access in Zanzibar and specialists often have to be flown in, it's crucial that the animals are regularly trained and can be examined without any problems. Many of them can no longer be released into the wild or come from poor living conditions – which makes the work done here all the more valuable. It's an aspect that might not be immediately apparent, but becomes very clear when you're there.
For us, it was an absolute 10/10 experience.

content:
It was an incredible experience. You learn so much about the animals and about the background and goals of the sanctuary. It's not about running a petting zoo, but about giving animals rescued from terrible situations, who can no longer be released, a good life.
You get closer to some of these animals than you probably ever will again in your life, which has an important reason behind it. There is no veterinary care for animals in Zanzibar. Therefore, it is essential that close contact is established between humans and animals on both sides.

content:
Cheetahs Rock
Wildlife Reservation in Zanzibar. Guests are allowed to interact with some of the animals.
A truly wonderful experience!
The visit is well organized. Guests are picked up by car from anywhere on the island and dropped off at the end.
The price is not cheap – $160. But the animals are kept in truly excellent conditions, so of course, all this comes at a significant cost.
Advance booking is required. Visits are not available every day.
There is also a service for swimming and playing with otters. However, for my trip, everything was already booked. Next time, I will definitely take this tour. They are incredibly adorable 🥰
I saw in other reviews that the staff doesn't know how to take photos. I completely agree. Indeed, the photos they take are so bad that they all have to be deleted, and this can be very frustrating, since you don't really have the opportunity to take photos of yourself. For myself, I solved this problem this way: I quickly realized the employees were having trouble with photos, so I started handing them my phone with video enabled. Each time, I reminded them not to change or touch anything in the shooting modes. Just keep the phone in video mode. Then, I took screenshots of the most amazing photos from the videos! Plus, the collection has incredibly interesting videos! Overall, I highly recommend this solution.

content:
INCREDIBLE!!
Magnificent animal sanctuary.
We spent the entire day at Cheetah's Rock.
In the morning, we had a special moment with the otters. We were incredibly lucky; we were the only ones there and met five exceptional otters in the company of Kevin, who took the time to explain and repeat everything to us since we don't speak much English. We learned lots of exercises so we could play with them.
At lunchtime, we ate at a nearby hotel with an incredible view and an excellent all-you-can-eat buffet.
In the afternoon, we were part of a group of about twenty with several zookeepers.
While everyone enjoyed the animals and took photos, a zookeeper provided information about each animal (its history, characteristics, etc.).
I loved the time with the lemurs; they roam freely in a large enclosure and come right up to us, and the photo with the cheetah was still very impressive. I recommend spending the morning with the otters; it remains my best memory.
A little tip: it's best if you understand English well to grasp all the explanations, but honestly, we speak very little of it, and we had a wonderful day. They take the time to explain things again in simpler terms if needed.
No jewelry, hats, or sunglasses, and dress modestly (black or white).
Please note that the entrance fee and any souvenirs purchased there go towards animal protection (paying for the care of animals that need it, food, etc.) and the conservation of endangered species. So yes, it's expensive, but it's for a good cause.

content:
We had an absolutely amazing day at Cheetah’s Rock in Zanzibar! We did both the private Otter Experience and the tour where we met ring-tailed lemurs, cheetahs, bushbabies, hyenas, monkeys, and many more incredible animals. Every moment was unforgettable — especially playing with the otters, which was truly heartwarming and magical. The animals are treated with so much care and respect, and it’s clear how much love and dedication goes into every interaction.
Cheetah’s Rock is not just an incredible place to interact closely with animals, but also a sanctuary full of compassion and purpose. So many of the animals here have suffered terribly at the hands of humans in the past, and it’s deeply moving to see how well they are cared for now. You can feel the team’s passion in every story they share and in the gentle way they handle each animal. Their mission to give rescued wildlife a safe and happy life is truly inspiring.
We are deeply grateful for the amazing work of the whole team and their commitment to giving these rescued animals a second chance at a happy life. This experience touched our hearts, and we highly recommend Cheetah’s Rock to anyone who loves animals. It is beyond beautiful to see how these once-suffering animals now live with dignity, love, and safety. The work done here not only heals broken lives but also contributes to the preservation of endangered species for future generations. Please support this wonderful place — they genuinely make a difference!

content:
In September, we had the opportunity to visit Cheetah's Rock and get to know the animals and the team.
What an incredibly unforgettable, wonderful, and unique experience!!! It was the highlight of a wonderful vacation in Zanzibar, and I wholeheartedly recommend visiting Cheetah's Rock.
Cheetah's Rock is a recognized sanctuary for rescued animals. From golden tabby tigers and white lions (of which there are only 38 left in the entire world!!!) to tiny Sykes' monkeys, there's a wide variety of sizes represented. The team, led by founder Jenny, does such a wonderful job with incredible love, patience, and above all, respect for the animals. They dedicate themselves to their work there every single day. The animals are never forced to do anything; if they don't want to interact with visitors, they don't have to.
Cheetah's Rock is a recognized sanctuary for rescued animals. I can only say that what I saw there deeply impressed and touched me, and that's why I decided to sponsor one of the Sykes' monkeys, the little diva. She completely stole my heart. Because of this, and especially because I saw firsthand how the animals are cared for there, it was incredibly important to me to support Cheetah's Rock.
I highly recommend that if you're ever in Zanzibar, visit Cheetah's Rock and support this wonderful organization with a visit, a sponsorship, or an adoption! Thank you from the bottom of my heart 💕 🦓 🐾 🐅 🦁 🦦

The team, led by founder Jenny, does such a wonderful job with incredible love, patience, and above all, respect for the animals.
They dedicate themselves to their work there every single day.
The animals are never forced to do anything; if they don't want to interact with visitors, they don't have to.
Cheetah's Rock is a recognized sanctuary for rescued animals.
I can only say that what I saw there deeply impressed and touched me, and that's why I decided to sponsor one of the Sykes' monkeys, the little diva.
She completely stole my heart.
Because of this, and especially because I saw firsthand how the animals are cared for there, it was incredibly important to me to support Cheetah's Rock.
I highly recommend that if you're ever in Zanzibar, visit Cheetah's Rock and support this wonderful organization with a visit, a sponsorship, or an adoption!
Thank you from the bottom of my heart 💕 🦓 🐾 🐅 🦁 🦦

content:
BEWARE: If it feels wrong, it’s because it is. Here are the key elements that the owner won’t tell visitors.
1. CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) has absolutely no connection with ethical practices or animal wellbeing. It only control border movement of the animals.
2. ZIPA (Zanzibar Institute of Protected Areas) only ensures the bare minimum standards determined by Zanzibar, which are notably poor.
3. Research has proven time and time again physical interaction with wild animals generates stress and its detrimental to the animals health. Specially in felines where they spend long periods of time alone. This place provides no opportunity for the animal to retreat, a fundamental welfare issue.
Quoting research:
[Poor Welfare Indicators and Husbandry Practices at Lion (Panthera Leo) “Cub-Petting” Facilities, 2022]
[University of Oxford's Wildlife Conservation Research Unit]
4. The breeding programs combined with lion cub petting and walking are serious red flags of “Canned Hunting” pipelines. Where animals are bred and used while they are “cute” and harmless, later they are sold to private owners for hunting in private land.
In conclusion, while the desire to have a close encounter with a magnificent animal like a lion or cheetah is understandable, the evidence strongly suggests that facilities offering petting of large carnivores are overwhelmingly unethical.

I didn't want to participate in any unethical exploitation of animals and Cheetah's Rock treats all of its animals extremely ethically.

Cheetah’s Rock isn’t just a place to meet incredible animals up close; it’s a true conservation centre run by people who genuinely care. We left feeling inspired and grateful for such a meaningful, ethical experience. Highly recommended!

content:
Cheetah’s Rock is an incredible experience and absolutely worth the price. This is not a zoo — it’s a conservation where every dollar goes towards the animals’ food, medicine, and care. You can truly see how well-loved and respected the animals are. The tour was very well organized and extremely informative, and my boyfriend and I enjoyed every minute of it.
They even accommodated my request last minute — I had assumed my boyfriend booked it in advance, only to find out he hadn’t. I reached out the night before, and they still managed to fit us in the very next day, which I deeply appreciated.
One tip: the tour can be lengthy, so I recommend bringing a snack or protein bar (i’m not sure if this was recommended on their site, I may have missed this). I also appreciated that the price included shuttle service — we stayed about an hour away, and that made the trip so much easier.
If you care about animal welfare and want a meaningful, educational experience, Cheetah’s Rock is worth every penny.

content: My husband and I decided at the last minute to visit Cheetahs Rock that same day. From the very first contact, we were amazed at how quickly we received a response and how easily we were able to book the tickets. We then received a detailed email with all the important information, allowing us to travel to the sanctuary well-prepared. Upon arrival, we were warmly greeted by the team with a fresh coconut and then waited until the maximum number of visitors had arrived. After a brief introduction, we went straight into Cheetahs Rock. From bushbabies, monkeys, and limas to white lions, tigers, and leopards, we saw almost every kind of wild animal. Our highlights were definitely the opportunities to interact directly with the animals, such as feeding the bushbabies and limas or brushing a leopard's fur. We also loved learning so much about the animals, which reinforced our sense of how respectfully they are treated there. We felt completely at ease throughout our stay and would like to thank the entire team at Cheetahs Rock for giving us such a unique experience. We wholeheartedly recommend the rescue center and are incredibly grateful that there are people like Jenny and her team who have such big hearts for animals and give them a second home.

content:
Don’t let the critics put you off with complaints about the $160 entry fee. Yes, it’s more than your average attraction—but Cheetah’s Rock is far from average. This isn’t just a zoo. It’s a sanctuary where conservation experts dedicate their lives to rescuing, rehabilitating, and training animals with compassion and respect.
Every encounter is deeply educational. The team takes time to share insights about each animal and guide you on how to interact in a way that honors their wellbeing. If you’re a true animal lover, visiting a place where animals are respected—not exploited—is non-negotiable. And at Cheetah’s Rock, the care is exceptional.
I finally met my favorite animal—the cheetah—and I’m grateful I waited to do it here, rather than in a cage at some neglectful zoo. If you’re just after a quick selfie and not interested in the animals’ stories or the meaningful work behind the scenes, this place might not be for you. But if you want a heartfelt, ethical, and unforgettable animal experience, this is the paradise you’ve been looking for.

content:
This is the most amazing place to get up close to many wild animals and learn all about them and conservation in Zanzibar. It's done in a way which visitors can have real hands on interaction with the animals but without placing any stress on them. The staff practise positive reinforcement with all the animals they look after so there's no pressure on them to engage with visitors. Something I wish all sanctuaries practised.

Cheetah's Rock is so well organised - they can arrange transport as part of the tour so it makes it easy to get there and back. It's great value for money as we got to spend the whole afternoon onsite and learnt so much about the animals in the santuary and conservation practices.
The staff ensure everyone is comfortable at all times and treated us to water and coconut juice on arrival plus a glass of prosecco mid-way through the tour which was an unexpected delight! The tour was so amazing; our only regret is that we didn't sign up to see the otters as well as the other wild animals as we loved it so much.
Honestly, if there's only one trip you plan to do in Zanzibar it has to be a visit to this place. It was the absolute highlight of our stay on the island.

content:
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A truly unique experience – beyond anything I have ever seen!
I visited Cheetah’s Rock yesterday, and I can say with all my heart – this place is one of a kind.The animals are not just cared for, they are protected, respected, and deeply understood by a team of experts who dedicate their lives to them.
What makes this place so different? The incredible closeness to the animals – done the right way. I have traveled a lot, but I have never seen anything like this. And the best part? You are not just a spectator. You learn, you connect, you understand.
One of the most fascinating moments was the positive reinforcement demonstration – done personally by the founder. Seeing how she works with the animals, using only trust and understanding, was truly incredible. She is a pioneer in this field, and witnessing her interaction with these animals is something you won’t experience anywhere else.
I also read a review complaining about finances and transparency. That review is completely misleading. Cheetah’s Rock does NOT ask for donations. The entrance fee goes directly into the care and protection of the animals. And trust me – this is money well spent.
But what truly sets this place apart is the founder. She is not just running a conservation center. She is a lioness, standing fiercely between her animal family and the world, protecting them with everything she has.
Cheetah’s Rock is not just a visit. It is an experience that changes the way you see wildlife.That’s why I am coming back for the VIP Otter Tour in some days – I simply cannot get enough of this place!
If you want to experience wildlife in a way that is ethical, unforgettable, and deeply moving – this is the place!

content:
I had a truly wonderful experience at Cheetah’s Rock, especially with the cheetahs.
I was amazed to see them so calm and trusting, even allowing a complete stranger to gently brush them.
It was an unforgettable feeling to be able to connect with these magnificent animals, from the graceful cheetahs to Beppo, the incredible zebra.
I truly believe that Cheetah’s Rock is a must-visit and that their work is a necessary initiative to protect these majestic big cats from extinction.
Their dedication to ethical wildlife conservation is inspiring.
One important note for future visitors:
Please be careful when booking via “beach boys”:
Unfortunately, I was misled by a beach boy closely working with a taxi driver. He claimed to take me to Cheetah’s Rock after having taken the tour fee. Instead of driving me to Cheetah’s Rock, he dropped me at a completely different, unethical place and left. The conditions there were shocking and heartbreaking and I realized that I got fooled and that this is definitely not Cheetah’s Rock.
It was a stark reminder that not all animal experiences are ethical.
To ensure you reach the real Cheetah’s Rock, I highly recommend booking directly through their official website (which I did after this, recommended by other tourists in my hotel.)
This way, you support real conservation efforts and avoid unethical places.
Thank you to the entire team at Cheetah’s Rock for this life-changing experience!

content:
We found Cheetah's Rock through Google. Since I'm pregnant, we wanted to check via email first whether participation was possible for me. Communication via email was quick and easy. There were no obstacles to my participation; I only had to sign a separate form.
The pickup, which we booked, was flawless. Upon arrival, everyone was offered water and a coconut. Unfortunately, we noticed right away that some guests weren't following the rules explained by the rangers, which were available both online and in the car. For example, some were using sunscreen, which isn't good for the smaller animals.
The tour itself was very interesting. Plenty of time was taken to explain everything and each animal in detail, and there was also ample time for taking pictures. You could really feel the close bond between the rangers and the animals.
The explanations from Jenny, the founder, were also extremely interesting. She told us how the park came about, how it's financed, and much more.
For anyone who loves and appreciates animals, this excursion is perfect.
I do have one small suggestion for improvement, though: perhaps you could incorporate shorter water breaks along the way. Drinking is, of course, possible at any time, but it's outside the enclosures, and that means you miss some of the presentation.
Warm regards from Germany to the whole team! You're doing a fantastic job, and we'll definitely visit you again when we return to Zanzibar.

content:
You should support this!
You should see it!
I'm absolutely speechless. It was simply incredibly beautiful. I want to emphasize that all the animals are extremely well cared for, they have plenty of space, and the enclosures are designed to be very realistic. The whole team is doing a fantastic job. They told us so much about the animals: how they actually live, why each animal had to be taken in, and what the plan is for its future.
They put in a lot of work to prepare the animals so they can return to the wild. This takes a lot of time and money. Unfortunately, it's not possible for every animal. Sometimes the animal wouldn't be able to manage it, or, as with lions, because the authorities currently prohibit their release back into the wild. Nevertheless, they continue with the training. Firstly, because it takes years, and secondly, because the regulations can change again.
We swam with otters first. It was so much fun that I was laughing so hard I cried.
After that, a Maasai man took us to an incredibly beautiful spot: Arnoldis on the Cliff Bar and Bites. Beautiful and delicious.
We were allowed to spend two hours there.
Afterwards, we continued for four hours at Cheetah's Rock with the other rescued animals. It's often quite shocking to learn why these animals had to be taken in.
It's wonderful that such a place and such people exist who care so much for the animals.
None of the animals were forced to come to us. Those that wanted to come came, and some monkeys didn't, and that was just how it was. Of course, you're given food to attract the animals, but it's not like they starve them to make them come. They are all very well-fed. Also, they don't allow an unlimited number of visitors. For example, there were only two of us with the otters, and it's not an everyday occurrence.
You can tell that the animals' well-being is their top priority, but they can't help them any more without visitors.
It was one of the best days of my life, and I would recommend it to everyone. If I could, I would give it 100 stars.

It was so much fun that I was laughing so hard I cried.
After that, a Maasai man took us to an incredibly beautiful spot: Arnoldis on the Cliff Bar and Bites.
Beautiful and delicious.
We were allowed to spend two hours there.
Afterwards, we continued for four hours at Cheetah's Rock with the other rescued animals.
It's often quite shocking to learn why these animals had to be taken in.
It's wonderful that such a place and such people exist who care so much for the animals.
None of the animals were forced to come to us.
Those that wanted to come came, and some monkeys didn't, and that was just how it was.
Of course, you're given food to attract the animals, but it's not like they starve them to make them come.
They are all very well-fed.
Also, they don't allow an unlimited number of visitors.
For example, there were only two of us with the otters, and it's not an everyday occurrence.
You can tell that the animals' well-being is their top priority, but they can't help them any more without visitors.
It was one of the best days of my life, and I would recommend it to everyone.
If I could, I would give it 100 stars.

Lara and Pier

content:
One of the most beautiful experiences of my life! At Cheetah's Rock, they rescue wild animals that have been mistreated, stolen from their mothers, and used for illegal purposes, animals rescued from zoos, or animals arriving from other contexts. Unfortunately, almost none of these animals can be released into the wild due to contact with humans or the impossibility of safely reintroducing them into their natural environment. All the animals in the reserve are respected, loved by their caregivers, and are free-roaming, vaccinated, and healthy.
For each animal, their story is told and the journey they took to arrive at this reserve.
It's important to visit this center, as it is self-financed through our visits. I absolutely recommend visiting Cheetah's Rock if you're in Zanzibar.
Thanks to everyone who works at Cheetah's Rock for their commitment to saving less fortunate animals!

content:
One of the highlights of our vacation!
The people were very friendly and shared a lot of stories about the animals. The founder herself was also there for a Q&A session and with the zebra, answering all questions thoroughly and providing additional information. You can tell that everyone is passionate about what they do and wants to give the animals the best possible life under the circumstances.
We were able to let the bush babies, monkeys, and lemurs jump all over us and feed them, and we even petted a cheetah and the zebra. The animals were free to move away at any time, and with the monkeys, you simply stayed seated, and they would approach you on their own (sometimes with the help of food). They clearly explain beforehand what you are allowed/supposed to do and what you aren't, and you can always say if you don't want to go near a particular animal. You feel well taken care of, and even during the cheetah encounter, there was only a little nervousness, more like excitement.
At first glance, the tour seems a bit expensive, but you experience something truly unique and support a worthwhile project at the same time.
For animal lovers, this is a must-see in Zanzibar!
