content:
I'm shocked by how many people in these reviews rave about the amazing experience of swimming with turtles.
I found it absolutely awful.
To be fair, we hadn't really done our research beforehand because we met two girls who spontaneously invited us along.
We paid the entrance fee ($15 for 30 minutes) and went in.
We immediately noticed the astonishing number of turtles gathered in one spot (something you don't usually see in the wild) and asked if the animals could actually swim in and out on their own.
We were told that was practically impossible, and that's when we finally realized that these weren't wild turtles, but rather captured turtles brought there to entertain tourists.
As soon as you start questioning the ethical aspects of the whole thing, you're immediately told that it's a "rescue center"—which is simply a blatant lie.
We were told that this was practically impossible. The animals clearly have no wounds or other externally visible problems; they can't be sick either, since sick animals in the wild are almost always infested with parasites.
Proper rescue centers therefore have various sterile pools where the animals' problems can truly be addressed.
Furthermore, rescue centers house WILD animals! This means that, for obvious reasons, it's not allowed for random tourists to enter the water with these animals. Besides, the animals would be sick or injured, which is why you shouldn't go in the water with them. (Generally, this is a good indicator of an ethical rescue center. In proper centers, visitors are not allowed to have direct contact with the animals.)
Then we were told that the animals are released again and again – after we asked several times and expressed our concerns, we were given a few more facts.
The turtles that end up in these "caves" are bycatch. (This includes animals that unfortunately get caught in large fishing nets, such as dolphins, sea urchins, squid, whales, and turtles.)
So, in the end, these are perfectly healthy animals that suffer because of our massive fish consumption.
They then serve as tourist attractions for a while until, under a grand guise of "animal welfare," they are released back into their natural habitat.
In short: after a few minutes of discussion, we left immediately and asked for a refund (15 dollars is easily a full day's budget for backpackers), which, of course, we didn't receive.
Please, in the name of animal welfare, do not support such facilities! In the wild, you can easily see turtles in their natural habitat on ethical boat tours without them having to suffer.

content:
If feeding turtles is on your Zanzibar itinerary, Salaam Cave is definitely worth considering.
The experience costs $12, and it was a lot more hands-on than I expected. Getting to the rock in the middle isn’t as easy as the videos make it look because the rocks under the water are uneven in some places. Once I got there though, I relaxed and really enjoyed being that close to the turtles.
A few things I’d tell anyone visiting: go early if you want fewer people around, take your own towel because you will pay extra if you need one there, and make use of the changing room after your swim. If you are traveling solo, you are allowed to use a tripod, which makes taking your own photos and videos much easier.
One thing I only found out afterwards was that green clothing can attract the turtles because it looks similar to the seaweed they are fed. I can’t say for certain that was why they kept coming towards me, but after hearing that, it made my experience make a lot more sense.

content:
One of the most unique experiences we had in Zanzibar.
When we first arrived, it was honestly difficult to imagine that such a beautiful cave was hidden there. The area was undergoing some improvements and construction work, so at first glance it does not immediately reveal what is waiting below.
Before entering the water, visitors are asked to shower thoroughly to remove sunscreen, body lotions and other products. We really appreciated this, as it shows how seriously they take the protection of the turtles and their environment.
Once inside, the experience is incredible. The water is crystal clear, the cave itself is beautiful, and we were even able to spot bats hanging from the ceiling. It feels like entering a hidden world.
The turtles are the main attraction and getting so close to them is something truly special. Visitors are given seaweed to feed them, and the turtles quickly swim over looking for a snack. Being able to observe them from such a short distance was unforgettable.
We paid for the one-hour experience, although for many visitors the 30-minute option would probably be enough. Either way, it was well worth it.
One funny piece of advice: avoid wearing green swimwear! My wife was wearing a green swimsuit, and one of the turtles apparently mistook it for seaweed and gave her a little bite on the back. Later, I had a small piece of seaweed attached to my arm and ended up getting a bite as well. Nothing serious at all, but it definitely gave us a good laugh and became one of the funniest memories of the experience.
The facilities are still being improved, and customer service could perhaps be a little more polished in some areas, but it was clear that the team is investing in the site and working to make the experience even better.
Overall, this was an immersive and memorable experience that allowed us to get closer to these amazing animals than we ever expected. The conservation aspect of the project was also very interesting, and learning that the turtles are cared for before eventually being released made the visit even more meaningful.
If you are visiting Zanzibar and enjoy nature and wildlife, Salaam Cave Aquarium is definitely worth adding to your itinerary.
Highly recommended.

content:
We visited Salaam Cave because the description gave the impression that it was a kind of sanctuary or refuge for turtles, where you could also learn about the animals and their habitat. That was our expectation.
However, our experience there was quite different. There were many people in the water with the turtles at the same time, and the animals were being fed so that visitors could interact with them. This made it feel more like a tourist attraction than a peaceful place where animal welfare is the priority.
Unfortunately, we received very little information about the turtles or about any conservation or educational work being done, even though that's exactly what we had hoped for. The way the animals were treated also left us with some questions.
We also found it somewhat disturbing that a monkey was being kept on a leash. This didn't really fit with our image of a place dedicated to animal welfare.
This review isn't meant to criticize anyone, but simply to share our personal experience. Anyone considering visiting Salaam Cave should perhaps do some research beforehand and decide for themselves whether this type of animal encounter is something they want to support.

Furthermore, if we're being completely honest, these turtles were most likely torn from their ecosystem and will end up dying in that horrible pool surrounded by Vikings who would do anything for a couple of vulgar photos.
MAN SHOULD LEARN THAT NOT EVERYTHING IS OWED TO HIM, natural experiences are not always possible to achieve and man should come to terms with it!

content:
Visiting Salaam Cave to feed my favorite animals—the turtles—was truly a wonderful and unforgettable experience. From the moment you arrive, everything is well organized and focused on both safety and respect for the animals. Before entering the cave, you’re required to shower off, and a staff member walks you through a set of simple rules to follow. You’re also given a small container of seaweed to feed the turtles.
The water is cold at first, which can be a bit of a shock, but once you’re in, it becomes comfortable. One of the best tips is to stay calm and move gently. Feeding the turtles small pieces of seaweed helps make the experience last longer and keeps them engaged.
I truly believe the turtles can sense energy and tension. By remaining calm, gentle, and not anxious, the turtles were very peaceful with me. Some tourists who were in the water at the same time seemed scared and tense, and they ended up getting bitten. I, however, did not get bitten at all, even after I ran out of seaweed.
Overall, it was a beautiful, peaceful experience. If you respect the rules, stay calm and treat the turtles gently, visiting Salaam Cave is an incredible experience I would highly recommend—especially for anyone who loves marine life as much as I do. We did not go with a tour guy- went on our own which is a lot better option. $12 per person for 30minutes

content:
⭐ SOS ⭐ Disturbing Treatment of a poor Monkey Baby 🐒
I visited Saalam Cave in November witnessed something extremely upsetting. A young monkey was kept on a short chain next to a “donations” box, apparently for paid photos with tourists. The animal showed clear signs of severe stress — it jumped at visitors and even bit someone. Its only “toy” was an electrical cable, which is dangerously unsafe.
After speaking with animal welfare groups, I learned that situations like this often involve young monkeys being taken from the wild, sometimes violently.
Supporting such practices — even unintentionally — contributes to more animals being captured and mistreated.
⚠️Please try to convince the handler to give you the monkey freely — and importantly, do not make any payment.
If you are able to take the monkey into your care, please contact the animal welfare organizations in Zanzibar immediately.
If you need a contact, feel free to message me on Instagram: @atzimieze ⚠️
I strongly urge all visitors:
• Please do not pay for photos or donate money when animals are being exploited.
• If you witness this monkey or others in distress, speak up and report it.
• Please also report this location directly on Google Maps (“Report this place”) so authorities and platforms are alerted. The more reports they receive, the faster something can change.
• Share this information with other travelers — your voice matters.
This experience was heartbreaking, and I sincerely hope that this monkey receives help as soon as possible. Tourism should never come at the expense of animal welfare. Let’s make sure practices like this have no place here.

The staff were friendly and explained that there's a program where injured animals are cared for and later released back into the sea. Of course, you can't really verify whether that's how it works, but the idea behind it is good. It's definitely worth it for some special photos and the experience of being so close to the animals.

content:
Sono profondamente scioccato e deluso da ciò che ho visto alla Grotta Salaam a Paje. Quello che viene promosso come un'esperienza naturale e tranquilla con le tartarughe è, in realtà, una situazione sovraffollata e sfruttatrice in cui gli animali selvatici vengono maltrattati per profitto, senza alcuna preoccupazione da parte di chi gestisce il luogo.
All'interno di una piccola grotta recintata, decine di turisti (più di 30 contemporaneamente) erano stipati, spingendo, strattonando e costringendo le tartarughe sott'acqua, afferrandole e tenendole con forza solo per scattare dei selfie. Queste tartarughe venivano nutrite senza sosta per tutto il giorno, insegnando loro ad associare gli esseri umani al cibo, lasciandole completamente vulnerabili quando verranno eventualmente rilasciate in natura. Gli animali erano chiaramente stressati, ma nessuno della gestione sembrava preoccuparsene.
Quando una turista preoccupata ha avuto il coraggio di parlare—dopo aver visto tartarughe essere afferrate, tirate e trattate brutalmente—anziché ricevere supporto, è stata affrontata aggressivamente dal manager e dal personale di sicurezza, che le hanno detto che questo tipo di abuso è necessario per far funzionare il posto. Le loro parole, e cito: 'Questo è un posto turistico

content:
What's being sold as a "turtle cave" is actually absolute animal cruelty!
We booked the excursion through our hotel's tour guide, who told us we could swim with turtles.
Upon arrival, we discovered it was an artificial cave containing approximately 25 turtles. They have no way to escape, and the flow of tourists isn't regulated by the operators. When we asked, they claimed the cave was there to protect the turtles, which is, of course, complete nonsense.
I'm truly speechless! Absolute animal cruelty 🥺 We regret booking this excursion! It's also very sad that many other tourists don't seem to have any real insight into the Salaam Cave.

content:
I went to Salaam Cave very early right when they opened at 7:30 am. I think the opening time is flexible. The cost to get in is 12 USD for 30 minutes in the water, it’s more for an hour. I believe this to be a fair price compared to many other attractions around.

The water can be difficult to navigate with many rocks, pebbles, and sea turtles coming at you. It is best to navigate slowly and calmly.
From my experience, sea turtles do not bite you randomly. The only rare instances of biting happen when you are not careful feeding them so they bite your hand. With caution you should be more than fine.
I used goggles and swam underwater. Underwater swimming is allowed, but be careful of your surroundings. Overall, it was an amazing experience and if you want to beat the crowds go super early right when it opens. When I arrived there was 10 minutes where nobody was there.

content:
We had an unforgettable visit to Salama Cave during our trip to Zanzibar! Hidden away like a true gem, this natural cave offers a unique and magical experience – swimming with turtles in crystal-clear water.
From the moment we arrived, the staff were welcoming and made us feel completely at ease. After a short introduction, we walked down into the cave, and what awaited us was simply breathtaking – turquoise water surrounded by stunning rock formations and majestic turtles peacefully gliding through the water.
Swimming alongside these gentle creatures was both surreal and calming. They were so graceful and curious, and we appreciated how respectful the guides were towards them, always reminding us to be gentle and not to disturb their natural behavior.
The environment felt clean, well-maintained, and authentic – not overly commercialized, which we loved. It felt like we were part of something truly special.
If you’re visiting Zanzibar, we highly recommend a stop at Salama Cave. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience that combines nature, tranquility, and a bit of adventure. Definitely one of the highlights of our trip!

content:
Absolutely not recommended – animal suffering for mass tourism
I am shocked by the way the turtles are treated here. It's pure mass tourism – far too many people are herded through at once, it's loud, chaotic, and completely disrespectful to the animals.
The turtles are kept in an artificial pool marketed as a "cave" – but there's no discernible exit or natural retreat for them. They are clearly being fed to get close to visitors. Some tourists touch the animals, even push them away or scream loudly. There's absolutely no consideration for the animals – and no real control by the staff.
From my perspective, the turtles seem completely stressed; some are even snapping at each other. This whole thing has absolutely nothing to do with respecting nature or animal welfare. For $12, you get 30 minutes in an overcrowded, noisy setting designed solely to rush tourists through.
For me, this was a disturbing experience. I can only advise everyone against it – please don't support such things.

content:
Salaam Cave Aquarium offers a unique opportunity to interact with turtles in a natural cave pool setting, but sadly, the overall experience falls short in many critical areas. The only standout feature was the excellent videography service provided by one of the staff members—though even this requires haggling to get a reasonable price.
Visitor management is lacking, with far too many people allowed into the pool at once, raising concerns about the turtles’ well-being. There’s no visible system to refresh or filter the water regularly, which is alarming considering the pollution caused by constant human activity. For an attraction that charges a premium fee, the showers and restrooms are subpar and in need of serious improvement.
There are also safety issues. The turkeys on site, likely stressed by captivity, can be aggressive and are prone to biting. Visitors should also tread carefully inside the cave—the uneven rock floor is quite slippery and could lead to injury if one isn’t cautious.
Most disappointing is the lack of education or orientation. A brief welcome speech explaining the cave’s significance and the conservation efforts for the turtles, including their eventual release, would go a long way in improving the experience.
Overall, an average and somewhat underwhelming visit.

Otherwise, the staff was friendly and even tried to calm a girl having a panic attack.

content: A terrible place. If anyone has even a shred of compassion or empathy for animals, I absolutely do not recommend it. I followed the group and didn't check where we were going, which is a shame. I was hoping for a cave where the marine world connects with the human world, where turtles somehow swim there for food as free beings, but instead I ended up in a hole in the middle of the parking lot with absolutely no water flow. A dozen or so beautiful turtles are trapped there, their natural instincts being to travel thousands of kilometers alone. The water is so greasy with oils and sunscreen that you can barely see the bottom. It's a turquoise slush. The turtles are fed only some kind of algae sold by farmers for a dollar. There are showers in front of the cave, but of course, no one uses them (I even saw a woman applying sunscreen just before entering the cave 🤦🏻‍♀️), which affects the quality of the water in which these animals live. And in the wild, they can live up to 100 years! In short, this place is a nightmare of majestic animals trapped for human enjoyment. If even one person skips this trip after reading my description, I'll be very happy.

content:
OMG, this place is amazing, I would give 10* if it was possible!!
It's a small cave where injured turtles are cared for and rehabilitated before being released back into the sea.
You pay a small fee at the gate for 1/2 hour or 1 hour and have a guide to explain the process. We brought some seaweed, and as we already had our swimmers on, we went down the ladder into the cave. They do have changing rooms you can use for free.
Once in the cave, we left our bags on the platform, I gave our guide my phone, and we went down another ladder into the water. The water is fresh at first and comes to waist height if you are 5ft 9, the floor of the cave was very rocky.
As soon as we were in the water, the turtles swam over to us, and we fed them some seaweed. Just watch your fingers as one turtle was quite greedy and nipped my thumb!
They don't mind you being there and swimming around you. They are very gentle, and you can pet them when they swim past. There are yellow birds that have made their nests above you in the cave.
We got out after half an hour, and our guide gave me my phone back with lots of amazing pictures and videos of me in the water with the turtles. It was a truly lovely time and not too busy when we visited, about 2pm.

content:
+ Amazing cave with seawater
+ Very clear water
+ You get algae to feed the turtles
+ Lots of turtles
+ Friendly staff
+ Lots of bats on the ceiling
- Since it's so new, there are hardly any rules. Many tourists behave terribly, picking up the turtles or trying to turn them over. One child even hung onto a turtle while diving, hoping it would pull them.
> I was very surprised that the staff didn't say anything.
- Entry to the cave should be limited to a certain number of people. We arrived 5 minutes before a group of 12 who were incredibly loud and inconsiderate. We were then asked to leave after 30 minutes, even though we wanted to leave ourselves anyway because it was getting too crowded.
- When it was less crowded, we were only allowed back in "as an exception" for a quick photo.
Overall, it's a great cave, and I think the price is justified for such an experience. Those who are easily startled and move suddenly in the water should, out of consideration for the animals (which also lie on the bottom and are at risk of being stepped on), watch from the rocks and not go into the water. Furthermore, sunscreen should be avoided for the 30 minutes to prevent polluting the water and the cave.
All in all, a fantastic experience!

content:
My boyfriend and I visited this place, run by locals who have a chameleon conservation project.
Before seeing the animals, we toured the caves with a guide, who gave us a detailed explanation of how the crystals form and provided a unique experience inside the cave (not suitable for those afraid of the dark). After visiting the caves, we went into the chameleon conservation area, where we were able to see several and even hold and feed them. The tour was very interesting and provided us with a wealth of information about this species and their conservation.
It's definitely worth it; one of the most beautiful experiences on the island!
The entrance fee is 15 euros (they also accept Tanzanian shillings and dollars, of course; converting could probably be cheaper; it was our mistake to only have euros).

Definitely worth checking out if you're around the area.

content: Chameleons are a family of lizards that can change their body color depending on the situation, primarily to protect themselves from danger, especially predators such as snakes and monkeys. They are adapted to an arboreal lifestyle, so here in the small garden, trees and small bushes have been created for them, along with burrows for burying eggs. The staff feeds them once a day, providing 5-7 insects each. The breeding center currently houses 18 adult chameleons. The chameleons live solitary lives, pairing up only during mating season. According to the guide, male chameleons may fight among themselves to assert dominance. These lizards are completely harmless to humans and very friendly. We got the impression that they perceive us as large trees, interesting to climb and explore. Chameleons use their paws and tail for balance and stability. When touching human skin, they do so very gently and tenderly. They catch insects offered for food with their tongues, which have a suction cup at the end. The process of ejecting the tongue lasts only 1/20th of a second—very quickly, as you can see in the video. Overall, we spent about half an hour here with a guide, and it was very interesting. The guide speaks excellent English and explains all the details of caring for the lizards, answering all questions very well. This is a place to visit for people of all ages. Considering the nearby caves, which I would recommend limiting to older people and children, a visit to the small chameleon nursery will fully justify your visit to Tazari village. The cost of visiting the nursery is only five dollars. The village is a 15-minute tuk-tuk ride from Nuvi. The road is mostly on the highway, but then you'll turn onto a secondary road. Tuk-tuk fares vary widely, but we settled on 20,000 shillings roundtrip and paid on the way back. This was the right decision, as the driver would likely have doubled the price if we'd paid 20,000 upfront.

content:
Avoid at all costs… I am so shocked by the lack of respect shown to animals on Earth for the sake of tourist entertainment.
Especially in Zanzibar. Between the various salam caves (turtle attractions) and dolphin fishing, you'll find these kinds of mini-zoos all over the island, like the one in Nungwi. The number of animals living on less than a hectare of land is appalling, and on top of that, the number of tourists disrupts their lives and natural rhythms.
Everything has become a business… for a quick photo with a chameleon on your hand, you can't imagine their tiny hearts and their tiny metabolisms, but they are very fragile, and what you are doing is cruel. It's a crime to make them suffer like this.
Please don't go! Even if they say they release them after getting them used to humans and feeding them, do you think they will be able to hunt insects and then adapt to their real environment? … I have so many questions.

content:
We visited Tazari Chameleon Reserve in Zanzibar, Tanzania, and it was a fantastic experience. The road to get there is a bit bumpy, but it’s worth it! The reserve is small but very welcoming, and the staff were incredibly friendly. Entry was $5 per person, and after paying, one of the staff members guided us through the reserve.
At first, we were asked to try spotting the chameleons ourselves—it’s surprisingly challenging! Then, he showed them to us and passionately explained all about these fascinating creatures and the important protective measures they’re taking to safeguard them from local threats. It was clear he truly loves and cares for the animals.
We also got the chance to handle the chameleons, including the young ones, under careful supervision. Overall, it was an unusual and highly rewarding 5/5 experience. No need to book in advance—just show up, and they’ll take great care of you. Highly recommended!

content:
I recently visited the Tazari Chameleon Reserve, and it was an absolutely incredible experience! Unlike a zoo, this reserve has a real purpose—to help and protect the chameleon population of Zanzibar. It’s all about conservation, and you can tell that every effort here is made with that mission in mind.
The guide was amazing—so friendly and full of knowledge about chameleons. You could tell he was deeply passionate about these unique creatures, and I learned so much from him. It wasn’t just a tour; it was an opportunity to understand the importance of preserving these animals and their environment.
I also highly recommend the cave tour, which was an exciting part of the visit and added a sense of adventure to the day. The whole experience was so peaceful and authentic. If you care about wildlife and want to support a great cause, Tazari Chameleon Reserve is the perfect place to visit.

The caves far exceeded my expectations. A large stalactite and many smaller, beautiful formations. Glittering rows of teeth and hemispheres, and three different colors: green, presumably containing copper; yellow, presumably containing sulfur; and pink. It was truly astonishing. We also saw the whip spider, which looks eerie but is completely harmless.
Be sure to wear good shoes!
This place is definitely worth a visit!!!

place_name: Dada Zanzibar Production and Cooking Site
content:
We spontaneously walked there from the hotel after I searched for a cooking class in Matemwe on Google Maps. Amina thought about it briefly when I inquired, and then we agreed. Amina ordered vegetables by phone, which arrived a few minutes later. Then we got started.
It's a very authentic cooking experience. Cooking on the floor, no running water, over an open fire. I wouldn't recommend it for those with sensitive stomachs.
The women are very friendly. I think we seem just as exotic to some of them as they do to us.
The food was delicious. You don't eat there, but take it home in jars that are meticulously labeled by hand.
Overall, a highlight for us. Alina speaks English. But don't assume that there will always be someone there who speaks English.
Google Translate can also do Swahili :-)

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
Absolutely Magical Experience – A Must-Visit Spice Farm in Zanzibar! 🌿✨
We had the most unforgettable experience at this incredible spice farm in Zanzibar! From the moment we arrived, we were warmly welcomed by the sweetest guide and the kind-hearted owner, who made us feel like VIP guests throughout the entire visit. What made this tour so special was that it was completely private — just the two of us — which allowed for a relaxed, intimate, and truly personal experience.
Our guide was not only extremely knowledgeable about every spice and plant, but also full of joy, passion, and humor. He took the time to explain everything in detail, encouraged us to smell, touch, and taste the different spices and fruits, and shared fascinating stories behind each one. You could tell that everyone working there truly loves what they do — and that made all the difference.
As if the amazing hospitality and rich knowledge weren’t enough, we were showered with thoughtful gifts before we left! From handmade spice necklaces to small samples of fresh local produce — it was beyond generous and heartwarming. We felt so appreciated and connected to the people behind this beautiful place.
This is not your average spice tour — it’s a heartwarming, authentic, and deeply personal experience that we will cherish forever. If you’re in Zanzibar, do yourself a favor and visit this farm. You won’t regret it for a second.
Thank you again for the unforgettable memories — we will carry them with us always! ❤️🌴

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We visited this farm with our family of four. We paid 25 each plus tips for the guides and tree climber. There was some confusion about the tour when we booked through Zantours who had not been to this farm before (we picked it because it was close to our hotel). They should have communicated in advance as we thought we were paying through Zantours and the spice farm wanted direct payment. Setting that aside, while the guide was nice and it was fun to see how all the spices are grown, the cost of this tour is not reflective of the experience. I thought that there was a cooking class included in this price but that is an add on. I ended up canceling another tour with Zantours because I felt ripped off after this one. The locals in Zanzibar think all North Americans are rich (and relatively speaking I guess we are) and so have no problem charging high tour rates for everything. They don’t realize that some of us saved up for a year to take this once in a lifetime trip. Wouldn’t recommend this tour to others.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
We did the Kisongoni Village tour with Bilal as our guide. I'm glad we chose this over a spice farm tour as visiting a village gave insights into the local way of life.
Bilal took us on a two hour walk explaining about the fruits and spices growing in his village and how they are used in medicine and cooking. Bilal is a great conversationalist, asking us questions while informing us about village life, giving the morning a friendly, relaxed vibe.
At just 19, it was inspiring to hear Bilal explain that he set his mind from a young age to study English and history to start a business that would benefit his village.
The tour ended with a fruit tasting and fresh coconut drink. There was an opportunity to buy spices at the end, which we did without haggling as happy to support the village. We booked the day before, and they helpfully arrange a transfer to and from our hotel.
An excellent option if you are staying near Kiwengwa beach and want to meet some local Zanzibaris and learn about their way of life.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
Unique and authentic experience to discover Zanzibar spices with local farmers. Highly recommended.
Bilal was our guide. He took care of the transfer and during the tour in the spice plantation of his village, despite his young age, he shared his extensive knowledge and taught us how to recognize plants, their fruit seasons and their several uses. We had the chance to taste many fruits, as well as coconut water and sugar cane. After the tour, we were lucky to join Mussa, his family and other people from the village for a cooking class to learn how to cook pilau rice. All together we prepared the lunch and then we had a delicious and gargantuan meal. After lunch, we could buy sone of the spices produced by the farmers. It was a great experience to appreciate the beauty of this island and its people, while also supporting their living. I suggest this place to all who are looking for genuinely local experiences and don’t mind going off the more touristic tracks.

Booking was super easy and we ended up booking for a same day visit.
Transfers were offered to us at a very reasonable rate and we were collected and returned to our hotel.
The visit was excellent and we learnt so much! Bilal was our tour guide and he was very knowledgeable. He took his time to show us all around the different spice and fruit trees/plants and sampling each one was great fun!
After the tour was finished, we enjoyed a fruit platter with Bilal and his colleagues and enjoyed wearing the hats and necklaces they made for us.
It was a fantastic afternoon spent in beautiful surroundings. It has also prompted us to try and become more self-sufficient at home!
The village children were also lovely to meet. There is an opportunity to purchase sweets for the children, along with spices to take home at the end of the tour.
Highly recommend a visit to this spice village. You will not be disappointed!
Thank you Bilal - Keep up the fabulous work!

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We chose this farm because it seemed unpretentious. The entrance is easy to miss, it is exactly where the sign is, so you must take the narrow winding dirt track to the parking. It is a community project, so they need your support. For $5 each our guide, Saka, gave us a detailed description of the plants grown on the farm, making the tour interactive and interesting. At the end of the tour we were shown how they climb the palm trees to harvest coconuts and finally we were given their fruit to sample. The visit was truly worthwhile. If you go there, make sure you ask for Saka, he’s the best!

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We found the visit incredibly interesting. Our guide, Bilal, took a lot of time to tell us all about the different spices, plants, and fruits. It was fascinating to learn how the spices grow and what they look like when you don't buy them from the supermarket. Tasting them fresh was simply fantastic. All the collected plants were presented in a basket made of palm leaves, along with accessories for us (free of charge). At the end, we were given plenty of fruit to eat, and we could buy various spices without feeling obligated to do so. It's a small spice farm, far removed from mass tourism, and that's precisely why we can highly recommend it. The people live in a small village, and everything is completely authentic. Keep up the great work, and we hope that Bilal will make it to Europe one day.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We had an awesome experience visiting this spice farm. Our guide, Bilal, was a young brilliant high school junior who loves history and languages and aspires to continue education in the university as an educator and tour guide. He was enthusiastic, knowledgeable and patient with good command of English. He provided thorough information about each plant, answered our questions, and offered us samples of each plant/fruit and even gave us some lemongrass to plant. At the end, they treated us with young coconuts and fruits. The grand finale was when their little helper, who was with us all along, and the lead guide Mohammad, made plant and flower crowns and Jewlery for us to wear. The tour took about 2.5 hours; an experience that we will never forget. We wish Bilal and his community all the best and may his wish and his mother’s wish for him come true and beyond. content:
Leaving this review only to counter the babies crying about the tide and sea urchins and lack of restaurants. It's a beach, in one of the few non-touristic parts of the island, and rich with life sustained by the rich, warm waters.
Only an absolute knob would not prepare for sea urchins (wear sea shoes..) - which Zanzibar is well known for. I swam and went snorkeling here pretty much every day for a week. place_name: TO THE HILL KIDICHI SPICE FARM
content:
Thank you to our guide, Adil, for his patient and professional explanations. He asked what kind of tour I wanted, and I said I wanted to learn more about spices without going into too much detail. I tasted and smelled spices throughout the tour, and he even showed me spice-based dyes and demonstrated their uses, which left a deep impression on me. This was a completely new experience for me, engaging all my senses—smell, taste, and touch. The guide was very knowledgeable; he even showed me the Chinese mimosa plant. The staff also wove straw hats for me and opened coconuts for me to drink. I thoroughly enjoyed it and was very happy.
The staff were also very helpful. Since I didn't have a ride back to Stone City, he called a friend of his who had a motorcycle to give me a ride. However, the friend didn't know where I was going and didn't speak English, so the owner decided to give me a ride. The owner was very talkative, asking about my impressions of the spice garden and Zanzibar, as well as how many languages ​​I spoke, which I enjoyed discussing. Thank you for the ride.
In short, I highly recommend this spice garden. I had a wonderful experience.

place_name: TO THE HILL KIDICHI SPICE FARM
content:
I spent a few wonderful hours there! It's a beautiful, peaceful place away from the hustle and bustle of Stone Town. A local guide, who inherited a wealth of knowledge about plants from his grandparents, took plenty of time to show me the various spices and plants, such as cardamom, cinnamon, star fruit, turmeric, ginger, vanilla, lychee, and more, and to tell me about their natural uses and medicinal properties. He even got me a coconut fresh from the palm tree and lychees from the tree.
Afterwards, you can also buy local spices there.
The whole place is easily accessible from Stone Town by taking bus line 511 for a small fare.
So far, it's one of my favorite things to do here.

place_name: TO THE HILL KIDICHI SPICE FARM
content:
Today we took our 9-year-old son to Stone Town (a short tour, 1.5 hours) and Prison Island to visit this lovely spice farm. Abdul from the spice farm gave us a truly entertaining tour. He explained a great deal, and we were able to smell and taste many spices and plants and learn about everything without it being overwhelming or boring. Even our son thought it was the best stop on our trip to Zanzibar. We were even given beautiful souvenirs woven from leaves, and there was plenty of time for questions and photos. Of course, they also want to sell things on the farm, as you'll see in every olive grove in Italy and every vineyard along the Rhine. We happily bought a few things as souvenirs for friends and would highly recommend this tour to anyone who has the time. We would like to give Abdul a special thank you; he speaks excellent German and only had to switch to his even better English twice.
After reading many negative reports about spice farms, we initially didn't want to do it, but we're glad this tour was recommended to us; apparently, it varies greatly from farm to farm. This one is a must-see in Zanzibar.

content:
A must visit when in Zanzibar.
I highly recommend visiting this farm when you are in Zanzibar. I was greeted by the owner Mr. Abdullah. This tour was really really amazing. We could see and touch so many different kinds of spices. Great opportunity to see all different types of spices as they grow and learn a lot. Our guide spoke very good English and broke down each product into interesting facts. Everything growing there where it has self-seeded or been planted. Jack fruit, star fruits, mango, papaya, Ginger, cardamoms, coffee, vanilla, oranges, cinnamon, bananas,etc etc. At the end of the tour we could also taste many of the local ripe fruits. Thanks Mr Abdallah for showing us your farm.

content:
It's interesting to stroll around since there's a lot of choice.
Unfortunately, as a tourist, you pay many times more than usual. :)
For example, a bottle of sugarcane juice normally costs 1000 TSN.
Here, they charge between 5,000 and 10,000 TSN, or even 1000 TSN for snacks instead of 200.
No matter how interesting it is, I definitely wouldn't shop here, because people can see that you're white and a tourist.
As a result, you only get inferior or old spices, since locals don't buy this stuff; they only buy it in certain shops, and they pay much more.
It's better to sell outside the city and do something nice for people who aren't being ripped off and are happy to receive money or even a tip.
Alternatively, there are parking lots that cost 1000 TSN per hour or 3000 TSN per day.
You're often asked if you'd like to donate money – just like everywhere else in Zanzibar :) Unfortunately, with the children it starts with a friendly hello, followed immediately by "Money, money"... a real shame for what is otherwise a lovely little island.

content: The local market is a place where you can find all kinds of spices, fruits, vegetables, and small ornaments. First of all, let me say upfront that it's not a very clean area. As for spices, black pepper, ginger, and cloves are really high quality. You can also buy vanilla twigs (orchid flower twigs) that grow in Zanzibar and are quite high quality. You can also buy liquid vanilla, banana, and mango extracts in small bottles; they are both reasonably priced and of good quality. Besides vanilla, Zanzibar is also famous for its cashew nuts. You can find both salted and unsalted nuts at very reasonable prices. They usually sell them in 100, 450, and 900-gram bags. Finally, they sell dried octopus and juvenile fish that they collect from the beach during low tide and salt. The juvenile fish are sold as fish chips; they're not hygienic, but they're worth trying.

Covid situation is very bad - but it is all over the island anyway, so no worse here than any place else except a resort.

content:
The historic market of Stone Town, Zanzibar, is one of the few places in sub-Saharan Africa steeped in history and stories.
You can find a bit of everything here: fruit, spices, meat, fish, herbs, and tea; it's also a great place to buy souvenirs.
Of course, you have to be prepared to put up with strong odors and a bit of dirt, but this also adds to its exotic charm.

I was wandering the alleys, when I bumped into this market, even though I knew that I had to visit it, I had no idea I was going on that direction, as I walk closer and closer, a veeeery distinctive smell was coming out of the fish section, lot of loud voices too. I walk straight in, spectacular experience!! I could witness the auctions, Hammer heads, other sharks, Big Marleys, giant Manta rays and heaps of other species of fish, the men negotiating the prices, chaos, very dirty, just like you see in documentaries, I went for lunch after and returned to it once again.
IT WAS AN AMAZING EXPERIENCE!! loved it so much!! they seem to be doing the same process for centuries.
That market is extraordinary to wander around. I recommend to do it alone and then maybe do it with a guide for better context.
I met a local guide nearby by accident, he gave me the tour then, he took me to the old slave market museum, then back to the market, where we went behind the scenes, sooo many hidden alley ways, I could see, where they butcher the chickens, where all market workers eat in what it seems to be communal kitchens, etc

content:
We heard about Zanzibar local (food and fish) market, now it was the time to see how it is, me and my friend, Colbet from South Africa decided to hv a look. We passed through narrow streets from stone town, and finally we reached to this place.
The Darajani market.
The Darajani Market is famous or known as Darajani Fish market or Darajani Food Market or even Darajani Local Market.
These are the names given by different people from different places according to their perspective and the way they categorize it as.
The Market is Open from around 07:30 Am to 10:30 pm and sometimes more depends on the customers.
The Darajani Market tour is one of things to do and you should never miss once you are in this Island, It became one of the most popular and most visited by tourist from around the world and local people, so its a tourist attraction.
Since it have More of the Variety of the Local food, and More Experience in Local trading and marketing experience, Small trade activities.
This is a cash only place, No Cards Services here.
This is One of the famous local food market in Zanzibar.
it's a place where you can find and have almost everything you need in the food section, (Fresh and at a very low / reasonable price.)
The market is very famous due to its unique style, arrangement (Specified Portions) and Running style.
The market has Beef Butches section, Fresh fish Section, Spice section , Fresh Fruits and mixed / different variety Section. so if you fail to find what you are looking for, just go to mixed / different variety Section, there you will get what you want.
so the Sellers have arranged them self in that way to make more life easy to their customers and quest visiting the market. Though the market is very populated especial during the afternoon since different people from part of Zanzibar going there for shopping but still you will find path ways to move around the market.
So if you need some fresh fruits, Vegetables, Fish and meat, Spices and further more even to experience Zanzibarian local life style this is the right place to visit.
I like the way people are so humble, everyone has his or her own internal motivation, Not only youth but even, Women and Older people they all seat together as a community with the aim of one goal to sell as the best they can,
once you are at the market it's a normal thing to see everyone is welcome you at his or her business. People from this area have high and good Customer care with pleasant language that will convince you to stop and buy from him or her and sometimes even just to have a look, this is what encourages them more.
The wonderful this you can come across a local guy Speaking your language, don't be surprised, or you hear someone speaks more than 3 Foreign language.
The market has the best products and cheap price ever,
For anyone you can go with your expensive camera to take pictures but with a request for a permission a person before taking the picture, Some they like to be in the picture some don't like to be in the pictures, so the better way is to ask the individual first.
Do you wanna have more fun, Say or talk to any local person a Swahili word there you go, you will love the moment of being there.
People are very friendly and its a Safe Market.
Thank you everyone these are some of my experiences of being there, i have much to say the beauty of this place but i leave for you to say more after passing to this place.

content:
The market itself is definitely worth a visit; it remains very authentic, and the meat and fish section is a real step back in time.
However, beware of tourist scams; prices are significantly inflated. For example, a 250g bag of black pepper was quoted at 25,000 shillings in the market stalls. After some haggling, I got it down to 15,000. Then, looking in the back alleys, where locals seem to shop, the price was 8,000. I bought two or three things there, but the vendor didn't have all the spices I wanted. He took me to a better-stocked supplier, and in that stall, the same pepper was 4,000 shillings. That's a price divided by... six! So I stocked up on spices and came back with over 3 kilos.
It's the same with fabrics; once you're at the market, cross the main street and wander through the alleyways on the other side. Here you'll find the stalls where the locals do their shopping. The prices are much lower and there's practically no room for negotiation.

content: Darajani Market is the perfect place to witness an authentic Zanzibari experience on the island. The market is usually boisterous from morning until late in the night, and the stalls are crowded with buyers looking to purchase a variety of items on display. With scents of spices filling the air, the market is a hive of activity and features an array of items for purchase including fabrics, fresh fruits, meats, spices, live chicken, DVDs and mobile phones. The best time to visit Darajani Market is in the morning when the perishable goods are fresh. However, you can visit Darajani Market in the afternoon when it’s less chaotic. If you have never been to an African market, this is the place to try out your haggling skills. The market is called the Estella Market and Marikiti Kuu.

A perfect way to understand the influence of different cultures on the Island.

Bilal's wasn't just a typical excursion to a spice plantation, but a true journey into a Zanzibar community that still lives almost entirely in traditional houses made of wood and mud. We visited the plantation and tasted all the spices picked from the trees, ate freshly picked fruit with Duly, a very friendly and expert guide who is learning Italian. We toured the village with Bilal, who told us about his community, meeting smiling and cheerful children (bring a bag of sweets; you'll make them all happy!). There's also the option, if you'd like, to make a small contribution by purchasing rice or other items at the village's small store. The entire visit took us
over three hours, spending about 20 euros each, half that if you just wanted to visit the spice plantation.
Thank you, Bilal and Duly, for this priceless experience!

content:
Visiting Bilal’s place for the spice and village tour was, without a doubt, one of the most meaningful, eye-opening, and unforgettable experiences I have ever had in Zanzibar.
As a European, being welcomed into the local community and having the opportunity to experience their culture, traditions, daily life, kindness, and incredible humility was something truly special. It gives you a completely different perspective and reminds you how much we can learn from people who live differently from us.
This is so much more than a tour. It is a genuine human experience, one that touches you deeply and stays with you long after you leave.
The village tour is an absolute MUST. Meeting the local people, seeing their everyday life, interacting with the children and families, and realizing how even a small donation can help provide food for the village makes the experience incredibly meaningful. What may feel like a small gesture to us can genuinely make a difference here.
You are not simply visiting Zanzibar. You are connecting with the real people who make this island so extraordinary.
I truly, truly recommend visiting Bilal and taking the time to discover this side of Zanzibar. And please, help spread the word. Tell your friends, recommend this experience to your hotel, and encourage other travelers to visit. The more people know about places like this, the more we can support local communities directly while experiencing something authentic and unforgettable in return.
Zanzibar is famous for its paradise beaches, but there is so much more behind them. If you come here, give yourself the chance to meet these wonderful people, listen to their stories, understand their way of life, and experience the true heart and soul of the island.
You may arrive thinking you are simply going on a spice and village tour, but you might leave with something much more valuable: a different perspective on life.
Please visit. Please support them. And most importantly, please speak about them.
Some experiences deserve more than five stars. ❤️
Highly, highly recommended.

content:
What we loved: it was authentic and supports the local village directly.
Budget extra beyond the quoted price for water/rice contributions. It's of course voluntary, but the whole village queues up for the rice after you commit to buying. I choose $20 and 20 eur (there were two shops). Bilal told us 20 euros is not enough for a bag of rice and I didn't understand how much was enough (probably because I already felt stressed about people queuing up). To be honest it was the only dent in an otherwise authentic and good experience. Having this information upfront would make it much better.
Also, prepare to be assertive when being offered to buy soap or oils, but that applies all around.
The village tour made us feel a bit uncomfortable because we were walking into peoples houses. Bilal explained villagers are grateful for the benefits it brings, but I wonder how sustainable that is. I would probably opt in for going into one home and actually sitting down to get to know the family (even if only a little).
We had an elderly person with us, so didn't go for the cooking class, but if we were to choose again I would probably go spice+cooking and pre agree for village contribution (eg. two bags of rice for $XX).

content:
This offers a fascinating and authentic introduction to the island’s famous spice heritage. During the tour, you walk through lush spice farms where you can see, smell, and taste a wide variety of spices and tropical fruits such as cloves, cinnamon, vanilla, ginger, fresh coconut,...
What makes the experience especially enjoyable is the friendly, knowledgeable and personal guidance, with explanations that are easy to follow and often interactive. You don’t just observe you actively engage by touching plants, tasting fresh produce, and learning how spices are used in both local cuisine and traditional medicine.
It was very fun with someone climbing a coconut tree which adds a playful and memorable touch to the experience.
I also did the local cooking class where you learn how to prepare local dishes using the fresh spices and ingredients you’ve just discovered. The atmosphere is relaxed and welcoming, and it’s a great opportunity to get involved, ask questions, and learn about Swahili cuisine in a very personal way.
I absolutely would recommend this!

content:
Highly recommended!
We did the Spice Tour, the Village Tour, and the Cooking Class. Everyone involved was very friendly, knowledgeable, and always helpful.
The Spice Tour offers many new impressions and insights into everyday spices. It's incredibly interesting to see the plants and raw fruits in person.
The Village Tour is fascinating. Friendly hosts in a typical village for the region. Living conditions aren't easy. You get to see traditional and modern housing and building styles. Afterward, you can support the residents by shopping at the local store. They sell classic souvenirs, sweets, and household items. The latter two support the village and are available for the children on weekends.
The Cooking Class follows. It's worth coming hungry for this, as the food is delicious! The cook cooks over five or six coals at once and makes it look effortless. The farm's spices are used liberally in all the dishes, from fish and pilau to banana dessert.
All in all, I highly recommend it!
You'll find classic souvenirs as well as sweets and household items. P.S. for my fellow Germans: The tour will be conducted in English.

content:
An incredibly impressive tour through a village and the flora of Zanzibar. Bilal, the company's founder, does amazing work in a very friendly way. The guided tour through the traditional village was deeply moving and incredibly grounding. The inhabitants live very simply and try to survive by selling their woven roofing materials, spices, and fruits. They also grow rice, but not enough. Unfortunately, it's not enough to get by, so they have two small shops selling basic foodstuffs (rice, beans, soap, diapers, and a few sweets—no, nothing from Ferrero). Anyone who wants to help can buy these items and donate them directly. Bilal raises awareness very sensitively and without pressure. And when you see the happy faces of the residents, especially the children with their lollipops, you know what €20 can do locally. I definitely had tears in my eyes. Such friendly and cheerful people, despite their very simple living conditions. After visiting the village, Ibrahim gave us a fantastic introduction to the world of spices and their uses, and I'm guessing he did it without ever having taken a sophisticated communication course. I learned some facts that I won't reveal here – I need them to show off! 😊 Of course, we also got to enjoy plenty of the local fruits (mangoes, melons, pineapples, coconuts, guavas, and bao bao, though they're not in season right now).
Booking the tour through the website is incredibly easy. Bilal responds to WhatsApp messages in no time. He also perfectly organized the transportation to and from Nungwi at a very good price. Everything was perfect – thank you, Bilal! 😍
It was an incredible day, and I'm so glad I stumbled across the website and chose this tour instead of a run-of-the-mill tourist trip.

content:
Bilal seems like a very nice and hardworking guy. My husband and I did a spice farm tour and visited his home village with him. There was no car transfer included — we used our own car and also gave him a ride. We paid $40 per person for the experience.
At the spice farm, Bilal and another young man who was helping him showed us and explained various spices, letting us smell and even taste some of them. Later, we cooked a few traditional dishes together with him and a local family (part of the farm owners), and we all shared the meal.
What I didn’t like was that, at the end of the tour, a man came over trying to sell us soap and essential oils at what I felt were very inflated prices. Another less pleasant moment was when we went to buy spices at a place Bilal took us to — again, I felt the prices were very high, just because we were tourists.
Overall, it was an enjoyable experience, but I don’t like feeling like we’re seen as just a source of money.

content:
As part of a Synchronization Journey in Zanzibar, a tour with Bilal at the spice farm is an exciting and unique experience. This journey offers not only an introduction to the variety of local spices, but also an in-depth look at the life of the local community and how they live in synergy with nature.
The tour includes a walk among rural houses, a glimpse into the shared and independent lifestyle of the residents, and an understanding of how local agriculture serves as the basis for the life of the community and the extended family. In addition, you will learn about the natural ecosystem and the ways in which spices contribute to health, nutrition, and daily life.
An integral part of the experience is tasting simple but special dishes, such as bananas cooked with cardamom, cinnamon, and coconut cream – a dish that demonstrates how the right seasoning can transform a basic dish into something extraordinary.
It is an experience that enriches all the senses and emphasizes the magic and importance of spices – not only in the kitchen, but also in everyday life.

content:
We visited Bilaly's farm, and it was wonderful. He's an ambitious young man trying to build something for himself, far from the tourist crowds on the beaches. He welcomed us to his farm and showed us all the spices during the tour, explaining how they are grown and their medicinal properties. It was truly interesting. We were allowed to taste everything on the plants, smell the leaves, and ask questions.
Towards the end of the tour, a young man climbed a palm tree especially for us and harvested fresh coconuts. We were able to taste the juice right away, and we used the coconut flesh in our meal afterward.
He then crowned us each with crowns, necklaces, bracelets, and rings he had crafted from banana leaves, making us the King and Queen of Coconuts. It was great fun!
After the tour, there was a cooking class. We cooked the local dish, Pilau, for which we had harvested all the ingredients ourselves! Spices, of course, too ;) For dessert, we had bananas cooked in coconut milk. Delicious!
In conclusion: It was a fantastic day, very educational, and the time flew by! We really hope Bilaly can build something here and we're keeping our fingers crossed!
Thank you so much for these unforgettable experiences :)

After the tour, there was a cooking class.
We cooked the local dish, Pilau, for which we had harvested all the ingredients ourselves!
Spices, of course, too ;) For dessert, we had bananas cooked in coconut milk.
Delicious!
In conclusion: It was a fantastic day, very educational, and the time flew by!
We really hope Bilaly can build something here and we're keeping our fingers crossed!
Thank you so much for these unforgettable experiences :)

content: We stumbled upon Bilal's by accident, but it was one of the best experiences we had in Zanzibar. Incredible flavors and unforgettable impressions—we'll try to recreate the dishes at home. We wholeheartedly recommend him if you're looking for something authentic. You certainly won't regret it. When we return to Zanzibar, we'll definitely visit this place, hoping that Bilal will expand his business in the future and perhaps even open his own restaurant.

content:
I walked into the Peace Memorial Museum in Stone Town without much expectation. From the street, the building looks as if it's been around for generations.
A white, round rotunda, old walls, shaded by palm trees. It was built in the early twentieth century, when Zanzibar was still a British protectorate.
The architect was John Sinclair, the same one who designed the Zanzibar House of Wonders. The architecture is a mixture of many elements: Arabic lines, a touch of colonial style, local plaster, and a feeling of the hot east coast.
Inside, the museum is simple, a bit chaotic, but there's a certain honesty to it. Old photographs of sultans, weapons, nautical charts, trade documents, and items from local homes are on display.
The exhibits look tired in places, but the objects themselves are powerful. The island's history is difficult, especially considering that Zanzibar was long a major center for the slave trade and maritime trade between Arabia, India, and East Africa.
I spent about an hour there. I walked slowly, reading the signs, listening to footsteps in the empty halls. I felt like I'd entered a place that remembers more than it tells. It's as if the museum stands at the junction of eras, where the colonial world, Arab culture, and African life have mingled and still remain connected.
If you love history and want to see Zanzibar not just from the beaches but through its roots, it's worth a visit. It's a quiet place, a little worn, but vibrant.

The Freddie Mercury display is beyond good and evil.
It's very sad that the museum is in such a state. It does have some interesting exhibits. I hope funding will be increased, renovations will be done, and better times will come for the museum.

content:
This is at the southern end of stone town, near the junction of creek road and kaunda road in the area called Mnazi Moja. It is also known by its local title: Beit El Amani (House of Peace). With its distinctive dome, arabesque windows and whitewashed walls, the building looks like a mosque or basilica church. It was designed by the British architect J H Sinclair, who also designed the high court, the British residency and several other public buildings around Zanzibar town.
'Museum' is a misnomer nowadays, as virtually all its viewable exhibits have been shifted to the rapidly developing museum in the House of Wonders and the place now serves as a library. Its well-known giant tortoises have been transferred to Prison Island.

content:
Disappointing and Disturbing Experience at Jozani Forest
I visited Jozani Forest hoping to witness the rare and critically endangered red colobus monkeys in their natural habitat. Unfortunately, what I saw was far from respectful or responsible wildlife tourism.
Despite clear rules to keep a 3-meter distance from the monkeys, many tourists completely ignored them—getting far too close, even standing on or over the animals to get their photos. The monkeys appeared visibly stressed, and it was heartbreaking to watch.
Even more concerning was the behavior of the guides. Rather than ensuring the safety and well-being of the animals, they seemed more focused on collecting tips and pleasing the tourists. I saw no efforts made to correct or guide inappropriate behavior. It felt chaotic and disrespectful.
We left early, unable to continue watching such blatant disregard for the welfare of these beautiful, vulnerable animals. I hope real conservation efforts are implemented soon—before it's too late for the red colobus monkeys.

Despite other discouraging reviews, we recommend the experience.

content:
This excursion is not worth it!
The park entrance fee is $12 USD per person, including a guide (not including tips, which the guide reminded us of several times during the visit).
We ended up with a guide who only gave us two 15-minute tours, without providing any explanation about the forest, the monkeys, or even the mangroves.
The first tour was supposedly about exploring the Jozani Forest, but we spent a good 20 minutes under a tree by the roadside watching monkeys (very cute, by the way) while the guide shouted into his phone. Then we entered the forest, walked 200 meters, and then returned to the starting point…
The second tour was a visit to the mangroves located 1.5 kilometers from the forest, where we walked 200 meters on a wooden boardwalk built in the mangroves before returning to the starting point. Beware if you don't have a car! The guide drove us but wanted to charge us for the ride!
A word of advice: avoid this place!

-On special days here in Zanzibar, don't even think of visiting this place, children might get lost, the queues are gonna be too long so u might as well visit just on a random normal weekend day.
-Id think they operate on work days.
-For me as a Zanzibari, i qould dwf recommend the Mtoni Marine Waterpark next to Hotel Verde more. And ride-wise, i would recommend the Legends in Kisakasaka, ofc not special days. Thank you for reading.

La Casa de las Maravillas o el Palacio de las Maravillas (en árabe: Beit-al-Ajaib, بيت العجايب) es un edificio emblemático en Stone Town, Zanzíbar, Tanzania.
Es el edificio más grande y más alto de Stone Town, ubicado entre el Fuerte Viejo y el antiguo Palacio del Sultán.
Es uno de los 6 palacios construidos por Barghash bin Said, segundo sultán de Zanzíbar, y se dice que está ubicado en el sitio del palacio de la reina Fatuma, quien vivió en el siglo XVII.
La Casa de las Maravillas alberga actualmente el Museo de Historia y Cultura de Zanzíbar y la costa Suajili.
El palacio fue construido en 1883 para Barghash bin Said, segundo sultán de Zanzíbar.
Fue concebido como un palacio ceremonial y sala de recepción oficial, celebrando la modernidad. Por eso fue nombrado 'Casa de las Maravillas'" porque fue el primer edificio en Zanzíbar con electricidad

content:
*House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib)*
History
- Built in 1883 by Sultan Bargash bin Said
- Served as a palace and a repository for Zanzibar's treasures
- Damaged by British warship HMS Philomel in 1896
- Restored in 2010-2012
Attractions for Tourists
1. *Exhibition halls*: Showcasing Zanzibar's history, culture, and natural environment
2. *Historic artifacts*: Including furniture, jewelry, and other relics from the palace
3. *Zanzibar's oldest elevator*: Built in 1883, it's one of the oldest in Africa
4. *Panoramic views*: Of Stone Town and the harbor from the top floor
Food and Beverages
1. *Traditional Zanzibari cuisine*: Including dishes like urojo (a spicy soup), mandazi (fried doughnuts), and chapati (flatbread)
2. *Seafood*: Fresh catches from the Indian Ocean, often served grilled or in curries
3. *Local fruits*: Like mangoes, coconuts, and pineapples
4. *Coffee and tea*: Served in traditional cafes and restaurants
Tips for Visitors
1. *Dress modestly*: Respect local customs and traditions
2. *Remove shoes*: When entering the palace or mosques
3. *Respect local rules*: No photography in certain areas, and no touching of artifacts
4. *Haggle politely*: When shopping in local markets
The House of Wonders is a must-visit attraction in Stone Town, Zanzibar. Its rich history, cultural significance, and stunning architecture make it an unforgettable experience.

content:
It was once the largest and most impressive house in Stone Town. Unfortunately, it's now closed (November 2022) due to the risk of collapse.
In 1883, a British naval officer built the house on behalf of Sultan Bargash. It was the first house, perhaps even in Africa, to feature Western technology: electric light, running water, a flushing toilet, and an elevator. Hence its name, the House of Wonders. The house combines Arabic and Victorian architectural styles. We don't know if or when it will reopen, but no construction activity was visible. 🤔

content:
The House of Wonders or Palace of Wonders (in Arabic: Beit-al-Ajaib, بيت العجايب) is a landmark building in Stone Town, Zanzibar. It is the largest and tallest building of Stone Town and occupies a prominent place facing the Forodhani Gardens on the old town's seafront, in Mizingani Road. It is located between the Old Fort and the Palace Museum (and former Sultan's Palace). It is one of six palaces built by Barghash bin Said, second Sultan of Zanzibar, and it is said to be located on the site of the 17th-century palace of Zanzibari queen Fatuma.[1] The House of Wonders currently houses the Museum of History and Culture of Zanzibar and the Swahili Coast.
The palace was built in 1883 for Barghash bin Said

content:
|The House of Wonders was once the most modern building in East Africa—it was the first building to have electricity and an elevator—and it mixes elements of European style and Zanzibari tradition by including cast iron columns, elaborate door carvings, coral rag, open central courtyards, and mangrove ceilings that together form a truly unique architectural achievement. Just next to it is the Palace Museum, built by the second sultan of Zanzibar in 1883, which is an opulent palace comprised of beautiful marble flooring, coral stone walls, and silver decorations. The palace was built in the Omani style as an extravagant Arab mansion, and holds many relics that offer a rare glimpse of a past era. The House of Wonders and Palace Museum have been converted into popular cultural destinations; the House of Wonders presents exhibitions dedicated to Swahili culture and the Palace Museum highlights its ties to Zanzibar's Omani history. |
Location: Unguja Island, Zanzibar city Tanzania.

content:
Nungwi Beach is truly beautiful. The white sand, the color of the water, and the scenery are spectacular.
Unfortunately, our experience was significantly marred by the sheer number of vendors and people constantly offering services.
While walking along the beach, you're approached repeatedly with offers of excursions, souvenirs, massages, and all sorts of other services. I wouldn't mind someone approaching you once to offer something; I completely understand they're trying to make a living. The problem is the frequency and, above all, the persistence. Often, politely saying "no, thank you" isn't enough.
Some people continue walking beside you, asking questions or trying to maintain a conversation even after you've made it clear you're not interested. When this happens every few minutes, something as simple as a peaceful walk on the beach becomes exhausting instead of relaxing.
My partner also felt particularly uncomfortable with the amount of attention she received, which made it even harder for us to enjoy the beach.
Hopefully, in the future they can manage this situation better so that visitors can enjoy such a spectacular place without feeling constantly harassed.

content: Zanzibar's beaches boast dazzling white sand and turquoise waters. Choosing the perfect beach depends on your preferences, so here are a few tips: For year-round swimming (no tides): Nungwi and Kendwa, located in the north of the island. These areas allow you to swim all day and offer magnificent sunsets. For kitesurfing and a local atmosphere: Paje, on the east coast, is a world-renowned spot for watersports enthusiasts, lined with lively cafes. For tranquility and authenticity: Jambiani and Matemwe offer wild and unspoiled stretches of coastline, ideal for long walks and snorkeling. You can explore these different locations and organize excursions through specialized platforms or simply ask the locals; they are very kind and help tourists with a big heart and without any sarcasm.

content:
Nungwi Beach is a beach in Tanzania, located in northern Zanzibar. It's a shame that such a beautiful beach loses all its charm due to the beach boys; they don't leave you alone, day or night. It's impossible to relax on these beaches.
What makes it special is its white sand, turquoise waters, and ideal sea for swimming for most of the day, even at low tide. Unlike other beaches on the island, the water here is usually more accessible. The beach contrasts sharply with the poverty inland, with high-end beach bars and beach boys right on the sand, and just 30 meters away... absolute poverty.
The sunsets are especially beautiful, with the traditional dhow boats creating a spectacular scene. In short, Nungwi Beach is a skippable stop in Zanzibar. A comfortable and different beach to enjoy the sea and the tropical atmosphere. If you can, look for other, more authentic options.
2025

We spent the day at Nungwi beach (northern part of the island) to jet ski and take a sunset cruise. It is a very busy and touristy part of the island (we stayed on the south east coast). The water is absolutely amazing and good vibes all round but the roads and parts of the beach are very busy.
Sunset Cruise on a Dhow: the entire experience lasted from about 4pm to 7pm. There is music on board, traditional songs and instruments. They also served fresh tropical fruit and drinks (drinks cost extra). At one point they stopped and allowed to jump off into the water, which my husband enjoyed! All in all a lovely experience!
Jet skis: we took a shorter ride option and it was safe and lots of fun! We negotiated the price down.
Be prepared with umbrella/chairs, else you pay to have shade and a lounger.
You will be approached by lots of locals trying to sell their services for jet skis and cruises, be prepared. We had our own guide with us so it was easy enough to avoid long talks etc. Understand that this is their way of earning a living, and they must make the most of the busy season as the island basically shuts down in the rainy months.

content:
Nungwi is exactly the type of beach where you realize why you travel thousands of kilometers for “ordinary” sand and sea. Fine white sand, turquoise water and palm trees like from a catalog, but without the sterile feeling of an artificial paradise. This is where it lives.
A big plus: minimal low tide. Unlike other parts of Zanzibar, you can swim practically all day, which sounds banal until you experience it elsewhere. The sea is calm, warm and ideal for swimming or just “standing in the water and staring into space”.
The atmosphere is a mix of local life and relaxed tourism. Fishing boats, Masai, beach boys, restaurants right on the sand, sunsets that really don’t deserve a filter. Nungwi is not a quiet haven for hermits – it’s a lively beach, but not annoying.
Food? Fresh fish, shrimp, octopus, simple beach bars and better restaurants. Prices are fair, if you know when to smile and when to say no politely.
Cons? More people, especially in high season, and sometimes overly active vendors. But honestly – that’s the price of a place that works.
Verdict:
Nungwi Beach is one of the best beaches in Zanzibar. Not only pretty for photos, but really great to stay. If you want a beach where you can live, swim, eat, drink and watch the sunset in the evening without thinking about the time – Nungwi is the right choice.

content:
The beach itself is genuinely stunning, with luminous turquoise water and a fascinating underwater landscape. Snorkelling is a treat: curious fish glide right up to you and the underwater reefs are beautiful . I also spotted three sea snakes with striking black-and-white bands, beautiful but venomous, so awareness is essential. As well as the cone snails to make sure you are aware of those and to avoid them. Lionfish, a lone jellyfish, and an abundance of sea urchins make appearances too, so reef shoes and a snorkelling mask are highly recommended.
That said, relaxing on the beach can be a challenge. You are frequently approached by vendors selling everything imaginable. While it’s easy to understand the economic reality behind this, the constant interruptions can be exhausting. The people are however quite respectful of a no thank you. The people on the beach too offering dolphin yoirs is something to research, they are often not licensed, uneducated about marine conservation and often do more harm to the natural life and harass the dolphins. I would recommend doing dolphin tours through the aquariums who actually add to marine conservation and do good.
All of this aside, the beach truly is beautiful. I would recommend staying somewhere with security or choosing a quieter, less crowded stretch of sand usualy at the end of the beach, and keeping your wits about you at all times. With the right precautions, it’s a place well worth experiencing

content:
Our guide took us to Nungwi, a traditional fishing village, not just a beautiful beach. This place made a huge impression on us. We saw carpenters hand-building a mahogany boat – an incredible process, without machinery, just craftsmanship and the strength of their hands. We also walked along the local houses. We could see women and children sitting at the entrances; there were so many children… The houses are very dark, and their condition reflects the early days of settlement.
We also visited the fish market, where fresh fish were being processed straight from the catch. We even stumbled upon an auction, vibrant, loud, and authentic, as if from another world.
The beach around the village is gorgeous! The white sand and the views are breathtaking. The contrast between the beauty of nature and the harsh everyday life of a fishing village is thought-provoking. It's a place that makes you stop for a moment and appreciate what WE have... 🥹
An incredible, valuable experience... not just for tourism, but for life.

content:
We have been going to Nungwi since 2010. Almost every year. This year was unfortunately the last time we visited Nungwi.
The Nungwi we've come to love, the Nungwi that's advertised, does not exist any more. What you will find now is a huge tourist trap.
Prices for everything is inflated now, and almost everywhere quoted in usd. You must ask to get a shilling price. The beaches and town is dirty, which always was the case. But now it's much worse.
The beaches are at times totally crowded. Literally hundreds of fake Masai everywhere. Look, there were always beach boys trying to sell you something. But now it's just gone nuts. In the late afternoon one can not walk on the public beaches without being harrased constantly. Not even mentioning any young female walking on the beach, having to deal with all the fake Massai guys trying to get friendly.
Take it from someone who's seen the Nungwi you see on advertisements now. It does not exist in Nungwi anymore. Sad but true.
