content:
I give this 2 stars for a few reasons. It is a lovely white sandy beach with beautiful turquoise water which is like getting into a bath it’s so warm, this is definitely has that Caribbean feel to it in Africa! Sections of the beach are private to hotels where others are more open which creates that buzzing bustling atmosphere with locals filling up for sundown,
Unfortunately I have to state this because I feel it will eventually ruin what is right now a beautiful destination albeit still a developing tourist location, but the waste and pollution Iv seen along the beach in the sea and on the sand especially during low tide is quite hard to look at. I managed to fill a bin up just during an afternoon in the sea,
I know the people are all doing there best and are lovely people but if there was some kind of incentive to help reduce and remove waste and recycle correctly it would do wonders for their main attraction.
Which goes to say about the beach boys, Iv done enough travelling to comfortably and politely steer away from them, but they seem to focus on young ladies on their own or groups applying a lot of pressure to buy local gifts from their associated shops, I know they’re doing what they have to earn money but this will put people off coming and give Zanzibar a bad name if it continues,
Otherwise yes I loved it here the beach area is quite small in non private sections when the tide is in but there are some nice relaxing beach bars you can also use.

content: Nungwi Beach is located on the shores of the village of the same name, in the north of Unguja Island. This island is the largest in the Zanzibar metropolitan area, and therefore is often referred to as "Zanzibar." Nungwi is one of the most densely populated villages on the island, not counting the capital, of course. It is primarily a fishing village, with its corresponding attributes. The Indian Ocean at this beach is warm and clear, mostly shallow in the coastal zone. As this is a fishing harbor, hundreds of traditional sailing fishing boats can be seen in the ocean. There are numerous starfish here, visible when walking in the shallow water at low tide. Sea urchins are almost absent, though they are abundant closer to the lighthouse. Low tides here reach a maximum of 500 meters, which is quite a bit. Therefore, low tide here is a fun way to walk along the ocean floor behind the receding water. The sand line is up to 50 meters wide, even at high tide. The beach is much wider in the section closer to the village of Kendwa. However, in Nungwi, the beach is also wide enough, even for playing soccer. The sand is white and fine as flour. The beach is very well-developed in terms of infrastructure. There are numerous restaurants, decent shops, souvenir stalls, and wonderful locals, who are a unique experience.

content: You arrive – and suddenly time stands still. The sand lies before you like sifted powdered sugar, dazzling white, soft as sleep, interspersed with tiny, pale blue stones that look like polished drops of the sky. They say they only exist here – noni stones, half myth, half memory. The sea? White. Clear. Immaculate. So pure it would seem like sparkling water – if it weren't so salty. 26 to 28 degrees Celsius, liquid light on your skin. No water. A temptation. Red and blue starfish glow between the waves, so clear it's as if someone forgot to turn them off. The sun? Non-existent. A magnifying glass. Anyone who walks along the beach for fifteen minutes without sunscreen or shade – even though the thermometer only reads 30°C – will burn their skin like in a microwave. Level three. Free. The ozone layer seems to exist here only as a memory. Shade is only found under the palm trees, and even they look stern. Sunscreen? SPF 50 is the polite start. Forgetting it makes you part of the geology – red like coral, silent like rocks. And yet: you stay. Because this beach – Nungwi, in the far north of Zanzibar – doesn't just dazzle, it transforms. There are guesthouses that seem like lost poems, two shops with everything and nothing, and they serve you the best fish barefoot, right at the grill, while the sea doesn't recede. There's low tide here too – but it comes quietly. No great retreat, just a whisper, a brief unveiling of the underworld before the sea reclaims it. Like a breath, not a withdrawal. And then: a tuna, yellow and blue like a painting, caught by fishermen, later served on the grill right on the beach. Smoke mingles with the salt air and the music of a guitar that no one is really playing – it emerges through the whisper of the wind, in the rustling of the palm trees swaying in the breeze. And they listen. Just like you. The place doesn't speak. It answers. Anyone heading south from here to Stone Town – about two hours – should budget between 40 and 70 euros for a taxi, or even 80 depending on their bargaining skills. I myself paid 70 euros from the airport to the Hilton in Nungwi – a fair deal. And it's worth it. In Stone Town, the narrow streets are fragrant with rosemary and fennel – a small Italian pizzeria, run by a woman from Abruzzo, bakes pizzas just like Mamma used to. They say she has the flour delivered directly from Italy – and you believe it when, in the hot streets, you suddenly think you can smell Naples. Anyone who's seen the film will also love visiting Freddie Mercury's birthplace – a small museum, a guided tour, a few minutes in which you feel like you're taking a step closer to him. And then there's Turtle Island – accessible by small boat. Some of the oldest animals in the world, they say. A hundred years old, some even older. And strong – so strong you'd think they could carry you. You can feed them, you can pet them – it's like a retirement home on the other side of the water, where time moves more slowly. And if you look closely: the old doors in Stone Town – massive, clad in iron – were built to keep elephants out. They used to roam these alleys. Now they're just stories. And somewhere among the shadows of these houses sit men making leather shoes, measured by foot, sewn by hand. A different pace, a different world. And then you're back. There, where the sky touches the sea, where the horizon seduces the dolphins with colors, consciousness hits you like a slap in the face – you recognize yourself… and forget your poem. The tuna isn't simply fried there, no – first charmingly advised by the waves, it leaps onto the grill with a hint of lemon – that was a meal. January 14-28

content:
Disappointed is the word. My visit to Zanzibar has been a profound disappointment, far removed from the idyllic image it usually projects. The experience has been marked by a series of negative points that have left me with a constant feeling of frustration and, at times, of being ripped off.
First of all, the initial costs are surprisingly high. Not only is transportation to the island expensive, but they also require payment for entry insurance, despite already having travel insurance purchased in my home country. This duplication of expenses is, to say the least, unjustifiable and makes you feel like you're being taken advantage of from the very beginning.
Hygiene is another of the most critical and disheartening aspects. The island is extremely dirty, with plastic and trash everywhere. The beaches, which should be the main attraction, are sadly polluted, marring the landscape and making the experience of enjoying them unpleasant. It's truly shocking to see such a level of environmental neglect in a place that depends on tourism.
Furthermore, the feeling of being constantly ripped off is palpable. Prices for tourists are blatantly higher than for locals, making you feel exploited in every transaction, from buying a simple souvenir to haggling over a service or taking the bus. To get from Stone Town to Nungwi, I was charged 10,000 tzh one way, while it costs locals 2,500, and then 5,000 tzh the return trip. It makes no sense. While food in restaurants can be affordable, eating on the street is a gamble and often results in being financially ripped off.
The only redeeming quality of my stay was the friendliness of the people. However, even this is overshadowed by their constant push to sell you something, which, while understandable in a tourist context, can become exhausting. Compared to my experience on the Tanzanian mainland, where I felt much more comfortable and at ease, Zanzibar didn't give me that sense of home or authenticity. I definitely feel let down and I, for one, will not be returning.

Zanzibar is actually really disappointing for me, online you see a paradise with beautiful beaches, people snorkelling and swimming with turtles but in reality it’s not at all glamorous, there is rubbish all over the ground everywhere you go, people are living in super run down houses right next to massive fancy hotels, low tide is during the middle of the day so all of the beaches you want to swim at are just sand and reef until high tide at night time and it’s EXPENSIVE. There are much nicer places with lovely beaches that you can travel to for much cheaper and are easier to get around! (Thailand and the Philippines especially)
As a young person travelling Africa with a currency that’s not USD, Euro or Pound (we’re travelling on the Australian dollar -Aud) it’s been pretty reasonable with the conversion but in Zanzibar specifically it’s been crazy expensive, they try to charge everything in USD so trying to hire a moped or scooter for three days they wanted not only $60 USD for the hire ($97 Aud) but also $15 USD ($25 Aud) for a “government driving permit” even when we both have an international license or an IDP (international driving permit) that’s the second “government” fee we’ve come across because you now have to get mandatory Zanzibar insurance when entering at the airport which was $45 USD ($73 Aud) aswell as the Visa I needed for entrance to Tanzania which was $50 USD ($80 Aud) what is the government doing with all this money they’re extorting from tourists if it’s not to try clean up atleast some of the rubbish that’s everywhere, making nice roads or helping with peoples housing.
All of the restaurant menus are in USD and obviously not what the local price is because what local is paying $7 USD ($12 Aud) for a stew, no one. It’s just frustrating because they do obviously make their livings off of tourists (especially the middle age demographic of Americans) which is what you would expect from a popular destination like this but it’s pushing the price of everything up for everyone else. It’s disappointing as someone who loves to travel because of course things cost money but this has got to a point of actually just being ridiculous.
We’re staying where we heard most people stay in Jambiani which was an hour from the airport (it cost us 90,000 TZS/ $35 USD which is $56 Aud) because they only do taxi there’s no ride share app in Zanzibar so trying to get to and from the airport is crazy expensive.
So because we’re staying in Jambiani if we wanted to go and do a snorkelling tour, the turtle sanctuary cave or anything like that it’s all up on the top of the island (roughly a 2 hour drive) in Matemwe which would already be hard on a rented scooter but because the scooter hire is expensive we’d have to try get either a tuk tuk, taxi or on the back of a motorbike all the way there and back for the day it would be not only hard to find someone who would do it but also costly as well, so if you’re planning on doing those things while in Zanzibar (snorkelling tour, swimming with dolphins, turtle sanctuary cave, anything like that) it’s most likely up near Matemwe so definitely spend the extra money on accommodation up there to save the hassle of trying to get there.
Zanzibar is a tourist scam. End of story.

content:
A great large beach at the northernmost tip of Zanzibar.
There’s plenty of space to walk along the shore or swim along the coast. White sand, calm warm water. The tides can be quite noticeable, especially in the area where women collect seaweed. But that’s part of the charm — watching them work and walking through the shallow water yourself.
You can swim, snorkel, ride horses, get a massage, or buy souvenirs, which are offered in abundance here. Nungwi has many restaurants, so you won’t go hungry. The best beachfront restaurants in Zanzibar are found here. You can enjoy a wide variety of cuisines, including a rarity for Tanzania — delicious desserts.
The vendors and dressed-up Maasai can be a bit annoying, but it’s the most touristy place apart from Stone Town. The beach is suitable for families, couples, groups, and solo travelers. The weather is always nice, and the water of the Indian Ocean is warm.

content: Nungwi Beach is often praised as a paradise, but my experience was far from it. The beach is overrated, with limited swimming time due to low tides in the morning and high tides from 3 PM onwards. The constant harassment by beach boys and fake Maasai trying to sell items or scam tourists is overwhelming, which explains why the beach is nearly empty—most tourists stay in their resorts to avoid the hassle. The beach itself is dirty, littered with plastic bottles and broken glass, and is strewn with seaweed, making it far less beautiful than the picturesque images suggest. The only positive aspect is the stunning sunset landscape, but even that isn't enough to redeem the overall experience. The beauty seen in photos only represents a small portion of the beach at specific times of the year. I wouldn’t return and wouldn’t recommend staying more than 2 nights.

content:
Pushy and disrespectful people (Marsais)
Unfortunately, we couldn't relax on the beach because every five minutes a vendor would approach us trying to sell us something. It's not inherently bad, but everyone wants to talk to you for four to six minutes before selling you anything, and if you don't want to, they become disrespectful.
My wife and mother were harassed, and when I said enough was enough and to move along, I was told that this was my country and that I should go back to Europe.
I've been to many countries, including some with pushy people, like Turkey, Morocco, and Egypt,
but I've NEVER seen anything like this.
There are so many beautiful beaches in the world, like in Indonesia, Mexico, Australia, and the Maldives.
This isn't the Zanzibar you see on Instagram.
I can only warn you: go somewhere else.
If you've already booked, go to a gated resort.

content:
In the north (ZaVa Nungwi restaurant and up north), there is a lot of activity with locals going about their daily business. Cows are on the beach, and there are many fishing boats in the water. Unfortunately, there is also a lot of garbage lying around, and the smell can be quite strong.
Further down in the south (around The Z Hotel), there are many restaurants, bars, and small shops to enjoy, but also many tourists, several beach boys, and Masaais, which can be overwhelming at times.
I highly recommend snorkeling in the area between The Sands Baobab and The Z Hotel. There are many colorful fish to observe. If you're lucky you can see moray eels, sea snakes or lionfish. Bring bathing shoes to protect your feet from the sea urchins and rocks.
One highlight is the sunset on this side!

content:
The road to Nungwi immediately gives you a sense of what a trip to this corner of Africa is like. Palm trees everywhere, people between cars, local shops that I have no idea what they were selling, lights nowhere, potholes that forced car owners to change their tires every 2 months, scattered houses with tin roofs, honking good mornings and smiles. The hotels are lined up on the beach, which is closed to locals and who can only access it from the village side. We visited 1 of the 3 schools in the village and after talking for a while with the teachers we gave stationery and toys to the children and took pictures with them after asking first of course. In Nungwi there is the phenomenon of tides and beach boys (whom we deal with with patience and kindness because they can be a little persistent but are generally polite and relaxed. If we say a polite and decisive no they will walk away saying hakuna matata, answer the same..)
All hotels have restaurants with traditional food pizzas fries pasta soups burgers seafood and alcohol. In the village there are bars and restaurants which we did not visit, but we did shop for local products and souvenirs (necklaces bracelets, fabrics, landscapes on banana leaves, paintings, wood carvings, drums and more). Support the locals!!. Except for those who sell shells and starfish (it is illegal). Among all of us are the young Maasai, a tribe that lives in the Serengeti desert from northern Tanzania, who have their own style and different way of approaching things (I should say that a little Maasai who followed us every day on our walk on the beach at low tide gave us a necklace as a gift..he was a very sweet and shy child). From Nungwi you can go to Mnemba for snorkeling, walk in Stone Town, to Nakupenda, visit Prison Island for its history and to see the huge turtles and take a sunset cruise.. we did all of that and it was all perfect ✨(all via beach boy Ricky). In Nungwi almost everyone speaks English because it is the second official language of the country. I think the important thing is to give these people a chance to talk to you, to get to know a little about their culture and their way of life, and they are all willing to tell you everything, about their family and the bond they feel, the political indifference and corruption, about the schools and the tuition they are forced to pay, while those who don't have them simply don't get an education, about their difficult living but everyone in the end smiles at you and says hakuna matata..no problem..!!!!!
I love you guys ❤️❤️❤️
ps: they don't care about the starfish that stay behind the low tide...a few seconds are enough for a single photo... out of water they die!!! We saw other tourists having these unfortunate beautiful animals out of the water for 3-4 and 5 minutes to take photos and selfies in all possible poses. Stop this..
Also be aware that at the airport, starfish shells raise an alarm and are confiscated..this does not offer anything to the animal, but it is a way to prevent theft from the sea or illegal trade..

content:
Immerse yourself in the tranquil waters of the Indian Ocean at Nungwi Beach in Zanzibar. This idyllic destination offers a serene and relaxing experience for those seeking to unwind and enjoy the beauty of the ocean.
As you step onto the soft white sands of Nungwi Beach, you'll be greeted by the crystal-clear waters of the Indian Ocean. The calmness of the sea creates a peaceful atmosphere, perfect for swimming, snorkeling, or simply floating in the gentle waves.
Dive beneath the surface and discover a vibrant underwater world teeming with colorful marine life. The coral reefs near Nungwi Beach provide an excellent opportunity for snorkelers and scuba divers to explore and observe the diverse ecosystem that thrives beneath the surface.
If you prefer a more laid-back experience, find a comfortable spot on the beach and listen to the soothing sound of the waves. Feel the warm sun on your skin as you relax under the shade of palm trees, letting the gentle ocean breeze wash away any worries or stress.
For the ultimate tranquility, consider booking a sunset cruise or a dhow sailing trip. Drift along the calm waters as the sun sets on the horizon, painting the sky with vibrant hues of orange, pink, and gold. It's a magical experience that will leave you in awe of nature's beauty.
Whether you choose to dive into the inviting waters or simply bask in the peaceful ambiance, the tranquil waters of the Indian Ocean at Nungwi Beach provide a serene escape from the hustle and bustle of everyday life. It's an experience that rejuvenates the mind, body, and soul, leaving you with lasting memories of tranquility by the sea.

We prefer a quiet corner of the island where we can be left in peace to enjoy the place.

content:
Superb beaches, divided into three distinct sections: the eastern section towards Kwenda, with its hotels and restaurants on stilts, diving clubs, and the tourist boat port—an area that isn't always very affordable.
Then there's the cape with its fish market and fishing port, and a fabulous beach restaurant between the Koranic school and the fish market.
Finally, the western section, past the Nungwi lighthouse, boasts a long, continuous beach accessible at low tide and during spring tides, and a string of hotels of varying quality. There are many touts offering excursions and Maasai people ready to take advantage of tourists with smiles and friendliness, but not always at the best prices. Avoid going to the beach alone at night to avoid ending up without even underwear (a misadventure experienced by an Englishman staying at the hotel)...
However, be aware that uncontrolled overexploitation of the beach (fishing for octopus, fish, crustaceans and shrimp, and harvesting of shellfish) and the reefs is sterilizing the area...

content:
I was told that this is one of the best beaches in Zanzibar, but after visiting it I have to say that I do not agree with this general opinion.
I have to say that I visited it on a cloudy day, which may have made me see it differently, but I walked along the entire beach and what I saw was a dirty beach, full of seaweed and full of fishing boats, quite far from an idyllic beach.
There were also many buildings (restaurants, hotels) built on the beach, on wooden pillars, which occupied the beach and that when the tide rises the sand disappears and it is difficult to walk on it.
On the other hand, very positive, it is a beach full of local life, since there are many local fishermen working on their boats, and children and women are continuously on the sand, playing or waiting for the men with their catches ... or even herds of cows sunbathing on the beach.
I should visit it on a sunny day and maybe my perception would be different... but even so, the walk was very pleasant.

content: Nungwi Beach is magnificent, although quite small compared to neighboring Kendwa. The sand is so white it's practically impossible to walk around without sunglasses. The sea is azure, especially beautiful on sunny days. The water has both high and low tides. At sunset, around 6:00 PM, the ocean begins to recede by 100-150 meters, and around 1:00 PM, it begins to rise, and by 4:00 PM, you can swim. During the day, Kendwa Beach is a 15-minute walk away; the low tide there is virtually nonexistent, or no more than 25-50 meters. The olive grove has its advantages – you can admire starfish and other ocean inhabitants while walking along the ocean floor. Bring coral slippers for walking. There are several restaurants and bars on the beach, as well as two liquor stores. Prices are quite reasonable. Between the Coco Cabana and Gelato Italiano restaurants, the small stretch of beach is filled with annoying beach boys, offering excursions and other things every five minutes. If you don't be friendly and start a conversation, they'll leave. But by sunset, this can get pretty annoying, which is a big minus. Between these restaurants, there's an excellent bar right on the shore with cold drinks. You can sit under an umbrella and watch the sunset. Five minutes from the beach, there's a minimarket, a pharmacy, and inexpensive fruit and souvenirs in the village. Bargain, bargain, and bargain some more.

content:
A fascinating and well managed addition to Zanzibar's tourist attractions.
It's a welcome short break from the beach, and shows you a completely different side to the island.
Good for couples, groups and families, and easily accessible with a short drive from any hotels on the north-east coast.
This cave system is in a vast & beautiful protected forest.
There's a professional reception area with good washrooms.
You take a guided walk through the forest and descend down some steps into the caves. You get to walk quite a distance comfortably, past wonderful natural rock sculpures, stalegmites & stalegtites, and tiny bats clinging to the roof of the cave. Look out for the beautiful sparkling crystal rock, and then you get to the 'Kiwengwa Challenge' area, where the cave tightens and gets very low, and you have to crawl a few metres on the ground till you emerge into a bright little grotto, open to the sky and surrounded by forest creepers. You don't have to do this, but it's good fun & worth it for the end view. Be prepared to get very dirty! You need good walking shoes - and don't wear your best clothes..
The attention to safety & conservation is impressive. You are guided to stay on the forest tracks to avoid the sink holes into the cave below, given safety helmets & torches, and advised not to touch the rock formations or shine light onto the bats.
The management is committed to protesting the forest flora & fauna.
There are several lovely forest trails you can also take.
The temperature is cooler, the birdlife is interesting, there are butterflies, and there are red colobus and blue monkeys.
You can spend just an hour, or more there, and it's definitely worth the trip!

content: We went there as a family and paid $3 per person. We were given helmets and flashlights. The guide was very relaxed and explained that the cave belongs to the government, but nobody really cares. We had asked because there were no signs along the road. content:

Some sections of the cave require crawling through narrow passages if you want to see everything, though even without that, you can explore about 75% of the cave comfortably. Of course, I left a generous tip as a thank-you for such a great experience, and Khalid was genuinely happy about it.
Highly recommended for anyone looking for something authentic and adventurous!

content:
The Kiwengwa Caves are located in the Kiwengwa-Pongwe Forest Reserve. These limestone caves extend over more than 150 meters and offer a fascinating underground ecosystem.
The caves are rich in stalactites and stalagmites, formed by the dissolution of calcium carbonate from coral rock. Various bat species, insects, and birds live inside the caves. Visitors can also see impressive tree roots and bark growing through the caves. Historically, local residents visited the caves to venerate their ancestors and made offerings at sacred stones.
Very nice caves for a reasonable price. Kassim was a nice guide who told us all sorts of things. I won't give everything away. In short, highly recommended.
PS I know a good guide with a van for a good price who can drive you around the island. You book him for a whole day. He knows nice spots and is very helpful. PM me for more info about this.

content:
Great company, great owner. We were staying near this beach, and from our accommodation, we were offered a dolphin-watching excursion for $100 USD for two people. So we decided to compare prices. The owner gave us the best offer directly, without any haggling, which saved us time. We also tried the excursion to Nungwi, which was cheaper (around $50 USD for two), but it was a shared tour with eight other people, and we didn't want to drive 50 minutes for that. So we contacted the owner the day before. He had prepared a large quantity of fruit for us, much more than we needed for two. His customer service was excellent: he asked for our feedback and made sure the skippers didn't pressure us to come back. We saw dolphins and were able to swim with them three out of four times. We then went snorkeling in one or two spots before relaxing on the sandbar. The sandbar was magnificent, one of the most beautiful beaches I've ever seen. We could have gone snorkeling again, but the water was starting to get a bit cold, so we decided against it. Some people have found starfish here.
The service was very professional. We had a local guide named Cappuccino, and the captain's name was Mobi. Cappuccino guided us in the water and also had a buoy with him for our safety throughout our snorkeling trip.
The journey from this beach to the dolphin watching site took longer than expected. Due to the low tide and shallow draft, the boat moved very slowly the whole way. It took almost an hour round trip. Factor this into your total time. We chose to leave at 7:30 a.m. (we left around 7:40 a.m.) and returned just after 12:10 p.m.
To avoid the crowds, I suggested leaving at 6:30 am as the owner had suggested, but that was too early, so we asked for 7:30 am. There were already a lot of boats. If you want to take pictures of the dolphins, be sure to do so before you go snorkeling, because you won't be able to turn back to see them again once they've left.

content:
A wonderful place to pass the time while waiting for food at the attached Bashasha Restaurant.
The tour begins with an introduction to the life stages of a butterfly, complete with plenty of visual aids. Before continuing, we were asked if we wanted to see a domesticated bushbaby. Of course, the children did. The guide then took it out of its sleeping box and held it. We were able to take photos, and the children could gently pet it. Contrary to other reviews, he never let go of it; in fact, he pointed out that this wasn't allowed. After the photo session, he let it run back into its sleeping box on its own.
Then we went to a small chameleon garden. At the time, there were only two animals. The guide told us a bit about the animals' habitat and the threats they face from the local population.
Finally, we went to the butterfly enclosure. They fluttered merrily about and could be attracted with flowers that the guide gave to the children.
We were able to stay in the enclosures as long as we liked. The guide found grasshoppers to feed the chameleons and flowers to feed the butterflies. He was always very careful to ensure we saw a lot while handling the animals gently.
All in all, a lovely little park.

content:
🇬🇧 Terrible experience, a place to absolutely avoid out of respect for the animals that are mistreated inside.
I visited the facility this morning with friends to see the butterflies and, between a chrysalis and a caterpillar, the guide brought out some galagos (bush babies) for us to take pictures with. The animals appeared stressed and terrified—one of them was even forcibly placed on my friend's hand and ended up biting him!
The guide didn't know what to do, so instead suggested we continue the cruel tour by holding other animals (chameleons).
We had to rush to the hospital to start rabies treatment, while the staff at the butterfly center made jokes about what happened, downplaying our reaction and repeatedly saying “hakuna matata, mzungu” (literally “white people, don't worry” in a dismissive tone), without offering a single apology.
It was disrespectful and dangerous toward tourists, but most of all, it was cruel to the poor animals kept in captivity.
We regret not having read the reviews beforehand, as this was a last-minute activity.
Please don’t support facilities that exploit animals in this way.

content:
If you think animal welfare is important, DO NOT VISIT THIS PLACE. IT IS NOT THE ZANZIBAR BUTTERFLY CENTRE. There was a bushbaby kept in a tiny cage without any enrichment! Awful to see. The guide also touched the animal, which was understandably very afraid and stressed out. He wanted to take it out to let us hold it, but we were not okay with that. It’s never okay to directly interact with wild animals to ‘please’ visitors. Also, bushbaby’s are nocturnal animals, so putting them on display in a tiny cage during the day, touching them, holding them,… is just pure animal cruelty. Keep them in their natural habitat, not in cages. We really didn’t expect to witness something like that and it made us very upset. There were also elephant shrews in an enclosure. The guide ‘chased’ them so they would move and we could take a ‘good picture’. We told him many times to stop, cause it scared them and we only wanted to see them in peace. He also grabbed a chameleon and put it on my partner’s hand. We put it immediatly back on the leaves, for the same reason as mentioned above. Don’t touch them, don’t stress them out, don’t keep them in cages. Let the animals be in peace. We visited because we thought it was the Zanzibar butterfly centre where they help them reproduce and then set them free in the wild, but it is not.
If we knew there were other animals there locked up and being handeld by humans, we would’ve never been there. I hope from the bottom of my heart that they release the shrews, squirrels, bushbaby’s, chameleons, lizzards, … back into the wild. And if that’s not possible because they wouldn’t survive cause they have been locked up too long, PLEASE make them a gigantic enclosure that resembles their natural habitat and don’t ever let visitors into their enclosure or touch them. Please leave them in peace…

While this type of attraction may support the local community economically I don’t think that can be said of the wildlife that it claims to be conserving.

content:
A lovely little facility where a guide shares fascinating information about native butterflies. The entrance fee also supports the local village community, which gave up managing the forest in favor of the national park and now relies primarily on tourism for its livelihood. Besides a small butterfly aviary, you can also experience chameleons up close and see bush babies and tortoises in a rescue/rehabilitation station. It was a wonderful experience for our children to be able to observe the animals so closely.
It's worth emphasizing that during our visit, the guide handled every single animal, egg, pupa, cocoon, etc., with the utmost care, respect, and consideration, and the animals' welfare was clearly the top priority. In my opinion, this principle should be binding for every visitor. At no point did I feel that the animals were being presented superficially to satisfy the sensationalism of paying tourists. Therefore, I highly recommend a visit, if only to support the local village community and thus the continued existence of the national park.

content:
There are many palaces on the Zanzibar coast over a distance of 5km from Zanjibar towards north towards Bububu. Noteworthy are the Marihubi Palace ruins historical sites and Mtoni Palace ruins.
As you move 4km north of Zanzibar town one reach the Maruhubi Palace located overlooking the coast. Built between 1880 and 1882 for Sultan Said Barghash for his secondary wives while he lived at the Palace in Zanzibar Town. The palace gets the name from the original owner of the land who sold it to Sultan Barghash. Coral stone and wood were used to build the Marihubi Palace and was one of the most beautiful structure on the island, which later distroyed by a fire and left in ruins. The photo of the palace taken at the end of the 19th century housed at the House of Wonders in Zanzibar Town, depicts its past glory. What now remains is massive stone pillars, the Persian-style bathhouses, a low stone basin containing water lilies and undulating lawns.
Come to Zanzibar. Reach Maruhubi Palace ruins Historical Sites and take a stroll through the history of this once magnificent place. The Maruhubi and Mtoni Palace ruins are a quiet peaceful places for a picnic away from the bustle of Stone Town and a place to wade through the history of Zanzibar. Good luck.

content: Our tour with Said was awesome. Said does this job because of his love for animals and the ocean and he is very knowledgeable. Our tour started right on the beachfront of our resort where we were picked up on an awesome little boat. We then went snorkeling and saw some amazing coral and many different fish species. After that we moved to a starfish area where we got to see hundreds of different coloured starfish! For lunch we were taken to a beautiful sandbank where Said prepared us a delicious seafood platter and some drinks. Once we were ready to head back we made our way to a mangrove forest where we were lucky enough to see the colobus monkey and where presented with a delicious fruit platter while we got to explore a bit of the shoreline. Said is ultimately an excellent guide and we loved our time with him!

content:
We booked three different Trips with Said and all of them exceeded our expectations.
The first lead us into the ocean by boat and gave us the chance to snorkel with a pod of dolphins. It was truly amazing to see these marine animals up close! After that we were taken to a reef with hundreds of colorful starfish. Finally we docked at a sandbank and we're offered fresh local fruit.
The second trip was Salaam Cave where we could swim with turtles.
The third trip was an entire day covering the Spice Farm, where a local guide showed us the trees and bushes where the spices are harvested. Then we went to Prison Island to watch the giant turtles and finally, we took a stroll in the narrow allies of ancient Stonetown and it's bustling market.
Altogether, we were very pleased with all the trips. Said is a charming and knowledgeable guide, an excellent organizer. Also he charged very fair prices. We can highly recommend him as he provided us with an unforgettable experience of Zanzibar.
Assanti Sana Said!

Don't go to this spice farm!

content: Shangani Public Beach is where Stone Town breathes—its pulse steady, its rhythm timeless. Here, the Indian Ocean whispers against the shore, carrying with it the voices of Zanzibar’s past. Dhow sails catch the breeze, their silhouettes sharp against the horizon, as if drawn from a canvas. The beach is not grandiose; it is humble, but its energy is magnetic. Locals gather to exchange stories, the scent of cloves mingling with the salty air. Children dart along the shoreline, their laughter a melody that merges with the waves. It is here, at twilight, that Omar, a quiet observer of life, finds his muse. Sitting at the edge of the sand, he watches the ocean meet the dusk, his thoughts weaving between tradition and ambition. This is more than a beach; it is the soul of Zanzibar—a meeting point of history, community, and dreams yet to unfold.

content:
Hello everyone. We are a family of two adults and two children, and we're currently in Zanzibar.
Yesterday we took this excursion, and I want to tell you about our experience. It was one of the most beautiful experiences we've had in Zanzibar so far. Our guide, Marcello, speaks excellent Italian and knows everything about the plants that grow on the island and are used in cooking and medicine around the world.
On this tour, you'll taste the spices and fruits they grow. I should point out that you're not obligated to buy the spices.
Aside from spices, the staff also sell natural soaps, massage oils, and scented essences.
For those who complain about the price, I'd like to point out that in Italy, a vanilla pod costs around €5, while the bags they sell cost 6-8. For two bags of vanilla, we spent €8.
As for Stone Town, it's an almost mandatory stop, not only to see how these people live, but also to admire the architecture, a legacy of different cultures.
Best regards

content:
Our visit to Old Dispensary was a delightful experience and a visual treat while exploring Stone Town. This building instantly stands out with its unique architecture and beautifully restored façade.
What makes the Old Dispensary so special is its intricate design. The carved wooden balconies, stained glass windows, and detailed decorative elements reflect a blend of Indian, Arab, and European influences. It’s one of those places where you can just stand and admire the craftsmanship for a while.
Originally built in the late 19th century, the structure has an interesting history and today serves as a cultural center. Walking through the building, you get a sense of its past while also appreciating how well it has been preserved and restored.
We enjoyed taking our time here, especially observing the finer details — from the ornate railings to the colorful glasswork. It’s not a place where you spend hours, but it definitely adds depth to your exploration of Stone Town.
Located close to the seafront, it’s easy to include this as a stop while walking around the area. Overall, the Old Dispensary is a great example of heritage preservation and architectural beauty — simple, elegant, and definitely worth a visit.

content:
I’d have been happy to pay an entrance fee, but the Old Dispensary is free to visit. So when the men working here (who sit at the front with the guest book doing nothing) pleaded me for a tip when I was leaving - I asked them ‘does it go towards the maintenance of the building? Or to your pocket?’ The response I received was ‘all tips go to the pocket’. So I’m supposed to tip you for sitting on your backside?
It would be nice if they set up a small admission fee to actually support the restoration and maintenance of this historical building, as opposed to all the visitors’ cash ending up in someones pocket. The men working here will continue to take advantage of this until something changes.

content: The Great Baobab Tree in Mzambarauni is a remarkable natural monument, prized for its enormous size and distinctive appearance. This ancient tree, often called the "Tree of Life," is a testament to nature's resilience and longevity. Its gnarled trunk and immense crown are not only photogenic but also a living testament to Zanzibar's unique blend of African, Arabic, and Swahili history. It served as a meeting place for local communities. Elders would gather beneath the Great Baobab to share stories, resolve disputes, or perform ceremonies. Tourists often stop here to admire its majesty and take unforgettable photos. The area is rich in diverse wildlife and lush vegetation, offering a peaceful environment for nature lovers and photographers alike.

content:
Review of Tour_Guide _Momba_zanzibar
During our holiday in Zanzibar, we decided to avoid the typical hotel-recommended guides from the beach. Instead, we found Momba – a certified guide recognized by the Tanzanian authorities with an education from a university in Kenya.
All of our initial skepticism was quickly put to rest. Momba showed us Zanzibar from a whole new perspective with his calm, knowledgeable spirit and a humor that made the entire experience both educational and unforgettable. His deep knowledge of the island’s culture, history, and nature was truly impressive, and it was clear that his education and passion for the area went hand in hand.
Momba took us to both well-known and hidden gems across Zanzibar, and his way of sharing stories and facts was engaging and captivating. It was also an important lesson for us to discover how many hotels attempt to recommend their own guides for financial gain instead of supporting the local community. Momba proved how much richer and more authentic an experience becomes when you choose a local guide who truly loves his work.
We can only give Momba the highest recommendations. Thanks to him for making our stay in Zanzibar absolutely fantastic and unforgettable!
Otto Lieber

content:
A truly special place on Pemba!
The lighthouse is definitely worth a visit. The view from the top alone is simply breathtaking – you have a fantastic panorama of the coast and the sea off Pemba.
But what truly makes this place special is the lighthouse keeper. He has been caring for this lighthouse for 30 years and tells its story with incredible passion. We were particularly impressed that he has learned the story and his explanations in several languages ​​– including German!
You can immediately tell how much the lighthouse means to him. His stories and his warm personality make the visit so much more than just a beautiful viewpoint.
For us, a real highlight on Pemba and highly recommended. Anyone visiting the island shouldn't miss this special place and the chance to meet its lighthouse keeper!

content: Mnemba Island is a single small island located about 3 km off the northeast coast of Unguja, the largest island of the Zanzibar Archipelago, Tanzania, opposite Muyuni Beach. It is roughly triangular in shape, about 500 metres (1,640 ft) in diameter and about 1.5 kilometres (0.9 mi) in circumference. It is surrounded by an oval reef seven by four kilometres in extent. These reefs have been declared a marine conservation area. Mnemba Island and its reef are sometimes called Mnemba Atoll which is incorrect because an atoll is an island that encircles a lagoon, which is not the case for Mnemba Island.

content:
The guide we were assigned on-site was a disaster—a total rip-off. He didn't even know the correct dates; he’d only be useful as a guide for blind people so they’d know where they were. We would have been better off just Googling the necessary information ourselves.
My negative review is primarily due to the poor treatment of the tortoises. Signs warn of a $50 fine for bypassing the fences, but many guides and tourists don't care; they ignore the barriers and wake up the oldest tortoise—allegedly 200 years old—just to take group photos for Instagram. I had heard about older animals dying recently, which comes as no surprise given how they are treated here. The security staff—at least three or four of them—were all making themselves comfortable in the ticket booth while total chaos reigned outside, largely driven by guides acting overzealously in hopes of better tips.
We found this animal cruelty appalling; what is the point of charging high conservation fees? It’s a complete farce—it’s all about the commercial exploitation of these poor animals. 😢
To top it all off, at the end of the tour—right at the exit—they actively solicit voluntary donations, despite the high conservation surcharge already paid. I don't even want to know where that money goes... perhaps to the 'hard-working'" security team?"

So apart from this experience, a nice trip. Recommend.

content:
Very disappointing experience – a real tourist trap at Prison Island (Zanzibar Turtle Sanctuary).
We paid around $50 for the round-trip boat (just a 10-minute crossing), plus $22 per person for entry. In total, nearly $90 for two people, for a visit that lasted only 30 minutes.
You see a few turtles and walk around a poorly maintained sanctuary. The boat captain suggests staying 1h30, but in reality, you’ve seen everything there is to see in half an hour. The island looks large from afar, but almost all areas are closed off, forcing tourists to stay in a tiny, restricted zone. It feels designed to extract as much money as possible while giving minimal value in return.
The whole thing is overpriced, underwhelming, and not well cared for. I strongly advise against it unless you’re an American tourist who doesn’t mind paying premium prices for very little.
Save your money and skip this one.

content:
I took a boat from Stone Town to Changuu Island, and even the crossing felt like stepping into another world: turquoise water, warm light, palm trees on the horizon. The island is small, but it carries history and nature with an intensity that deeply moved me.
Our guide not only showed us the turtles on the tour—which was incredible in itself—but also gave us a concrete and well-informed introduction to the island's history: In the 19th century, Changuu was first used by Arab slave traders as a place to hold restless or unruly enslaved people before they were sold on to Stone Town and beyond. Later, the British planned a prison there, but it never functioned as such and instead served as a quarantine station for yellow fever and other diseases. Today, only the ruins of these facilities remain, standing as a silent but powerful witness to what happened here.
What impressed me most was how respectfully our guide conveyed this history – not embellishing it, not sensationalizing it, but clearly, factually, and with empathy. We walked through the ruins, listened, asked questions, and understood that this place is far more than just a photo spot.
But Changuu is also a wonderful place of nature. The Aldabra giant tortoises there make you stop and think: These ancient animals, some over a hundred years old, move serenely through the shade of the palm trees, take food from your hand, and appear so peaceful and dignified that you really want to remember that moment.
The tour is well-planned: Information panels explain both the ecological significance and the historical context. The guides answer every question – not just superficially, but with in-depth knowledge, authenticity, and respect for the people and nature that have shaped this island.
What also impressed me: The island isn't just a "zoo destination," but a place where conservation, education, and visitor experience work together seamlessly. You can sense that it's not just about attractive presentation, but genuine protection and explanation – and that makes the visit a truly profound experience.
The boat trip, the ruins, the ancient stories, the encounter with the tortoises – everything comes together to create a picture that has changed my perception of Zanzibar. Anyone who truly wants to understand how islands, wildlife, and history intertwine should start here.
My conclusion: Changuu Island isn't just a worthwhile day trip from Stone Town. It's a place of encounter – with nature, with history, with truth. A recommendation that will stay with me for a long time.

content: Pricing information is sketchy, so we paid $40 each, thinking we'd paid for everything. Before boarding the boat, we had to pay the government tax ($10 each), so we thought we'd paid for everything. Before entering the park, we had to pay another €11 each, and only then did we actually pay for everything. The fact that there's a place where this red-listed species continues to breed is already a positive thing. Seeing visitors touching the turtles without considering it's prohibited is quite sad. The museum shop has ridiculously high prices, but we still bought a few small items. A positive note is that the €40 boat ticket included nakupenda, so after Prison Island, we went to the sand spit. The advice is to negotiate the excursion with the people at the boat departure area and combine the two visits (Prison Island and the sand spit).

content:
You have to pay for a boat across from Stone Town (included with our pre-booked guided trip).
Before getting on said boat, you must pay 3usd tax to a government desk on the beach, per person. No idea why. This will increase to 10usd from 1st September 2025.
To board your boat, it's feet in the filthy water. A choppy 25 minute crossing and you do the same the other end, although at least the water is clean here. There are taps upstairs to wash your feet off before refitting shoes etc.
At this point, you then find out that it's actually a zoo. The remains of the 'prison' (actually a quarantine facility) have been converted into a zoo, which they rarely refer to as a tortoise sanctuary but they're captive, you can't get away from it. From what I understand as soon as a tortoise appears near the path everyone flocks to it for photos which I imagine would be very stressful for them. The young are taken away from them and put in cages until they're older.
It costs an additional 12usd per person to enter the zoo when you arrive. After realising what it was we decided not to pay and returned to stone town on our dhow.
All information we found out previously suggested 'Prison Island' was the site of a long since ruined prison where giant tortoises are free to roam, unhindered. This is absolutely not the case, our guide told us that it used to be like that, but the government realised there was money to be made as a tourist attraction.
Waste of time and money.

content:
Our visit to Slave Market was one of the most powerful and emotionally heavy experiences of our trip. This is not just a place you visit — it’s a place that makes you pause, reflect, and truly understand a difficult part of history.
Walking through the site, especially the underground chambers where enslaved people were once held, gives you a stark sense of the extreme conditions they endured. The spaces are small, dark, and suffocating even today — it’s hard to imagine how many people were confined there under such inhumane circumstances. It’s an experience that stays with you long after you leave.
The memorials and exhibits around the site help provide context and tell the stories of those who suffered here. The displays are informative and thoughtfully put together, helping visitors understand the scale and impact of the slave trade in this region.
The area also includes the Anglican Cathedral, which stands as a symbol of hope and transformation, built on the very grounds of the former market. The contrast between the painful history and the present-day setting is quite striking.
We would definitely recommend taking a guide here, as it helps you better understand the historical significance and the stories behind what you’re seeing. It adds depth and meaning to the visit.
Overall, the Slave Market is not an easy place to visit, but it is an important one. It offers a sobering reminder of the past and leaves you with a deeper appreciation of history and humanity.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content: Informative museum on the East African slave trade. Dark times for humanity. The shame of many prosperous countries in the world. It really gives you a lump in your throat here, looking at the depictions of villages being burned and families split up and shipped away. The East Africans were sent as slaves to mainly Arabia, after being imprisoned and bought here in Stonetown, Zanzibar. I knew a lot about the slave trade to the Caribbean, but not so much here, so it was very educational. Lots of history, pictures and illustrations in the museum, and stories on individuals. I got a good background on how Dr. Livingstone was on the side of the slaves and tried to promote trade of resources to phase out slavery. There are also some stories on the individual slave traders, if you can stomach their greed and heartlessness. There is also a basement under the church where the slaves were imprisoned, that you can explore. A guide is allocated to you with the price of admission. Our guide was really good.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content:
My visit to the Old Slave Market/Anglican Cathedral in Zanzibar, Tanzania, was a sobering and thought-provoking experience. The site was formerly a slave market, where thousands of enslaved Africans were bought and sold during the 19th century.
The history of the site is presented in a clear and informative way, with displays and exhibits that detail the brutal reality of the slave trade. The guided tour was insightful and provided a greater understanding of the horrific conditions that the enslaved people were subjected to.
The Anglican Cathedral, which now stands on the site of the former slave market, is a beautiful and striking building that provides a fitting tribute to the victims of the slave trade. The architecture is impressive, with high ceilings, stained glass windows, and intricate details.
Overall, my visit to the Old Slave Market/Anglican Cathedral was a powerful and moving experience that left a lasting impression. It is a reminder of the inhumanity and cruelty of the slave trade and serves as a call to action to continue to work towards a more just and equitable society. I highly recommend a visit to this historic site for anyone looking to gain a deeper understanding of the history of Zanzibar and the impact of the slave trade.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content:
Zanzibar was a hub of the slave trade in East Africa during the 19th century. At the slave market, people were inspected and their value determined based on their age and health.
Now, a simple museum tells the story, and you can visit the cellars that served as living quarters. Up to 80 slaves were crammed into these tiny spaces—simply oppressive.

No val la p na la visita, l'únic que veuràs es una exposició que de plafons amb informació que pots trobar en internet, una església simple i una obra d'art morbosa que es el reclam turístic a 5$ l'entrada i uns guies que t'assalten a l'entrada i que expliquen coses no certes i venen un passat vergonyos com una atracció.
Història de la catedral:
Es va construir en set anys, posant la primera pedra el dia de Nadal de 1873 fins a l'obertura el Nadal de 1879, basant-se en una visió d' Edward Steere , tercer bisbe anglicà de Zanzíbar, que va contribuir activament al disseny. Com la majoria dels edificis de Stone Town, està fet principalment de pedra corall . Té un sostre de formigó únic amb forma d'una inusual volta de canó (això va ser la idea de Steere) i l'estructura general barreja detalls gòtics perpendiculars i islàmics . La catedral va ser consagrada el 1903 i va rebre el nom de la catedral de Canterbury .
L'església es troba a Mkunazini Road, al centre del nucli antic, i ocupa una gran àrea on antigament hi havia el mercat d'esclaus més gran de Zanzíbar; de fet, la construcció de la catedral estava destinada a celebrar la fi de l'esclavitud. Es diu que l'altar es troba al lloc exacte on abans hi havia el 'post de fuet'" principal del mercat. A la plaça hi ha un conegut monument als esclaus (unes quantes figures humanes encadenats que surten d'una fossa) així com un museu sobre l'esclavitud.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content:
Apparently there is more than just the exhibit with panels and pictures, and a place underground also. We couldn't find it, and you might need to pay a guide extra for that (on top of admission to the exhibit).
A few rooms details the history of the market in display panels with photos and renderings and a lot of reading. There is a monument that you can see in the photos. The interior of the cathedral is nice. They have services on Sundays in Swahili. There is a service in English at 8AM in the chapel. The price of admission is high, but you're not paying for new information, simply just to get past the gates to see the monument and read some panels, and be in the same place where it all happened. The information presented is definitely sobering and good knowledge to have when visiting and touring Stone Town, but if you can read about it online and have no need to be in the same location as where it happened (and could be content with just looking past the gate--or visiting on Sunday for church to get on the grounds), you won't be missing much.

content:
Absolutely beautiful place and definitely one of my favorite spots in Zanzibar! 🤍
The cave itself is stunning and the whole place has such a peaceful and special atmosphere.
The staff are incredibly friendly, welcoming and helpful, which makes the experience even better. They also offer to take photos for you, and honestly, the pictures turned out SO good! 📸 I also really loved the little clothing corner, where you can find handmade clothes made and sold on site. It’s such a nice touch and a great way to support local creativity.
Overall, this place is absolutely worth visiting if you’re in Zanzibar. Whether you want to swim, relax, eat, take beautiful photos or simply enjoy a unique and peaceful place. I can highly recommend it! 🩷

content: We were really excited for our cave trip, but it turned out to be nothing like what's advertised, and we were really disappointed. The cave itself is nice, cool clean, deep water and tiny fish which are very cute. However there was something else in the water that looked like little lice, that bit really hard and meant we couldn't stay swimming for as long as we would have liked to. The advertised facilities (the restaurant, showers, yoga area, seating area, lockers) were all closed or out of order - we were told we couldn't even buy a bottle of water, and it was a very hot day. We mentioned this to the staff and even to the manager, but we were told there was nothing that could be done. We felt it would have been fair to tell us about the closed facilities before we'd paid 15 dollars entree fee each, or if the price would have been adjusted to reflect the total lack of facilities at the time. As it was, we were really disappointed, especially by the manager's total lack of care.

content: We were so looking forward to this, after reading the reviews, and so disappointed. The admission fee was quite high, at USD15 each, and the reception staff didn't warn us that almost all the facilities were unavailable. The cave itself is nice and cool to swim in, with some tiny fish and but also a lot of small stinging creatures. The advertised changing space and lockers didn't appear to exist. There were 2 toilets, one with a door that didn't close, no electricity, and a shower that didn't work. It was a very hot day, and we had planned to have lunch in the advertised restaurant, but it was closed (long-term) and there was nowhere even to get a bottle of water. The gardens are pretty, but the sitting areas were out of action and cushions wet or moldy. We read that there was a second beach, but found no sign of this, nor of the advertised yoga space. The cave is about 20 minutes' walk along a narrow bumpy track from the main road. We asked politely if we could have a reduction in the price once we realised the advertised facilities weren't available, but were told this was impossible.

content:
Overpriced.
Entry fee is 10$ (no card payment accepted, no receipt given, as usual for a lot of Zanzibar places), a bit to much imho for the whole tourist attraction, which basically consists of a cave with a natural pool and some sofas and chairs to sit and have a drink. Drinks are overpriced as well. I took an African Coffee and it cost 5000 shillings (2€; you can buy an espresso in the expensive Milan for a smaller price) to just have a cup, some boiled water and a tin of coffee as many you can find in a supermarket. A sign in the entry said “Free Wi-Fi” but we found no Wi-Fi network and the staff also didn’t even asked us if we wanted a password/voucher. Everybody just sitting and chilling there in their pole pole way, almost forgetting customers needs.
I definitely don’t recommend this place.

content: The photos are of Kuza Cave, the name Kuumbi Cave is incorrectly described. It's located within the cultural center (formerly part of the village) and also associated with the local sacred area. Today, it features bathrooms, a changing room, a small restaurant, souvenirs, several buildings, music (a local sang two Polish songs), and a semi-open cave with very clear water, similar to a cenote in Mexico... up to several meters deep, about 30 meters long, with approximately 30 steps carved into the rock, plus a few meters along the rock in front of them and down them to the water itself. The water temperature is around 25 degrees Celsius.

content:
We are a family of 3 people and were very happy to experiment a 3days safari with our wonderful guide Bidan
Everything was perfectly planned and organised. We stayed in comfortable lodgings and had great food. Everything was included in the package (entry-fees of the national parks, accommodation, food and water).
The communication with Bidan was simple and fluent before and during our stay in Tanzania.
As soon as we met we felt like family members and Bidan our guide did all he could to make us feel great,
to please us and show us the most beautiful things (animals, landscapes, waterfalls etc.)
Even though it was the rainy season in April, we managed to see lions, girafs, impalas, elephants and many more.
Concerning the payment of the safari the good thing was that we could pay on arrival, so absolutely safe and without surprises.
In conclusion, these 3 days with Bidan were rell the trip. We start from Dar Es Salam to go to Mikumi National Park. We traveled in a confortable 4×4, the perfect way to enjoy the road and to see all te were very lucky to see a lot of animals (lions, éléphants, buffalo, hippopotamus, girafes, baboons, impalas, etc). We also visited an authentic Masaï Village near Mikumi. The last day we went to Udzungwa to see the highest waterfall in National parks. After the trip our guide (Bidan) brings us back to the harbor to go to Zanzibar but you can choose where you want to go after the safari.
The guide (Bidan) was always very kind and professional, we ate together every day and we spend good time with him. He did his best to see animals we wanted to see like lions. And he also help us to speak with the local people and to book our boat trip to Zanzibar.
Conclusion: we recommend you BLACKWILLOW SAFARIS if you want to have a great safari tour in Tanzania and meet nice people.

Arsheen is a professional in the stand up paddling, so she even made some photos of us without waterproof cases. This is so much better than photos than I made with a waterproof case. After the tour, we were offered homemade snacks in the backyard. It was very romantic to watch the sunset near the ocean. I definitely recommend that tour to everyone who is visiting Zanzibar. Mangroves were even better than in the Jozani forest. Also, the host helped us with the transfer from the Nungwi. The taxi had a fixed price and driver was very friendly.

content: We have really enjoyed our little sup journey in mangroves, a once in a life time experience! We swam into the depth of the forest first, and then we went closer to the sea, where the route was less evident and therefore more adventures. Our instructor told us about the mangrove forest, how it grows in salted water - some amazing staff. He also explained us how the landscape would change when the tide was low. Eventually we got to the front side of the forest and paddled along it enjoying beautiful views and the sunset. Then we had a nice rest - we got off the boards and swam until the sun was down. That was a moment I'd never forget - peaceful, charming, magical... When we arrived back to the base, we had a shower and had a wonderful dinner (I just can't call it snacks - there were so much fruits, homemade cookies, popcorn and more!) - all on the terrace with a stunning sea view. I should also mention that the 2 Winds team had arranged a driver for us, and we had managed to visit the Jozani Forest on our way to the padding tour. Thus we had a full day filled with fantastic emotions, one to remember for many years to come.

content:
I can’t recommend this Stone Town tour enough — truly a five-star experience from start to finish. The history, culture, and architecture came to life in a way that guidebooks just can’t capture. Walking through the narrow winding streets, learning about the island’s Swahili, Arab, and European influences, and hearing the stories behind the carved wooden doors and historic buildings was absolutely fascinating.
Lee was incredibly knowledgeable, friendly, and passionate. He answered every question with depth and made the experience feel personal rather than scripted. I especially loved visiting the old slave market site and the bustling market — it gave such powerful context to Zanzibar’s past and present.
The pace was perfect, the insights were thoughtful, and the views were stunning. If you’re visiting Zanzibar, this tour is a must-do. It gave me a much deeper appreciation for Stone Town and its rich heritage.
Highly recommend! 🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟

place_name: Lee The Don Tours & Safaris Zanzibar
content:
Our time in Zanzibar was truly unforgettable, and a huge part of that was thanks to our wonderful guide, Lee. From the moment we met him, he welcomed us with the biggest smile and genuine warmth, instantly making us feel comfortable. He didn’t just show us around – he shared his love for Zanzibar, its culture, history, and natural beauty in a way that made every moment special.
He guided us through Stone Town, bringing its history and culture to life with fascinating stories. Our visit to Prison Island was both educational and great fun – Lee made sure we got to see the giant tortoises up close and even took brilliant photos for us too!
Our Safari Blue day was absolutely magical – snorkelling in crystal-clear waters, relaxing on a sandbank, and enjoying a delicious seafood lunch, all perfectly organised by Lee.
We also went on a dhow sunset cruise, swam with turtles, relaxed at Kendwa Beach, and even experienced the incredible Mikumi National Park, spotting elephants, giraffes, and lions. Every trip was seamless because Lee took care of every detail with professionalism and kindness.
What really made this trip stand out was Lee himself – always smiling, patient, and such fun to be around. By the end of our journey, he wasn’t just our guide anymore – he’d become a friend. We shared laughs, great conversations, and so many unforgettable memories.
If you’re visiting Zanzibar and want more than just a tour – if you want an experience filled with warmth, joy, and genuine friendship – ask for Lee. He’ll make your trip truly special.
Lucca and Scott x

place_name: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour
content:
An amazing experience with Jozani Long Tours!
I had a fantastic time exploring Jozani Forest with my guide Kesi. We hiked over five miles through the forest and it was worth every step. The highlight was finding the Zanzibar Red Colobus monkey which is endemic to Zanzibar!
Kesi was incredible - so knowledgeable about all the animals, plants, and birds. He had the eye of a hawk! He could spot birds hidden deep in the trees that I would have never seen on my own, and he could even tell what kind of bird it was just from hearing its sound.
You can really tell Kesi is passionate and an expert at what he does. He made our long hike fun, educational, and unforgettable. If you visit Zanzibar, I highly recommend booking with Jozani Long Tours and asking for Kesi. 5 stars!

place_name: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour
content:
Visit here! You wont regret it! We were surrounded by countless Red / Blue Colobus monkeys, we got really close and were able to take loads of close up photos... The mangrove was beautifully set up for visiting - very interesting...We also went to the butterfly farm with chameleons and a bush baby... At first I didn't feel comfortable because the chameleons were kept in a small cage, as was the bush baby. But our guide told us that both species were rescued from the forest as locals hunt them to kill believing they are either poisonous (chameleons), or evil spirits (bushbaby). They keep them there during the day to sleep and let them out at night as they are nocturnal, so they meet with their families, eat and come back voluntarily to the centre because they get given fruit...
The guide also informed us that the project is crucial for local community support because the proceeds go to local school development etc.
A great experience Jozani forest and not to be missed!

content:
I had an absolutely fantastic private birding tour in Jozani Forest on Zanzibar Island. It was a real pleasure to be guided one-on-one by Kesi, who is incredibly experienced and knowledgeable.
What truly amazed me was his ability to identify birds purely by their calls — it was honestly crazy (in the best way!). He would hear the faintest sound and immediately know which species it was and where to look. Thanks to his sharp eye and exceptional ear, I was able to spot and photograph some beautiful birds — including a few that are quite rare.
Beyond bird identification, he also explained the habitats and overall ecology of the forest in a very engaging and easy-to-understand way. The private setting made the experience even more special and relaxed.
Another additional highlight was seeing the endemic Zanzibar red colobus monkeys up close.
The booking process was very easy and smooth. I would absolutely do this tour again — especially with Kesi as my guide. Highly recommended for anyone interested in birding and nature!

place_name: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour
content:
Our first time in Zanzibar and today we visited Jozani forest. We chose the 3 hour/middle tour which was very enjoyable; it was quite hot and humid so for those interested in doing this tour I would definitely advise bringing plenty of drinking water and appropriate shoes (the terrain is not suitable for flip flops!)
We were part of a small group of just 5 people which made the tour very manageable. Our tour guide Kasi was very knowledgeable and had an excellent eye for pointing out a variety of animals - lizards, millipedes, snakes, elephant shrews, cicadas, crabs (the final part of the tour involves a short visit to the mangrove part of the forest).
It was lovely seeing the Colobus monkeys and they came very close to us on their own accord. As they have no predators on the island they were not shy to get close to us!
I would highly recommend a tour of Jozani forest, especially as a nice change from your typical day of water sports / time on the beach / snorkelling etc

content:
Visiting Jozani Forest was one of the highlights of our trip to Zanzibar!
The forest is breathtaking with centuries old trees, mysterious mangroves and an atmosphere that makes you feel small but deeply connected to nature.
Our guide Beka was incredibly knowledgeable and shared so many fascinating facts about the plants, animals and history of the park. We were lucky enough to spot the famous red colobus monkeys, playful and unique to Zanzibar as well as a tree snake quickly slipping into the palms.
It’s amazing to think that such a rich ecosystem is protected here. Jozani Forest is not just a visit, it’s an experience peaceful, wild, and unforgettable. Highly recommended for anyone visiting Zanzibar!

place_name: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour
content:
Our nature walk with Kesi in Jozani National Park was nothing short of spectacular. We started our adventure walking through the mangroves spotting small crabs in the mud and learning about the mangrove tree species. Kesi found some mangrove seed pods and we were able to drop them in the mud to plant a new mangrove tree. Then we found ourselves amongst a troop of blue monkeys. These monkeys are difficult to capture on camera due to their quick movements and inability to sit still. Kesi gave us plenty of time to observe their habits, munching on fruit and leaves, swinging through the trees, grooming each other and even engaging in creating the next generation. We continued our hike, Kasi pointed out birds, giant snails, lizards and skinks along the way. Eventually we made our way to a red colobus monkey troop. Picturesque in nature, these monkeys were playful and exhibited the same behaviors as the blue monkeys. This red colobus subspecies endemic to Zanzibar was giving us a show. We saw up to 5 young red colobus playing together, rolling around and nipping and chasing each other around the trees. We saw plenty of baby red colobus breastfeeding from their mothers and eventually settling into the trees for an early afternoon nap. We eventually found another troop of red colobus a little deeper in the forest, these ones seemed a little less keen on humans observing their behaviors and stayed high up in the trees. Kesi spotted a snake and an elephant shrew. It was a great tour but bring something to eat and plenty of water.
Also, Abdul, our driver serenaded to and from the destination with his soulful voice.

content:
I really enjoyed visiting Stone Town and staying for two nights.
It’s the oldest part of Zanzibar City and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The narrow, maze-like streets are full of souvenir shops, and wandering around is part of the fun, even if you get a bit lost.
Darajani Market is a must-see for fresh fruit, fish, spices, and local products, while the Forodhani Gardens night market is perfect in the evening.
Stone Town also has great rooftops with Arabic and African-inspired décor.
The Freddie Mercury House is nice for a quick photo, and some shops selling tanzanite are worth checking out.
I felt completely safe and really enjoyed the experience.
Stone Town is authentic, vibrant, and full of charm — definitely worth spending a night or two here.

The narrow, maze-like streets are full of souvenir shops, and wandering around is part of the fun, even if you get a bit lost.
Darajani Market is a must-see for fresh fruit, fish, spices, and local products, while the Forodhani Gardens night market is perfect in the evening.
Stone Town also has great rooftops with Arabic and African-inspired décor.
The Freddie Mercury House is nice for a quick photo, and some shops selling tanzanite are worth checking out.
I felt completely safe and really enjoyed the experience.
Stone Town is authentic, vibrant, and full of charm — definitely worth spending a night or two here.

content:
We booked the original Safari Blue experience, and after doing a few other snorkelling tours around the island, I can confidently say this was the best one.
We didn’t manage to see any dolphins, but the snorkelling spots we visited were absolutely amazing. There weren’t many boats around, and the Safari Blue boats seemed to coordinate with each other really well to make sure that none of the spots became too crowded. We saw plenty of fish and sea stars, and the masks provided were also surprisingly good quality. On all the other snorkelling tours we did, the masks would constantly leak, so this made a big difference!
The lunch was absolutely amazing — probably one of the best meals we had during our holiday. Everything was very fresh, and the seafood was excellent quality. There were also plenty of soft drinks and fresh fruit available throughout the trip.
The staff were really fun and friendly and definitely added to the experience. The only thing missing was a bit of music on the boat — otherwise, it was a fantastic day and I would highly recommend it!

content:
The transfer and the guide were excellent and greatly contributed to the success of the excursion. The snorkeling, the sandbar, and the natural pool were also very enjoyable.
However, lunch definitely needs improvement. I informed them the day before the activity that my mother suffers from severe food allergies, particularly to lemon, which can be life-threatening. The organizer confirmed that this information had been passed on to the team. As a precaution, we also checked with the guide on the day itself, who assured us that everything had been taken care of.
Imagine our surprise when my mother tasted the fries and discovered they had been drizzled with lemon juice. As for the seafood, not only were pieces of lemon arranged on the platter, but the entire dish contained lemon. As a result, my mother had an allergic reaction and was unable to eat almost any of the planned dishes.
Luckily, she had her medication and reacted quickly. Such negligence regarding a repeatedly reported allergy is unacceptable. Despite our messages, we received only apologies and no response to our request for compensation, even though this meal was included in the price of the excursion. Being a small, local business cannot justify such a lack of diligence on such a serious matter.
